CASH BALANCE, NET BURN, MONTHS OF RUNWAY, fundraising status

title: Write a plain-English matter update letter for a client
description: A periodic client update on where their case or deal stands, what is next, expected costs, and any decisions they need to make.
content:
Write a status update to a client about their legal matter.

**Client and their sophistication:** [e.g. "individual, first time with a lawyer" / "in-house general counsel"]
**Matter:** [TYPE AND SHORT DESCRIPTION]
**What happened since the last update:** [EVENTS, FILINGS, CALLS, DOCUMENTS RECEIVED]
**Upcoming dates:** [HEARINGS, DEADLINES, CLOSING DATES]
**Decisions the client needs to make:** [e.g. "whether to accept mediation" - or "none"]
**Fees billed to date vs. estimate:** [NUMBERS - or "skip"]
**Anything they will not like hearing:** [SETBACKS, DELAYS, COST OVERRUNS]

Structure:
1. Bottom line in two sentences: where things stand and whether anything changed.
2. What happened, in plain language; explain any legal term the first time you use it.
3. What comes next, with dates in bold, and what the client needs to do and by when.
4. Decisions needed, with the options and the practical trade-offs. Do not choose for them; say the attorney will discuss a recommendation.
5. Budget: spend so far against the estimate and any expected change.
6. How to reach us.

Rules: give bad news early and plainly. Do not predict outcomes or use percentages of success. Do not invent facts, dates, or amounts; use [CONFIRM]. Keep it under 400 words. Note that sending this by unencrypted email or to a work account the client's employer can access may risk privilege; remind me to confirm the client's preferred secure channel. Have the responsible attorney review before sending.

title: Write a polite reminder for an overdue action or deadline
description: Gives you a friendly first reminder, a firmer second one, and a final notice for something someone still owes you.
content:
Write a polite reminder for something someone still needs to do.

**What's pending:** [THE ACTION - e.g. "approve the budget", "submit timesheets", "send the signed contract"]
**Who owes it:** [PERSON OR GROUP, and their seniority relative to me]
**Original deadline and how it was agreed:** [DATE; email, meeting, process]
**Why it matters now:** [WHAT IS BLOCKED OR AT RISK, and the new deadline]
**What happens if it's still not done:** [REAL CONSEQUENCE - e.g. "payroll runs late", "I escalate to their manager" - or "none"]
**Reminders already sent:** [none / once / twice]
**Channel:** [email / Teams / Slack]

Write three versions I can use in sequence:
1. **Friendly nudge** - assumes good intent, restates the ask, makes it easy (link, attachment, exact step).
2. **Second reminder** - clearer about the impact and the new deadline, still courteous.
3. **Final notice** - firm and factual: what happens if it isn't done by the date, and who else will be informed, if relevant.

Rules for each:
- The ask and the deadline in the first two lines; put the date in bold.
- Under 90 words. No guilt-tripping, sarcasm, or "per my last email".
- If it's a group reminder, make it work without singling anyone out.
- Use only the consequence I gave; never invent or exaggerate one. If I gave none, keep the final notice to the new deadline and the impact.

Also suggest when to send each one, and whether the final notice should copy anyone.
variables: PERSON OR GROUP, and their seniority relative to me
WHAT IS BLOCKED OR AT RISK, and the new deadline

letter / email / form answers; word limit

title: Write a stronger opening line for my email or message
description: Gives you several sharper opening lines that get to the point and make the reader keep reading.
content:
Write a stronger opening for my email or message.

**My draft:** [PASTE THE FULL MESSAGE]
**Reader:** [WHO, and how busy or interested they are]
**What I want them to do or understand:** [GOAL]

First, tell me in one sentence what my current opening does and why it is weak (e.g. warms up too long, starts with background, buries the ask, opens with an apology or "I hope you're well").

Then give me 5 alternative openings, each one or two sentences, using different approaches:
1. **Bottom line first** - the conclusion or ask straight away.
2. **Reader's benefit** - what's in it for them.
3. **The key fact** - the number, change, or news that matters most, taken from my draft.
4. **The question** - a direct question they will want to answer.
5. **The connection** - a link to something they said, asked for, or care about.

For each, note when it works best and the risk (e.g. too blunt for a first contact).

Rules:
- Use only facts in my draft; no invented statistics or hooks.
- No clickbait, false urgency, or flattery.
- Each opening must lead naturally into the rest of my message; tell me if a sentence after it needs adjusting.

Finish with your recommended opening and a matching subject line.
variables: WHO, and how busy or interested they are

title: Write a thank-you email after a meeting
description: A short, specific thank-you to a client or senior colleague that shows you listened and confirms the next step.

Write a thank-you email to send after a meeting.

title: Write a weekly sales team update that drives action
description: A short weekly update for your sales team with the number, wins, priorities, and asks, written so reps actually read it.

Write my weekly update to my sales team.

**Wins this week:** [deals closed, great calls, behaviors worth recognizing, with names]

title: Write a word-for-word script for a difficult conversation
description: A word-for-word conversation script with opening lines, key questions, and phrases to avoid so you stay direct without being harsh.
content:
Write a script for a difficult conversation so I can be direct without being harsh.

**Who I'm talking to and our relationship:** [e.g. "peer in another team", "my manager", "a long-time client"]
**The issue, in facts:** [WHAT HAPPENED, with examples]
**The one message they must hear:** [KEY MESSAGE]
**What I want to happen afterward:** [OUTCOME]
**How they're likely to feel or react:** [e.g. defensive, surprised, upset]
**Setting:** [in person / video call / phone]

Give me:
1. **Opening (first 30 seconds)** - 2 alternative opening lines that name the topic plainly, without a long warm-up or a fake compliment.
2. **The structure**, with suggested words for each part: the facts, the impact, my key message, their perspective, agreeing next steps, and the close.
3. **What to say** - 5-6 key sentences I should get out, in my own plain voice.
4. **What to ask** - 4-5 open questions to understand their side and reach agreement.
5. **What to avoid saying** - a table: Phrase to avoid | Why it backfires | Say this instead. Include blame, sarcasm, "always/never", "no offense, but", and over-apologizing.
6. **If it goes sideways** - short lines for when they get angry, cry, go silent, or change the subject.

Rules: keep sentences short and spoken, not written. Be firm on the issue and respectful to the person. Don't invent facts I haven't given; use [ADD EXAMPLE] where one is needed.

title: Write a work apology email that owns the mistake without over-explaining
description: Drafts a professional apology that takes responsibility, states the fix, and rebuilds trust without groveling or excuses.
content:
Help me write an apology email for a mistake at work.

**What happened:** [THE MISTAKE, plainly]
**Who was affected and how:** [PEOPLE, CUSTOMERS, OR TEAMS; THE IMPACT]
**My share of responsibility:** [WHAT WAS MINE vs. OUTSIDE MY CONTROL]
**What I've already done to fix it:** [ACTIONS]
**What I'll do to stop it happening again:** [CHANGES]
**Recipient:** [WHO, and the relationship]

The email should follow this order:
1. **Own it** - a clear apology in the first sentence, using "I" (or "we" if it was genuinely a team failure).
2. **Name the impact** on them, briefly and specifically.
3. **The fix** - what's been done and what's still in progress, with dates.
4. **Prevention** - one or two concrete changes.
5. **Close** - an offer to talk, without asking for forgiveness.

Rules:
- Under 150 words.
- No excuses, blame-shifting, or "sorry if you were upset". Context only if it helps them understand the fix, in one sentence at most.
- Don't over-apologize or repeat "sorry" more than twice.
- Don't promise things I haven't listed.

Return the email, a 2-line Teams or Slack version, and a note on anything in my notes that reads as defensive. If the mistake has legal, contractual, or regulatory consequences, tell me to check the wording with my manager or legal before sending.
variables: PEOPLE, CUSTOMERS, OR TEAMS; THE IMPACT
WHAT WAS MINE vs. OUTSIDE MY CONTROL

title: Write an inbox delegation agreement with my executive

title: Write an RFI that gets a fast, usable answer

Also give me a one-line log entry for my RFI log: number, date sent, subject, ball-in-court, date needed.

title: Write internal status updates during a live production incident
description: Drafts clear, regular updates for engineers, leadership, and support while an outage is still happening, without guessing at causes or ETAs.
content:
Help me write internal status updates for a production incident that's happening right now.

**What's broken (user impact):** [e.g. "20% of logins failing in EU", "dashboards loading slowly"]
**Started at:** [TIME AND TIME ZONE]
**What we know so far:** [SYMPTOMS, SUSPECTED CAUSE, RECENT DEPLOYS OR CHANGES]
**What we're doing:** [CURRENT ACTIONS, e.g. "rolling back", "scaling the database"]
**Severity level:** [e.g. "SEV1", "SEV2"]
**Roles:** [INCIDENT LEAD, COMMS OWNER, WHO IS INVESTIGATING WHAT]

Write one update per internal audience:
- **Incident channel (engineers):** current hypothesis and evidence, what has been ruled out, who is doing what, what help or access is needed, and changes that must be paused (deploys, migrations).
- **Leadership:** impact in business terms (users, customers, revenue affected - use [CONFIRM] where I haven't given numbers), current status, decisions they may need to make, and next update time. No jargon.
- **Support team:** what customers will notice, approved wording to use, known workarounds, and what not to promise (causes, ETAs, credits).

Rules for all updates:
- Lead with impact and current status, in the first line.
- Separate what we know from what we suspect. Never state a root cause that isn't confirmed.
- Never give a fix ETA we can't stand behind; give the time of the next update instead.
- Use UTC or one stated time zone throughout.
- End each update with "Next update by [TIME]".

Also give me:
1. A fill-in template I can reuse every 30 minutes as the incident evolves.
2. A "mitigated, monitoring" update and a "resolved" update for each audience, including what follow-up (postmortem, customer comms) happens next.
3. A short timeline log format to keep during the incident so the postmortem is easy to write later.

title: Write past-due fee reminders to a law firm client
description: A three-step escalation of reminders for unpaid legal fees that protects the client relationship and follows the ethics rules on collections and withdrawal.
content:
Write a sequence of past-due payment reminders to a client of my law firm.

**Client type:** [individual / small business / corporate]
**Matter status:** [active / closed]
**Amount past due and invoice dates:** [DETAILS]
**What the engagement letter says about payment, late fees, and withdrawal:** [PASTE THE CLAUSES]
**Trust funds on hand for this client:** [AMOUNT - and whether the engagement letter allows applying them]
**Payment options we offer:** [card, payment plan, ACH]
**Upcoming deadlines in the matter:** [DATES - or "none"]

Write three messages:
1. Friendly reminder (around 15 days past due): a neutral tone, invoice details, payment link, and an offer to talk about questions on the bill.
2. Firm follow-up (around 45 days): restate the engagement letter terms, propose a payment plan, and ask for a response by a date.
3. Final notice (around 75 days): state the consequences allowed by the engagement letter. If the matter is active, explain that the firm may seek to withdraw, without threatening to harm the client's case, and note any court permission withdrawal may require.

Rules:
- Never threaten to hold the client's file or original documents hostage, report them to authorities, or neglect their matter; check my state's rules on retaining liens.
- Do not apply trust funds to fees unless the engagement letter and state rules allow it and the fees are earned and billed.
- Do not disclose confidential information to anyone other than the client.

Also give me a short phone script and a note on when to stop work versus keep protecting the client's interests. This is general guidance; review with the responsible attorney before sending.

title: Allocate capital across competing bets in my company

Help me decide where to put limited money and people across competing initiatives.

4. Recommend a portfolio within the budget, including what's funded fully, funded in stages with a milestone gate, or not funded.

Return the table, the recommended portfolio, and a short memo I can share with my leadership team explaining the choices.

title: Allocate nonprofit expenses across program, management, and fundraising
description: A documented method for splitting shared costs by function for your statement of functional expenses and Form 990.
content:
Help me allocate our nonprofit's expenses by function.

**Our programs:** [LIST]
**Expense data:** [PASTE trial balance or expense list by natural category: salaries, benefits, rent, utilities, technology, printing, travel, etc.]
**Staff and time:** [each role and estimated % of time on each program, management and general, and fundraising, ideally from timesheets or a time study]
**Space:** [square footage used by each function, if relevant]
**Shared activities:** [e.g. a newsletter that educates and asks for gifts, a gala with a program component]

Steps:
1. Classify direct costs to a single function where possible.
2. Choose a reasonable, consistent allocation basis for each shared cost (time for salaries, square footage for rent, headcount for technology) and explain why.
3. Treat activities with both program and fundraising elements under the joint-cost rules (purpose, audience, and content criteria under ASC 958-720); if the criteria are not met, the costs go to fundraising.
4. Watch for common errors: putting the executive director entirely in program, leaving fundraising at zero, or allocating to make the program ratio look better.
5. Build a functional expense matrix (natural category rows by function columns) that ties to total expenses.

Return: the matrix, the allocation methodology memo our auditor can review, the resulting program, management and general, and fundraising percentages, and a note on how to document time going forward.

Use only the numbers I provide. This is general information; have our auditor or CPA review the method before we use it in financial statements or the Form 990.

title: Analyze a rental property deal before making an offer

Analyze this rental property as an investment before I make an offer.

**Planned renovation budget:** [IF ANY]

Calculate and show the math:
1. Gross scheduled income, effective gross income, operating expenses, and net operating income (NOI). Debt service is not an operating expense.
2. Cap rate at asking price and at my offer.

5. Break-even occupancy and break-even rent.
6. Stress tests: rents down 10%, vacancy up to 10%, rate up 1 point, taxes reassessed at purchase price.
7. The maximum price that still meets my target return.

Return a summary table, then the key risks and what to verify in due diligence (rent roll vs. leases, T-12 statements, utility bills). Use only my inputs, marking assumptions. This is general analysis, not investment advice; confirm with a lender, CPA, or advisor.

title: Analyze financial statements
description: Reads a P&L, balance sheet, and cash flow statement and summarizes performance, health, and risks.
content:
Role: Act as a financial controller analysing a company's financial statements.

Context: Statements provided (P&L, balance sheet, cash flow) and periods: [STATEMENTS_PERIODS]. Sector and any peer/benchmark data: [SECTOR_BENCHMARK]. Known events affecting comparability: [EVENTS]. Audience and their question: [AUDIENCE_QUESTION]. Accounting-policy notes that matter: [POLICY_NOTES].

Goal: Explain what the numbers actually say about performance and financial health, and what deserves management attention.

Task: Produce: (1) trend and common-size analysis of the P&L; (2) key ratios across profitability, liquidity, working-capital efficiency and leverage, each with the calculation, the trend, and a plain reading; (3) the quality-of-earnings and cash-conversion picture; (4) 3-5 findings that need management attention; (5) an executive summary (~150 words) answering the audience's question.

Constraints: Use only the figures in the statements; show every ratio formula. Adjust for the comparability events and say how. Do not opine beyond what the statements support - flag where you would need more data (e.g. segment detail).

Examples: Ratio line: 'Gross margin: 61% -> 58% -> 55% over three periods; driven by [X per notes]; below the [sector] benchmark of ~60%.'

Format: Sections: P&L trend & common-size | Ratio analysis (table) | Earnings quality & cash conversion | Findings for management | Executive summary. ~700 words.

Verification: Recompute a sample of the ratios and reconcile net income to operating cash flow; list any figure that does not tie.

Validation: Review as an audit partner: is any conclusion stronger than the statements justify? Soften or evidence it, and name what disclosure would settle the open questions.

title: Apply ASC 606 revenue recognition to my SaaS contracts

Work through the five steps:
1. Identify the contract (and whether any amendments create a new contract or modify the old one).
2. Identify performance obligations - say whether each item is distinct, and why. Note that setup fees in SaaS are often not distinct and get recognized over the subscription or customer life.
3. Determine the transaction price, including variable consideration (usage, credits, refund rights).
4. Allocate the price using standalone selling prices; tell me what SSP evidence I need.
5. Recognize revenue - ratably for the subscription, as delivered for distinct services.

Return:
- A month-by-month schedule: billed, recognized revenue, deferred revenue balance, contract asset if any.
- Sample journal entries for billing, cash receipt, and monthly recognition.
- Judgment calls I need to document in a policy memo.
- How this affects reported revenue versus ARR and bookings, in one paragraph.

Show your math. Use only the numbers I give you; mark assumptions as [ASSUMPTION]. This is general information - confirm treatment with my accountant or auditor.

title: Audit freight invoices for overcharges and billing errors

content:
Help me audit freight invoices for overcharges.

**Invoices:** [PASTE OR SUMMARIZE: INVOICE NO., SHIPMENT ID, DATE, ORIGIN, DESTINATION, WEIGHT, CLASS OR DIMS, CHARGES BY LINE]
**Contracted rates:** [RATE TABLES, FUEL SURCHARGE FORMULA, DISCOUNTS, MINIMUMS, ACCESSORIAL SCHEDULE]
**Our shipment records:** [BILL OF LADING DATA, ACTUAL WEIGHTS AND DIMENSIONS, PROOF OF DELIVERY, APPOINTMENT TIMES]
**Dispute window in the contract:** [e.g. 90 or 180 days]

Check each invoice for:
- Rate not matching the contract for that lane, weight break, or class.
- Fuel surcharge applied at the wrong index or percentage.
- Reweigh or reclassification charges without supporting inspection evidence.
- Accessorials we didn't request or can disprove (liftgate, residential, inside delivery, detention without appointment evidence).
- Duplicate billing for the same shipment.
- Minimum charges applied incorrectly.
- Late delivery where service guarantees allow a refund.
- Math errors.

Rules: only flag an error if the data supports it; if I'm missing the contract term or record needed, list it as [NEED DATA] rather than guessing. Do not estimate refunds without showing the calculation.

Return:
1. An exceptions table: Invoice | Shipment | Issue | Billed | Should be | Difference | Evidence.
2. Total overcharge and the top recurring error types.
3. A dispute email to the carrier listing claims with evidence and the response deadline.
4. Process fixes to prevent these errors (pre-audit rules, accessorial approvals, dimensioner checks).

title: Audit our software subscriptions and recurring office costs
description: A list of every recurring charge with owner, usage, and renewal dates, plus what to cancel, downgrade, or renegotiate.
content:
Help me audit our recurring office and software costs.

**Recurring charges:** [PASTE - vendor, what it is, cost, billing frequency, payment method, renewal date if known]
**Seats or licenses vs. people using them:** [if known]
**Owners or users:** [who requested each, which team uses it]
**Contracts and notice periods:** [if known]
**Budget target:** [e.g. "cut 15%"]

Do this:
1. **Inventory table:** vendor | category (software, utilities, cleaning, leasing, subscriptions, services) | annual cost | billing | owner | licenses paid vs. used | renewal date | notice period | auto-renews?
2. **Findings:** duplicates or overlapping tools, unused or underused seats, subscriptions on personal or forgotten cards, people who've left still holding licenses, monthly plans that would be cheaper annually (or the reverse), price increases at renewal.
3. **Recommendations:** cancel / downgrade / consolidate / renegotiate / keep - with estimated annual savings, based only on the figures I gave.
4. **Renewal calendar:** what to review 60-90 days before each renewal.
5. **Messages:** a note to owners asking whether they still need the tool, and a renegotiation email to a vendor.
6. **Ongoing process:** how new subscriptions get approved and recorded.

Mark missing data [ADD]. Check contract terms before cancelling anything.
variables: who requested each, which team uses it

title: Bill a shipper for detention and accessorial charges with proof
description: Builds an accessorial invoice backed by timestamps and contract terms, plus a firm email that gets detention paid.
content:
Help me bill a customer for detention and other accessorial charges and get paid.

**Charges to bill:** [detention, layover, lumper, TONU, driver assist, redelivery, extra stop]
**Our rate terms:** [e.g. "2 hours free, then $X per hour", from rate confirmation, contract, or tariff]
**Notice requirements in our agreement:** [e.g. "notify within 1 hour of free time ending", "submit within 7 days"]

Do the following:
1. Calculate billable time from appointment or arrival (whichever our terms use) minus free time, and show the math.
2. Check whether we met every notice and paperwork condition; flag anything that weakens the claim.
3. List the documents to attach.
4. Draft the invoice line items with descriptions.
5. Draft a short email to the customer's AP or carrier rep: facts, terms, amount, documents, due date.
6. Draft a firmer follow-up for if they deny or ignore it.

Also give me 3 process changes so detention is captured automatically next time (driver check-in prompts, rate con language, geofence reports).

Use only the rates and times I give you; mark gaps [ADD]. Do not overstate what the contract says.

title: Break down revenue and margin changes into price, volume, and mix
description: A price-volume-mix bridge that shows exactly why revenue and gross margin moved between two periods.
content:
Help me build a price-volume-mix (PVM) bridge explaining the change in revenue and gross margin between two periods.

**Periods compared:** [e.g. "Q3 this year vs. Q3 last year" or "actual vs. budget"]
**Data by product/SKU/segment:** [PASTE: units, revenue, and cost of goods for both periods]
**Level to analyze at:** [product / product family / customer segment / region]
**Other effects to isolate:** [FX / new products / discontinued items / acquisitions - or "none"]

Steps:
1. Compute average price and unit cost per line for each period.
2. Split the revenue change into price, volume, and mix effects. State the formulas you use and the order of calculation, because the order changes the split.
3. Do the same for gross margin, adding a cost (rate) effect.
4. Treat new and discontinued lines separately so they do not distort price or mix.
5. Check that the effects sum exactly to the total change; show the reconciliation.

Return:
- A bridge table: Starting value | Price | Volume | Mix | Cost | FX/Other | Ending value.
- The top 5 lines driving each effect.
- 4-6 bullets of plain-English commentary for management.
- Any data issues (zero units, negative prices, returns) and how you handled them.

Use only the numbers I provide. If something needed is missing, mark it [ADD DATA] rather than estimating.
variables: e.g. "Q3 this year vs. Q3 last year" or "actual vs. budget"
PASTE: units, revenue, and cost of goods for both periods
product / product family / customer segment / region

title: Build a budget vs. actual variance analysis in Excel
description: Sets up a budget vs. actual sheet with correct variance formulas, favorable/unfavorable logic, materiality flags, and a YTD view.
content:
Help me build a budget vs. actual (or forecast vs. actual, or this year vs. last year) variance analysis in Excel.

**What I'm comparing:** [budget vs. actual / forecast vs. actual / current vs. prior year]
**Line items:** [PASTE - e.g. revenue lines, cost categories, headcount, departments]
**Numbers:** [PASTE budget and actual by line and month, or a sample]
**Period:** [e.g. "September 2026 and YTD"]
**Materiality threshold for comments:** [e.g. "over $10k and over 5%"]
**Who will read it:** [e.g. "department heads", "CFO"]

Build:
1. **Layout:** Line | Budget | Actual | Variance $ | Variance % | Fav/Unfav | Comment, for the month and YTD side by side, with subtotals that add up.
2. **Sign logic:** for revenue, actual above budget is favorable; for costs, below budget is favorable. Give one formula approach that handles both (e.g. a +1/-1 "type" column), so the Fav/Unfav label is never wrong.
3. **Formulas:** variance %, protected from zero or blank budgets (show "n/a" instead of #DIV/0!), and a materiality flag that only lights up lines needing explanation.
4. **Conditional formatting** for material adverse variances.
5. **Checks:** totals tie to the source, budget totals tie to the approved budget, and months without actuals are excluded from YTD.
6. **Questions to ask each budget owner** for every flagged line: timing or permanent, price or volume, one-off or recurring.

Return the layout, all formulas, the checks, and a short summary of the biggest variances using only my numbers. Do not invent reasons for variances - leave [ADD REASON] for owners to fill in.
variables: PASTE budget and actual by line and month, or a sample

title: Build a business budget with driver assumptions
description: An annual or project budget built from clear drivers and assumptions.
content:
Role: Act as an FP&A analyst building a driver-based annual budget.

Context: Entity / cost centre: [ENTITY]. Prior-year actuals and current run-rate: [PRIOR_ACTUALS]. Business plan inputs (volume, headcount, pricing, initiatives): [PLAN_INPUTS]. Known cost drivers and their rates: [COST_DRIVERS]. Constraints / targets from leadership: [TARGETS]. Chart of accounts structure: [COA].

Task: Produce: the driver tree linking business inputs to P&L lines; an assumptions log (each assumption, its value, source, and owner); the build sequence (which lines to model first and dependencies); the key sensitivities to test; and the review checkpoints before submission.

Format: Sections: Driver tree | Assumptions log (table) | Build sequence | Sensitivities | Review checkpoints. ~450 words.

Verification: Flag every assumption without a named source or owner, and any P&L line not connected to a driver. Do not invent rates - mark [INPUT NEEDED].

Validation: Sanity-check the implied totals against prior-year run-rate: are the growth/cost movements explainable by the plan inputs? Flag any line that jumps without a reason.

title: Build a capex case for automating a manual process
description: A capital request for an automation project with full costs, realistic savings, payback, and risks, ready for the approval committee.
content:
Help me build a capital expenditure (capex) request to automate a manual process.

**Process today:** [what operators do, number of operators per shift, shifts, cycle time, quality issues, safety or ergonomic risks]
**Proposed solution:** [e.g. "collaborative robot for machine tending", "vision inspection system"]
**Costs:** [equipment quote, integration, guarding and safety, installation, utilities, training, spare parts, software licenses, downtime during installation]
**Expected benefits:** [labor hours, scrap reduction, throughput gain, overtime, injury risk reduction]
**Volumes and product life:** [annual volume and how many years the product will run]
**Company hurdle rules:** [payback limit, IRR or NPV hurdle rate, discount rate]

Steps:
1. Build the total installed cost, flagging common items left out (safety risk assessment, guarding, changeover tooling for other parts, engineering time, ramp-up losses).
2. Calculate annual savings with my rates and volumes. Count labor savings only if the people will be redeployed to real open work or the roles will not be backfilled; otherwise say so.
3. Add ongoing costs: maintenance, programming support, spare parts.
4. Calculate simple payback, NPV, and IRR. Show the math.
5. Run a sensitivity check: what happens if volume drops 20%, the ramp-up takes twice as long, or savings come in at 70%.
6. List non-financial benefits and risks: ergonomics, quality consistency, flexibility for future products, single point of failure, skills needed to support it.

Return: an executive summary (under 150 words), a cost and savings table, the financial results, the sensitivity table, risks with mitigations, and the decision being asked for.

Use only my figures; mark gaps [ADD]. Do not overstate savings. Have finance check the numbers before submission.
variables: annual volume and how many years the product will run
payback limit, IRR or NPV hurdle rate, discount rate

title: Build a fixed asset register and depreciation schedule
description: Sets up a fixed asset register with useful lives, methods, and monthly depreciation, and flags items that shouldn't be capitalized.
content:
Help me build a fixed asset register and depreciation schedule.

**Assets purchased or held:** [PASTE - description, purchase date, cost, in-service date, location]

**Disposals or impairments this year:** [DETAILS or "none"]
**Fiscal year end:** [DATE]

Steps:
1. Classify each asset (e.g. computers, furniture, vehicles, leasehold improvements, software) and check it meets the threshold.
2. Flag items that look like repairs or maintenance, items that should be bundled (e.g. 20 laptops bought together), and leasehold improvements whose life should be capped at the lease term.
3. Apply the policy and calculate monthly and annual depreciation, starting from the in-service date (state the convention used - full month, half month, etc.).
4. For disposals, calculate accumulated depreciation to date and the gain or loss.

Return:
1. The register: Asset ID | Description | Class | In-service date | Cost | Life | Method | Monthly depreciation | Accumulated depreciation | Net book value.
2. A summary by class that ties to the general ledger accounts.
3. The journal entry for this period's depreciation.
4. Open questions.

Tax depreciation (e.g. bonus or Section 179 in the US, capital allowances elsewhere) follows different rules - list it as [TAX PREPARER TO CONFIRM] rather than calculating it.
variables: method and useful lives by class, or "help me propose one"

title: Build a flat-rate price book for my service trade business
description: Flat-rate task prices built from real labor, material, and overhead costs, so every tech quotes the same profitable price.
content:
Help me build a flat-rate price book for my trade service business.

**Trade:** [PLUMBING / ELECTRICAL / HVAC / HANDYMAN]
**Common tasks:** [e.g. "replace toilet flapper", "install GFCI receptacle", "replace 50-gal water heater" - list 10-40]
**Typical time per task:** [HOURS, INCLUDING SETUP AND CLEANUP - or "estimate and mark"]
**Typical material cost per task:** [COSTS]
**Annual overhead:** [RENT, TRUCKS, INSURANCE, SOFTWARE, OFFICE STAFF, MARKETING]
**Billable hours per tech per year:** [e.g. "1,100 of 2,000 paid hours"]
**Tech pay and burden:** [WAGE, PAYROLL TAXES, BENEFITS, WORKERS' COMP]
**Target net profit:** [e.g. 15%]
**Current service call fee and warranty policy:** [DETAILS]

Steps:
1. Calculate my break-even cost per billable hour (labor + burden + overhead), showing the math.
2. Calculate the hourly selling rate that hits my target net profit.
3. Set material markup tiers (e.g. higher markup on low-cost parts).
4. Price each task: (hours x selling rate) + marked-up material, rounded to a clean number. Show a column for the margin.
5. Suggest good/better/best add-ons where natural (e.g. shut-off valve upgrade with a faucet install).
6. Flag tasks where my times or costs look unrealistic or where a fixed price is risky (unknown conditions); recommend diagnostic or T&M pricing for those.

Return: the cost and rate calculation, a price book table (Task, Hours, Material, Price, Margin %, Notes), a list of tasks to price as T&M, and rules for techs on when to deviate from the book.

Never invent costs; mark guesses as [ESTIMATE - CONFIRM]. Check pricing and disclosure rules for my state with my accountant.

RENT, TRUCKS, INSURANCE, SOFTWARE, OFFICE STAFF, MARKETING

title: Build a grant budget and budget justification

Help me build a budget and budget justification for a grant application.

**Funder type:** [federal / state / private foundation / corporate]
**Funder's budget rules:** [PASTE guidelines: allowable costs, indirect cap, match requirement, budget categories]
**Project and period:** [DESCRIPTION, start and end dates]

**Other costs:** [supplies, travel, contracts, equipment, participant support, evaluation]

Steps:

2. Calculate personnel as salary x % effort, plus fringe, with any cost-of-living increase stated.
3. Apply indirect costs to the correct base. For US federal awards, note whether we use a negotiated rate or the de minimis rate on modified total direct costs, and which costs are excluded from that base. [CONFIRM the current rate and rules in the award's terms.]
4. Flag costs that are commonly unallowable (e.g. entertainment, alcohol, lobbying, fundraising costs) or that need prior approval.

Return: the budget table, the justification, a list of assumptions, and the questions to ask our finance lead. This is general guidance; verify against the funder's rules and our auditor's advice.

CONFIRM the current rate and rules in the award's terms.

title: Build a headcount plan with fully loaded employee costs

- Cost new hires from their start month only, and apply the hiring delay above.
- Separate one-time costs (recruiting, equipment) from recurring costs.
- Show backfills for expected attrition separately from net new roles.

Return:

2. A per-role cost summary showing how base salary becomes fully loaded cost.

title: Build a month-end close checklist with owners and deadlines
description: Creates a day-by-day close calendar with tasks, owners, dependencies, and review steps so the books close on time every month.
content:
Help me build a month-end close checklist and calendar.

**Team:** [WHO does what - e.g. "me (staff accountant), AP clerk, controller reviews"]
**Systems:** [accounting software, payroll provider, bank feeds, billing system, spreadsheets]
**Entities and bank accounts:** [NUMBER of each]
**Target close timeline:** [e.g. "books closed by business day 5"]
**Key recurring items:** [e.g. payroll accruals, revenue recognition, inventory, credit card statements, intercompany, depreciation]

Build the checklist in close order, including: pre-close (cut-off reminders, open PO and invoice sweep), cash and bank reconciliations, AR and AP, payroll, accruals and prepaids, fixed assets and depreciation, revenue, inventory if relevant, balance sheet reconciliations, flux review, reporting, and period lock.

Return:
1. A table: Day (BD-2 to BD+N) | Task | Owner | Depends on | Output/evidence | Reviewer.
2. The critical path - which tasks hold up everything else.
3. Fixes for the problems I named (e.g. earlier cut-off emails, a standing estimate method).

Keep tasks specific and checkable ("Reconcile operating account to bank statement, tie to GL"), not vague ("review cash").

title: Build a profit-and-loss estimate for a book acquisition
description: A title P&L that tests the advance, print run, pricing, and royalties to show the break-even point and whether an offer makes sense.
content:
Help me build a profit-and-loss estimate for a book we are thinking of acquiring.

**Formats and list prices:** [hardcover / paperback / ebook / audio - with prices]
**Sales forecast by format:** [UNITS for year one and lifetime, based on comps or our data]
**Average discount to retailers and wholesalers:** [e.g. "48% blended"]
**Returns rate assumption:** [e.g. "25% on print"]
**Unit production cost:** [printing, paper, binding per copy, by print run size]
**Plant and one-off costs:** [editing, design, typesetting, proofreading, permissions, audio production]
**Royalty rates in the proposed deal:** [e.g. hardcover 10%/12.5%/15% escalators on list, ebook 25% of net receipts]
**Proposed advance:** [AMOUNT and payment schedule]
**Marketing budget and overhead allocation:** [AMOUNTS or % of revenue]

Calculate:
1. Net revenue per format after discounts and returns.
2. Cost of goods, royalties earned, and whether and when the advance earns out.
3. Gross margin and contribution after marketing and overhead.
4. Break-even units, and the maximum advance that still meets our target margin of [TARGET %].
5. Scenarios: low / expected / high sales, and a different first print run.

Return a P&L table by format, the scenario comparison, and a short note to the acquisitions meeting: the offer I can justify, the key assumptions, and the biggest risk.

Show every formula. Use only my inputs; label any assumption you add as [ASSUMPTION - CONFIRM]. Have finance review before making an offer.
variables: hardcover / paperback / ebook / audio - with prices
UNITS for year one and lifetime, based on comps or our data
printing, paper, binding per copy, by print run size

title: Build a project cost estimate with a contingency reserve
description: A structured cost estimate by work package with explicit assumptions, risk-based contingency, and a range you can defend.
content:
Help me build a cost estimate for my project, including a contingency reserve.

**Project scope:** [SUMMARY or work breakdown]
**Labor:** [roles, number of people, time on the project, loaded rates if known]
**Non-labor costs:** [software, hardware, vendors, travel, facilities, training]
**Known risks that could add cost:** [LIST]
**Estimating basis:** [past similar projects, vendor quotes, expert judgment]
**Currency and budget period:** [e.g. USD, fiscal year]

Steps:
1. Organize costs by work package or phase, separating one-time from recurring costs.
2. List every assumption behind each line (rate, duration, quantity) so a reviewer can challenge it.
3. Rate each line's estimate confidence (high / medium / low) based on its basis.
4. Size a contingency reserve from the identified risks (probability x cost impact), and explain why it differs from a flat percentage. Mention that a separate management reserve for unknown risks is usually held by the sponsor, not the project.
5. Flag commonly forgotten costs: internal staff time, licenses after go-live, data migration, testing environments, change management, hypercare.

Rules: do not invent rates or prices. Use [QUOTE NEEDED] or [RATE NEEDED] placeholders. This is planning support, not accounting advice - have finance validate it before approval.

Return:
1. An estimate table: work package | item | quantity | rate | cost | basis | confidence.
2. A contingency table: risk | probability | cost impact | expected value.
3. Totals: base estimate, contingency, and a low-high range.
4. An assumptions list for the business case.
variables: software, hardware, vendors, travel, facilities, training
past similar projects, vendor quotes, expert judgment

title: Build a should-cost model for a purchased part

title: Build an ARR bridge and net revenue retention analysis
description: A recurring revenue waterfall from new, expansion, contraction, and churn, with retention metrics and commentary.

Help me build an ARR (annual recurring revenue) bridge and retention analysis.

title: Build an open-to-buy plan for next season
description: A month-by-month open-to-buy plan at retail and cost that shows how much I can still buy and where I'm overbought.
content:
Help me build an open-to-buy (OTB) plan for my next season.

**Category or department:** [NAME]
**Planning period:** [e.g. "Feb-Jul, by month"]
**Planned sales by month:** [AT RETAIL - or last year's actuals plus my growth assumption]
**Planned markdowns and promotions by month:** [$ OR % OF SALES]
**Beginning-of-month inventory now:** [AT RETAIL]
**Target inventory levels:** [e.g. "BOM stock-to-sales ratio of 3.0" or planned EOM inventory by month]
**Inventory already on order:** [BY DELIVERY MONTH, AT RETAIL]
**Initial markup %:** [to convert retail to cost]

Use the retail method: planned purchases = planned sales + planned markdowns + planned end-of-month inventory - beginning-of-month inventory. OTB = planned purchases - on order.

Return:
1. A month-by-month table: BOM inventory, sales, markdowns, EOM inventory, planned purchases, on order, OTB at retail, OTB at cost.
2. Months where OTB is negative (overbought), with options: cancel, push delivery, shift to another month, or plan a promotion.
3. How much OTB to hold back for in-season reorders and opportunistic buys, with reasoning.
4. Sensitivity: OTB if sales come in 10% below and 10% above plan.
5. Assumptions I should confirm with finance.

Show the formulas so I can rebuild this in a spreadsheet. Do not fill gaps with made-up figures; mark them [ADD].
variables: AT RETAIL - or last year's actuals plus my growth assumption

title: Build financial projections for a business
description: 3–5 year revenue, cost, profit, and cash projections from clear assumptions.
content:
Build financial projections for my business.

**Business model and stage:** [DETAILS]
**Period:** [e.g. 36 months, monthly for year 1]
**Revenue drivers:** [price, volume, customers, growth, churn]
**Costs:** [cost of goods, salaries, rent, marketing, tools — fixed vs. variable]
**Funding and starting cash:** [AMOUNTS]

Deliver:
1. An assumptions table (every input, its source, and confidence).
2. Projected P&L, cash flow, and key metrics (gross margin, burn, runway, break-even month).
3. Three scenarios — conservative, base, optimistic — and what drives the difference.
4. A sensitivity check on the 3 assumptions that matter most.
5. A layout I can recreate in a spreadsheet (with formulas described).

Projections, not predictions — label every assumption. Have an accountant review before relying on them for lending or investment.

title: Calculate CAC payback, magic number, and burn multiple for my SaaS
description: Your core SaaS efficiency metrics calculated correctly, benchmarked by stage, and turned into a short diagnosis.
content:
Calculate the go-to-market efficiency metrics for my SaaS business.

**Period data (quarterly preferred):** [new ARR, expansion ARR, churned and contracted ARR, sales and marketing spend, gross margin %, net burn, starting and ending ARR]
**Number of new customers and average ARR per new customer:** [DATA]
**Business model:** [self-serve / sales-led / hybrid] **Stage:** [e.g. seed, Series A, $5M ARR]
**How we account for S&M:** [what is included - salaries, commissions, tools, agencies]

Calculate, showing the formula and inputs for each:
1. CAC (blended, and paid if I give channel data).
2. CAC payback in months = period S&M spend / (new ARR added in the period x gross margin %) x 12, using prior-period spend if I specify a lag. Keep units consistent (ARR is annual) and state them.
3. Magic number = (this quarter's revenue minus last quarter's revenue) x 4 / prior-quarter S&M spend (net new ARR / prior-quarter S&M as an approximation).
4. Burn multiple = net burn / net new ARR.
5. Net revenue retention and gross revenue retention, if data allows.
6. LTV:CAC, only with a stated churn assumption, and a note on why it can mislead at early stage.

Then:
- Compare each metric to commonly cited ranges for my stage and model, labeled as rough rules of thumb, not standards.
- Diagnose the biggest drag (low win rates, high churn, low margin, overspend) and what data would confirm it.
- List 3 actions ranked by likely impact.
- Flag any inconsistent or missing inputs instead of guessing.

Output: a metrics table, a 150-word diagnosis, and the action list.
variables: what is included - salaries, commissions, tools, agencies

title: Calculate my freelance rate from my income goal
description: Works back from your target income, real billable hours, and costs to a day rate, project price, and minimum.
content:
Help me work out what to charge as a freelancer, starting from what I need to earn.

**Target take-home income per year:** [AMOUNT]
**Business costs per year:** [software, equipment, insurance, accountant, coworking, training]
**Benefits I now pay myself:** [health insurance, retirement, paid time off]
**Weeks I plan to work per year:** [e.g. 46]
**Hours per week I can work:** [TOTAL]
**Location for tax purposes:** [COUNTRY / STATE]
**Typical project:** [WHAT I DELIVER, and roughly how long it takes]
**Previous step (optional):** [PASTE my niche and positioning, so pricing matches the clients I'm targeting]

Do this:
1. Estimate billable hours realistically: subtract time for sales, admin, and gaps between projects (assume 50-70% of working time is billable unless I say otherwise), and explain the assumption.
2. Calculate the revenue needed: take-home + costs + benefits + an estimated tax set-aside (mark the tax rate [CONFIRM]).
3. Turn that into an hourly floor, a day rate, and a price for my typical project.
4. Show 3 pricing options for that project (hourly, fixed fee, monthly retainer) with pros and cons for my niche.
5. Set a walk-away minimum and explain how to raise rates for new clients over time.

Show the math step by step in a table. This is general information; confirm tax and insurance figures with an accountant or local professional.
variables: health insurance, retirement, paid time off
WHAT I DELIVER, and roughly how long it takes

title: Calculate product margins before I stock my store
description: Works out landed cost, fees, and true profit per item so you only launch products that make money.
content:
Help me check whether the products I want to sell will actually make money.

**Products (name, expected selling price):** [LIST]
**Cost per unit from supplier:** [AMOUNTS, plus minimum order quantity]
**Shipping from supplier, duties, and import fees:** [AMOUNTS or "not sure"]
**Packaging cost per order:** [AMOUNT]
**Where I'll sell:** [own store / Etsy / Amazon / other - fees vary]
**Shipping to customers:** [what I'll charge vs. what it costs me]
**Expected return rate:** [% or "not sure"]
**Marketing budget per sale:** [AMOUNT or "not sure"]

Do this:
1. Calculate landed cost per unit (product + inbound shipping + duties + packaging).
2. Subtract platform and payment fees. Use the fee rates I give; if I don't know them, show them as [CONFIRM CURRENT FEE] rather than guessing.
3. Account for returns, damaged goods, and free-shipping costs.
4. Show gross margin and contribution margin per unit, and the maximum I can spend to acquire a customer and still break even.
5. Flag any product with a contribution margin under 30% (or my own threshold) and suggest fixes: price change, bundle, cheaper packaging, different supplier, or drop it.
6. Calculate the cash needed for my first order across all products.

Output: a table (Product | Price | Landed cost | Fees | Contribution margin $ | % | Max acquisition cost | Verdict), then the cash-needed total and recommendations.
variables: own store / Etsy / Amazon / other - fees vary
what I'll charge vs. what it costs me

title: Calculate the cost of poor quality at my plant
description: A cost of poor quality (COPQ) breakdown across scrap, rework, warranty, and appraisal, with the biggest money leaks ranked for action.
content:
Help me calculate the cost of poor quality (COPQ) for my plant or product line.

**Period and scope:** [e.g. "last 12 months, Plant 2"]
**Internal failure data:** [scrap quantities and values, rework hours and labor rate, re-inspection, downgraded product, line stoppages for quality]
**External failure data:** [warranty claims, returns, customer chargebacks, field service, premium freight to replace bad parts, recall costs]
**Appraisal costs:** [inspection and test labor, lab costs, calibration, audits]
**Prevention costs:** [quality planning, training, FMEA work, supplier development]
**Revenue or cost of goods sold for the period:** [AMOUNT]

Steps:
1. Sort every cost I give into the four buckets: prevention, appraisal, internal failure, external failure.
2. Calculate each bucket's total and COPQ as a percentage of revenue (or COGS).
3. Flag hidden costs I probably haven't counted: overtime to recover output, expedited freight, extra inventory held as a buffer, engineering time on firefighting, lost capacity on the bottleneck. List them as [ESTIMATE NEEDED] rather than guessing amounts.
4. Rank the top 5 failure costs by product, defect type, or line using a Pareto view.
5. For the top 3, suggest what prevention spend could reduce them, and a simple payback estimate based only on my numbers.

Return: a summary table by bucket, the Pareto ranking, the hidden cost list, and a 150-word summary for leadership.

Use only figures I provide. Show calculations. Where scrap is valued at material cost only, note that it understates the true cost (labor and overhead already spent).
variables: inspection and test labor, lab costs, calibration, audits
quality planning, training, FMEA work, supplier development

title: Categorize messy bank and card transactions to my chart of accounts
description: Sorts a raw transaction export into the right accounts, with confidence levels and a short list of items that need a human answer.
content:
Help me categorize bank and credit card transactions for bookkeeping.

**Rules I already follow:** [e.g. "software subscriptions under $500 go to Software", "owner's personal Amazon orders go to Owner Draws"]
**Accounting basis:** [cash / accrual]

For each transaction:
- Suggest the account, a cleaned-up payee name, and a confidence level (high / medium / low).
- Flag likely transfers between the business's own accounts, loan payments (split principal vs. interest as [NEED LOAN SCHEDULE]), owner draws or contributions, refunds, and sales tax collected - these are the usual miscategorizations.
- Flag possible personal expenses, duplicates, and anything over [AMOUNT] that might need to be capitalized.
- Do not guess on vague descriptions (e.g. "POS 4471", "Zelle J. Smith"). Mark them [ASK CLIENT].

Return:
1. A table: Date | Description | Cleaned payee | Suggested account | Confidence | Note.
2. A short list of questions for the business owner, grouped so they can answer in one pass.
3. Suggested bank rules I could set up in my accounting software for recurring payees.

title: Challenge a department's budget submission before approval
description: A line-by-line review of a budget request with probing questions, red flags, and a negotiating position.
content:
Help me review a department's budget submission and prepare to challenge it.

**Department and owner:** [DETAILS]
**Their submission:** [PASTE: line items for this year's request, last year's budget, and last year's actuals]
**Their stated rationale:** [WHAT they wrote or said]
**Company targets or guardrails:** [e.g. "opex growth capped at 5%"]
**Strategic priorities this department supports:** [DETAILS]

Review for:
- Growth vs. last year's actuals (not just last year's budget).
- Run-rate errors: annualizing one-offs, double-counting hires, missing savings from leavers.
- Padding signs: round numbers, large "other" lines, contingency hidden in multiple lines.
- New initiatives without measurable outcomes.
- Spend that does not link to a stated priority.
- Timing: costs front-loaded with no reason.

Return:
1. A table: Line | Requested | Prior actual | Change % | Concern | Question to ask.
2. The 8 most important questions for the review meeting, in order.
3. Three options: approve as is, approve with conditions, or a reduced version with the specific cuts and their impact.
4. A short, respectful opening statement for the meeting.

Stay constructive: the goal is a credible budget, not winning an argument. Do not assume bad faith; flag concerns as questions.

title: Check a financial model for errors before it goes to leadership
description: A structured model review that finds formula errors, broken logic, and weak assumptions before anyone relies on it.
content:
Review my financial model for errors and weaknesses.

**Purpose of the model:** [e.g. "3-year plan for board", "acquisition model", "pricing model"]
**Structure:** [DESCRIBE tabs and flow - inputs, calculations, outputs]
**Key formulas or sections:** [PASTE formulas, or paste tabs as tables with cell references]
**Known concerns:** [anything I am unsure about]

Check for:
1. Mechanical errors: hard-coded numbers in formulas, inconsistent formulas across a row, wrong ranges, circular references, sign errors, mixing units (thousands vs. units, monthly vs. annual).
2. Integrity: does the balance sheet balance, does cash reconcile to the cash flow statement, do subtotals foot?
3. Logic: timing (annual vs. monthly), growth compounding, double-counting, tax and depreciation treatment, working capital direction.
4. Assumptions: any that look out of line with history or benchmarks I have provided.
5. Usability: inputs clearly separated, labeled units, version and source notes.

Return:
- An issues log: # | Location | Issue | Severity (high/medium/low) | Suggested fix.
- The top 3 issues that could change a decision.
- A list of standard checks (balance check, cash proof, totals) to add to the model.
- Questions I should answer before sharing.

Only review what I paste. If you cannot see a cell or formula, say so rather than assuming it is correct.
variables: DESCRIBE tabs and flow - inputs, calculations, outputs
PASTE formulas, or paste tabs as tables with cell references

title: Check loan covenant compliance and draft the lender certificate
description: Calculates each financial covenant from the loan agreement's definitions, shows headroom, and drafts the compliance certificate.
content:
Help me test our loan covenants and prepare the compliance certificate.

**Covenant definitions from the loan agreement:** [PASTE exactly - e.g. "Fixed Charge Coverage Ratio", "Senior Leverage", "Minimum Liquidity", and the definitions of EBITDA, Funded Debt, Fixed Charges]
**Test period and frequency:** [e.g. "trailing 12 months, tested quarterly"]
**Financials for the test period:** [PASTE P&L, balance sheet, cash flow items needed]
**Adjustments allowed by the agreement:** [e.g. one-time costs, non-cash compensation, caps on add-backs]
**Lender reporting deadline:** [DATE]

Steps:
1. Calculate each covenant strictly using the agreement's definitions, not standard accounting definitions - show every component.
2. Show the add-backs used and confirm each is allowed and within any cap.
3. Compare to the required level and calculate headroom (in ratio and in dollars of EBITDA or cash).
4. Project next quarter's result if I give you a forecast, and flag a likely breach early.

Return:
1. A calculation table per covenant: Component | Source | Amount | Notes.
2. Summary: Covenant | Required | Actual | Pass/Fail | Headroom.
3. A draft compliance certificate in neutral language, with [OFFICER SIGNATURE] and [CONFIRM AGREEMENT TERMS] markers.
4. If any covenant is tight or failed, talking points for a proactive conversation with the lender.

Definitions in the agreement control. Have the calculation reviewed by our CFO or counsel before submitting.
variables: PASTE P&L, balance sheet, cash flow items needed
e.g. one-time costs, non-cash compensation, caps on add-backs

title: Check whether a client project is making money
description: A profitability check comparing budget to actual hours, my effective hourly rate, where time leaked, and what to fix now.
content:
Help me work out whether a client project is profitable.

**Fee structure:** [fixed fee / retainer / hourly with a cap, and the amount]
**Budgeted hours by phase or task:** [ESTIMATES]
**Actual hours logged so far by phase or task:** [ACTUALS]
**Other costs:** [subcontractors, software, travel]
**My target hourly rate or margin:** [TARGET]
**How much is left to do:** [REMAINING WORK]

Analyze:
1. Effective hourly rate so far and projected at completion, showing the math.
2. Budget vs. actual by phase, with the biggest overruns highlighted.
3. Likely causes of overruns: unpaid scope creep, extra revision rounds, meetings, my own underestimate, or client delays. Separate what was in my control from what wasn't.
4. Projected final margin under a best, likely, and worst case for the remaining work.
5. Actions for this project: what to raise as a change request, what to streamline, and what to stop doing for free.
6. Lessons for pricing the next similar project: a revised estimate per phase.

Use only the numbers I provide. If key data is missing (e.g. untracked time), say how that affects the result instead of guessing.
variables: fixed fee / retainer / hourly with a cap, and the amount

title: Check whether a design project will finish within its fee
description: A fee-burn check comparing fee spent with percent complete by phase, with an estimate at completion and recovery options.
content:
Help me check whether my architecture or engineering project will finish within its fee.

**Contract fee by phase:** [e.g. "SD $40k, DD $60k, CD $120k, CA $80k"]
**Labor and consultant cost to date by phase:** [PASTE from the project report]
**Percent complete by phase:** [the project manager's honest estimate of work done, not fee spent]
**Approved and pending additional services:** [AMOUNTS and status]
**Remaining staffing plan:** [hours by role through completion]
**Billing and collections:** [billed to date, unbilled work in progress, receivables over 60 days]
**Target project profit margin:** [e.g. "15%"]

Calculate and explain:
1. Earned value per phase (percent complete x phase fee) against cost to date, and the spent-vs-earned gap.
2. Estimate at completion: cost to date plus estimate to complete, and the projected profit or loss vs. target.
3. Effective multiplier or net revenue per hour, if I give raw salary costs [OPTIONAL].
4. Which phase is causing the overrun and the likely cause (scope creep without an additional services request, rework from coordination errors, extra client meetings, longer construction period).
5. Billing health: over- or under-billed position and collection risk.

Return:
- A phase table: fee | earned | cost to date | estimate to complete | estimate at completion | variance.
- The top three drivers of variance.
- Recovery options ranked by impact: additional services to request, staffing changes, scope clarifications, schedule changes.
- A short summary I can send to the principal in charge.

Use only my numbers; mark gaps [NEED DATA]. Show formulas.

title: Choose a fair method to allocate shared overhead costs
description: Compares allocation bases for shared costs across departments, products, or locations and shows the results and trade-offs of each.
content:
Help me allocate shared overhead costs.

**What's being allocated:** [e.g. rent, IT, HR, executive salaries, utilities - with amounts]
**Receiving units:** [departments / product lines / locations / clients / grants]
**Data I have for each unit:** [headcount, square footage, revenue, labor hours, machine hours, transactions, usage]
**Purpose of the allocation:** [pricing / profitability analysis / management reporting / grant or contract cost recovery / transfer pricing]
**Rules I must follow:** [e.g. "federal grant cost principles", "contract terms", "none"]

Steps:
1. For each cost pool, suggest 2-3 possible allocation bases and say which best reflects what drives the cost.
2. Calculate the allocation under the recommended basis, and under one alternative for comparison.
3. Show how each unit's profitability changes under each method.
4. Flag pitfalls: allocating by revenue hides real cost drivers; fixed costs allocated to a unit don't go away if the unit is cut; allocations that shift with another unit's volume cause confusion.

Return:
1. A table per cost pool: Basis | Unit | Driver quantity | Share % | Allocated $.
2. A side-by-side profitability view under each method.
3. A recommended method with one-paragraph rationale I can share with managers.
4. A simple monthly process to repeat it.

If this is for grants, government contracts, tax, or transfer pricing, mark the method [CONFIRM WITH SPECIALIST] - those have specific rules.
variables: departments / product lines / locations / clients / grants

title: Classify a lease and calculate the opening lease entries
description: Works through lease classification, the lease liability and right-of-use asset, and the first entries, with every assumption made visible.
content:
Help me account for a lease.

**Framework:** [ASC 842 / IFRS 16]
**Lease terms:** [PASTE - asset, commencement date, term, renewal/termination options, payment schedule and escalations, free-rent periods, purchase option, residual value guarantees]
**Initial direct costs and lease incentives:** [AMOUNTS]
**Discount rate:** [rate implicit in the lease if known, or our incremental borrowing rate, or the risk-free rate election if we're eligible]
**Our policy elections:** [short-term lease exemption, combine lease and non-lease components, etc.]

Steps:
1. Confirm it contains a lease (identified asset, right to control).
2. Determine the lease term, including options we're reasonably certain to exercise - explain the judgment.
3. Classify it (finance vs. operating under ASC 842; IFRS 16 lessees use a single model) and show each test.
4. Calculate the initial lease liability (present value of payments) and right-of-use asset.
5. Build the amortization schedule for the first 12 months.

Return:
1. Classification conclusion with the reasoning.
2. A calculation table I can rebuild in a spreadsheet (period, payment, interest, principal, liability balance, ROU asset balance).
3. Opening journal entry and the first monthly entry.
4. A list of inputs marked [CONFIRM] - especially the discount rate and term.

Show the math, don't just state results. Verify final numbers in a spreadsheet and with our auditors before booking.

title: Classify SaaS costs into COGS and calculate gross margin
description: A defensible split of hosting, support, and services costs into cost of revenue, with a gross margin view investors will accept.
content:
Help me classify my SaaS costs between cost of revenue (COGS) and operating expenses, and calculate gross margin.

**Cost lines:** [PASTE my expense list with amounts - hosting, third-party APIs and AI model costs, monitoring tools, support team, customer success, implementation team, payment processing, DevOps salaries, etc.]
**Revenue split:** [subscription revenue vs professional services revenue]
**Team allocation:** [e.g. "DevOps spends 60% on production uptime, 40% on new features"]
**How we classify today:** [CURRENT approach, or "everything is in opex"]

Return:
1. A table: cost line | amount | COGS or opex | allocation % | reasoning. Cover the usual SaaS judgment calls: production hosting vs development environments, support vs customer success (retention vs expansion work), DevOps and SRE time, payment processing fees, amortized capitalized software, and AI inference costs.
2. Subscription gross margin and services gross margin calculated separately, then blended. Show the math.
3. How my margin compares to commonly cited SaaS ranges, labeled as rough rules of thumb.
4. The top 3 drivers of margin and ideas to improve each (e.g. hosting efficiency, support deflection, pricing of AI-heavy features, services packaging).
5. A short policy note to keep classification consistent month to month, with the allocation method documented.
6. Red flags investors look for, such as moving support costs to opex to flatter margin.

Use only the figures I give; mark assumptions as [ASSUMPTION]. This is general information - confirm the classification with my accountant.
variables: subscription revenue vs professional services revenue
CURRENT approach, or "everything is in opex"

title: Compare insurance quotes side by side before renewal
description: Extracts the key terms from several insurance quotes into one comparison table, highlights coverage gaps, and lists questions for the broker.
content:
Help me compare insurance quotes side by side.

**Type of insurance:** [e.g. group health benefits, commercial property, general liability, fleet, cyber]
**Who it covers:** [e.g. "85 employees and dependents", "two warehouses"]
**Current policy and what we want to keep or fix:** [DETAILS]
**Quotes:** [paste the text of each quote or schedule of benefits, labeled by insurer]
**What matters most to us:** [e.g. lowest premium, broad coverage, specific benefit, insurer service]

Do this:
1. **Extract** each quote's key terms into a table, one row per benefit or term and one column per insurer: premium, deductible or excess, limits and sub-limits, co-pay or co-insurance, waiting periods, exclusions, territory, policy period, and any benefit specific to this insurance type. Copy figures exactly as written and note the page or section. If a quote doesn't state a term, write "Not stated" - never fill in a typical value.
2. **Differences that matter:** flag where quotes differ meaningfully, especially lower limits, new exclusions, and conditions that could deny a claim.
3. **Like-for-like check:** note where quotes aren't comparable (different limits, periods, or assumptions) and what would make them comparable.
4. **Cost view:** total annual premium plus a rough worst-case out-of-pocket per quote, showing the math.
5. **Questions for the broker or insurers** to close each gap.
6. **Summary:** which quote looks strongest for my priorities and why, with the trade-offs.

Format the extraction table so I can paste it straight into Excel or Google Sheets. This is general information; confirm terms with my broker before deciding.

title: Compare loan term sheets from different lenders side by side
description: A side-by-side comparison of financing offers by true cost, flexibility, and risk, with negotiation points.
content:
Help me compare financing term sheets from different lenders.

**Our situation:** [purpose of the financing, amount needed, current debt, cash flow profile]
**Term sheets:** [PASTE key terms for each: facility type, amount, interest rate and margin, fees (arrangement, commitment, exit, prepayment), tenor, amortization, security, covenants, warrants or equity kickers, reporting requirements]
**What matters most to us:** [e.g. flexibility to raise more, low cash cost, no personal guarantees]

Steps:
1. Calculate the all-in cost for each offer over the expected life, including fees and any equity value given away. State assumptions such as expected draw and repayment timing.
2. Compare flexibility: prepayment terms, covenant tightness against our forecast, restrictions on further debt, dividends, or acquisitions.
3. Compare risk: security and guarantees, cross-default, material adverse change clauses, change-of-control terms.

Return:
- A comparison table: Term | Lender A | Lender B | Lender C | Which is better and why.
- All-in annual cost for each.
- Red flags in each offer.
- The 5 most valuable points to negotiate with our preferred lender, with suggested asks.
- A recommendation with reasoning.

Use only terms I provide; mark unknowns [ASK LENDER]. Have legal counsel review the final documentation.

title: Compare my booking channel costs and plan a shift to direct bookings
description: Calculates net revenue by distribution channel and gives a realistic plan to grow direct bookings.
content:
Help me analyze my distribution channel costs and grow direct bookings.

**Room nights and revenue by channel (last 12 months):** [DIRECT WEB, PHONE/EMAIL, BOOKING.COM, EXPEDIA, GDS, WHOLESALE, GROUPS]

title: Compare my college financial aid offers side by side

Help me compare my college financial aid offers so I understand what each school will really cost.

title: Compare startup investor term sheets and what I'm giving up

Help me compare equity term sheets from investors.

title: Convert cash-basis books to accrual basis
description: Identifies and calculates the adjustments to move a set of cash-basis financials to accrual, with entries and a bridge.
content:
Help me convert a set of cash-basis financial statements to accrual basis.

**Why we're converting:** [e.g. "lender wants GAAP-basis statements", "investor due diligence", "monthly management reporting"]
**Period:** [DATES, plus opening date]
**Cash-basis P&L and balance sheet:** [PASTE]
**Unpaid customer invoices at start and end of period:** [AMOUNTS or AR aging]
**Unpaid bills at start and end:** [AMOUNTS or AP aging]
**Other items:** [prepaid expenses, accrued payroll and bonuses, customer deposits/deferred revenue, inventory, accrued interest, depreciation if not booked]

Steps:
1. For each item, calculate the opening and closing balance and the effect on the period's income (e.g. revenue + closing AR - opening AR).
2. Draft the adjusting entries, including the opening equity adjustment.
3. Build a bridge from cash-basis net income to accrual net income, item by item.
4. Flag items where I haven't given enough data, marked [NEED BALANCE].

Return:
1. An adjustments table: Item | Opening | Closing | P&L effect | Entry.
2. The cash-to-accrual net income bridge.
3. Adjusted P&L and balance sheet (only if all inputs are provided).
4. A short note on whether to keep accrual books going forward and what that requires monthly.

Note that tax reporting basis may differ from book basis - mark any tax implication as [TAX PREPARER TO CONFIRM].

title: Cost a menu dish and set its menu price
description: A recipe cost card with yields, food cost percentage, and price options that hit my target margin.
content:
Help me cost a dish and set its menu price.

**Dish and portion:** [NAME, PLATED PORTION SIZES]
**Recipe ingredients:** [EACH INGREDIENT, QUANTITY PER PORTION, PURCHASE UNIT AND PRICE - e.g. "salmon fillet 180 g; case 10 lb at $98"]
**Known yields or trim loss:** [e.g. "whole salmon yields 60% usable", or "unknown"]
**Garnish, sauce, bread, and sides served with it:** [DETAILS]
**Target food cost %:** [e.g. 28-32%]
**Comparable prices on my menu and nearby competitors:** [PRICES]
**Concept and price positioning:** [e.g. neighborhood bistro, fine dining]

Steps:
1. Convert each ingredient from as-purchased (AP) cost to edible-portion (EP) cost using the yield; where I have not given a yield, use a clearly labeled typical estimate and mark it [VERIFY BY YIELD TEST].
2. Build a cost card: ingredient, portion qty, AP unit cost, yield %, EP cost per portion.
3. Add a "Q factor" allowance (2-5%) for seasonings, oil, and waste, and say what I chose.
4. Calculate total plate cost and the price needed for my target food cost %.
5. Give three price options (e.g. ending in .00, .50, or psychological pricing that fits my concept), with the food cost % and gross profit dollars for each.
6. Note the dollar contribution margin, not just the percentage, and whether a higher-cost dish might still earn more per plate.

Return the cost card as a table, the price options table, and 3 ways to lower the plate cost without hurting the dish (portion, substitution, cross-utilization). Use only the prices I give; do not invent supplier prices.

title: Cost and price a multi-day tour package
description: A tour costing sheet with fixed and per-person costs, break-even group size, markup, and a sellable inclusions list.
content:
Help me cost and price a multi-day tour package.

**Tour outline:** [DAYS, DESTINATIONS, ACTIVITIES, ACCOMMODATION LEVEL]
**Supplier costs (net rates):** [HOTELS PER ROOM/NIGHT AND OCCUPANCY BASIS, TRANSPORT PER VEHICLE/DAY, GUIDES, ENTRANCE FEES, MEALS, INSURANCE]
**Group size range:** [MIN AND MAX PASSENGERS]
**Currency and exchange risk:** [SUPPLIER CURRENCIES vs. SELLING CURRENCY]
**Sales channels and commissions:** [direct, travel agents at X%, OTA at Y%]
**Target margin:** [e.g. 20-25% gross]
**Taxes or regulatory charges:** [e.g. VAT on margin, tourism levies - or "unsure"]

Steps:
1. Split costs into fixed per departure (vehicle, guide, tour leader comps) and variable per person (beds, meals, entries).
2. Calculate cost per person at several group sizes and the break-even group size.
3. Price per person on twin share, plus a single supplement calculated from actual single room costs.
4. Build in currency buffer and agent commission so margin holds on every channel; show net margin by channel.
5. Flag where a minimum numbers clause, final payment date, and cancellation scale are needed to protect the departure.
6. Write the inclusions and exclusions list as a guest would read it.

Return a costing table, a price table by group size and channel, the break-even point, and the inclusions/exclusions list. Use only supplier rates I give; mark gaps as [GET QUOTE]. Package travel rules and tax treatment vary by country; confirm with my accountant and any travel trade body I belong to.
variables: direct, travel agents at X%, OTA at Y%
e.g. VAT on margin, tourism levies - or "unsure"

title: Cut the number of days it takes to close the books each month
description: A diagnosis of the month-end close timeline with bottlenecks, quick wins, and a plan to close faster.
content:
Help me shorten our month-end close.

**Current close length:** [e.g. "business day 9"]
**Target:** [e.g. "business day 5"]
**Close task list:** [PASTE: task, owner, start day, end day, dependencies]
**Systems used:** [ERP, spreadsheets, reconciliation tools, consolidation]
**Known bottlenecks:** [e.g. late vendor invoices, manual intercompany, waiting on payroll]
**Team size and constraints:** [DETAILS]

Steps:
1. Map the critical path: which tasks determine the close date.
2. Identify bottlenecks and their causes: late inputs, manual work, rework, review queues, approvals.
3. Sort improvements into: move work before period end (pre-close), remove or simplify, automate, and change materiality thresholds or estimates.
4. Check that faster does not weaken controls: keep reviews and segregation of duties.

Return:
- A critical path summary.
- An improvement table: Change | Days saved | Effort | Risk | Owner | Timing.
- A revised close calendar by day.
- Metrics to track (days to close, post-close adjustments, late reconciliations).
- A 90-day rollout plan.

Base estimates on my task list; label estimated savings as estimates and mark unclear tasks [CONFIRM].
variables: PASTE: task, owner, start day, end day, dependencies

title: Decide whether to lease or buy an asset
description: A lease-versus-buy comparison on after-tax present value, plus the cash, accounting, and flexibility trade-offs.
content:
Help me decide whether to lease or buy an asset.

**Asset:** [WHAT, expected useful life]
**Purchase option:** [price, financing rate if borrowed, maintenance, residual value]
**Lease option:** [term, payments and timing, fees, maintenance included?, end-of-term options]
**Our discount rate / cost of debt:** [%]
**Tax rate and depreciation rules to apply:** [DETAILS - or "pre-tax only"]
**Other considerations:** [cash constraints, covenants, technology obsolescence risk, expected usage]

Steps:
1. Lay out after-tax cash flows for each option over the same period.
2. Calculate the present value of each and the difference.
3. Identify the break-even lease payment or residual value at which the decision flips.
4. Note how each option affects the balance sheet and reported EBITDA under the lease accounting standard I use [ASC 842 / IFRS 16], and any covenant effect.
5. Weigh qualitative factors: flexibility, upgrade path, maintenance risk, and cash preservation.

Return:
- A side-by-side cash flow table and PV summary.
- The break-even analysis.
- A short recommendation with the conditions under which it would change.

Treat tax and accounting treatment as general information to confirm with your accountant. Mark missing inputs [CONFIRM].

title: Design or clean up a chart of accounts
description: Produces a structured, right-sized chart of accounts with numbering, mapping from the old one, and rules to keep it from sprawling again.
content:
Help me design or clean up a chart of accounts.

**Business and industry:** [WHAT IT DOES, how it makes money]
**Size and complexity:** [revenue range, number of entities, locations, departments]
**Reporting needs:** [e.g. "P&L by location", "gross margin by product line", "grant tracking", "lender covenant reporting"]
**Framework and tax regime:** [US GAAP / IFRS, country, entity type]
**Current chart of accounts:** [PASTE, or "starting from scratch"]
**Accounting software:** [e.g. QuickBooks Online, Xero, NetSuite - and whether it supports classes, tracking categories, or dimensions]

Principles to apply:
- Use accounts for what the transaction is; use classes/departments/locations for where it happened. Don't create "Rent - Store 1", "Rent - Store 2".
- Group accounts so the statements roll up cleanly (assets, liabilities, equity, revenue, COGS, operating expenses, other income/expense).
- Keep enough detail for tax return lines and lender reporting, and no more.
- Leave numbering gaps for future accounts.

Return:
1. The proposed chart: Number | Account name | Type | Detail type/tax line | Notes.
2. Which dimensions (class, department, location, project) to use instead of extra accounts.
3. If I gave a current chart: a mapping table (Old account -> New account | Action: keep / merge / rename / inactivate) and the risks of merging accounts with history.
4. Five rules for adding new accounts in future.

Flag tax-line mapping as [CONFIRM WITH TAX PREPARER].
variables: WHAT IT DOES, how it makes money
revenue range, number of entities, locations, departments
US GAAP / IFRS, country, entity type

title: Document a financial model so someone else can run it
description: A model user guide covering structure, inputs, update steps, checks, and known limits for a clean handover.
content:
Help me document a financial model for handover.

**Model purpose and users:** [e.g. "monthly rolling forecast used by FP&A and the CFO"]
