Context: Learning objectives: [OBJECTIVES]. Content covered: [CONTENT]. Audience and level: [AUDIENCE]. Item formats allowed: [FORMATS]. Number of items and coverage weighting: [BLUEPRINT]. Stakes (formative / certification): [STAKES].

Task: Produce an assessment blueprint (objective x number of items x cognitive level), then the items: for each, the stem, options (with plausible distractors based on real misconceptions), the key, a one-line rationale for the key and for why each distractor is wrong, and the objective it assesses. Aim for application-level items, not just recall.

Format: Sections: Blueprint (table) | Items (numbered, each with stem/options/key/rationale/objective).

Verification: Flag items that are ambiguous, have grammatical give-aways, test recall of trivia, or do not map to an objective. Ensure exactly one defensible key each.

Validation: Answer a sample of items as a knowledgeable learner and as a guessing one: do the strong learners pass and can the items be gamed? Fix any that can.

title: Create a rubric and give feedback on student work
description: Clear rubrics and consistent, constructive feedback on assignments.
content:
Help me assess student work.

**Assignment and level:** [DESCRIPTION, grade/course]
**Rubric (paste) or "create one":** [RUBRIC]
**Student work:** [PASTE — remove names and personal details]

If no rubric is provided, first create one: 4–5 criteria, 4 performance levels each, with clear descriptors.

Then for the work: score each criterion with a quoted example as evidence, give 2 strengths and 2 specific improvements (with how to fix them), and a short, encouraging summary addressed to the student.

The final grade is the teacher's decision — treat this as a draft.
variables: PASTE — remove names and personal details

title: Create an apprentice training plan toward journeyman licensure
description: A structured on-the-job training plan that tracks required hours, skills, and classroom work for an apprentice in my trade.
content:
Help me create a training plan for an apprentice in my trade.

**Trade:** [ELECTRICAL / PLUMBING / HVAC / CARPENTRY / OTHER]
**State and licensing path:** [STATE, REGISTERED APPRENTICESHIP OR NOT, LICENSE GOAL - e.g. journeyman electrician]
**Hour and classroom requirements I know about:** [e.g. "8,000 OJT hours, 576 classroom" - or "not sure"]
**Apprentice's current level:** [YEAR, HOURS LOGGED, SKILLS ALREADY SIGNED OFF]
**Type of work my company does:** [e.g. "residential new construction and service", "commercial tenant improvements"]
**Who supervises and mentors:** [JOURNEYMAN/MASTER NAMES OR ROLES, SUPERVISION RATIO RULES]

Build:
1. A skills matrix grouped by work process (e.g. for electrical: safety, layout and rough-in, service and panels, conduit bending, troubleshooting, controls, code), with levels: Observed, Assisted, Did with supervision, Competent.
2. A phase plan by year or by hour band, showing which skills to target and which job types give that exposure. Note where my company's work leaves gaps and how to fill them (rotation, partner company, classroom labs).
3. A monthly check-in template: hours logged by work process, skills signed off, safety notes, goals for next month.
4. Safety milestones before more independence (e.g. lockout/tagout, ladder and fall protection, trenching awareness).
5. A hour-log format that matches what licensing boards typically ask for, with a note to confirm the exact form.

Rules:
- Hour requirements, supervision ratios, and what counts toward licensure vary by state and program. Mark every requirement as [VERIFY WITH STATE BOARD OR APPRENTICESHIP SPONSOR].
- Apply evaluation standards the same way to every apprentice.
variables: e.g. "8,000 OJT hours, 576 classroom" - or "not sure"
YEAR, HOURS LOGGED, SKILLS ALREADY SIGNED OFF
JOURNEYMAN/MASTER NAMES OR ROLES, SUPERVISION RATIO RULES
VERIFY WITH STATE BOARD OR APPRENTICESHIP SPONSOR

title: Create discussion or critical-thinking questions
description: Questions that spark real discussion for classes, book clubs, or workshops.
content:
Create discussion questions.

**Topic, text, or video:** [DETAILS]
**Group:** [students (age/level) / book club / team workshop]
**Goal:** [comprehension / critical thinking / debate / personal reflection]
**Time:** [MINUTES]

Give me 12 questions moving from easy to deep: 3 recall/understanding, 4 analysis ("why", "how"), 3 evaluation/debate (no single right answer), and 2 personal connection. For the best 3, add follow-up prompts to keep the discussion going.

title: Create flashcards and memory aids
description: Spaced-repetition-ready flashcards and memory techniques for anything you need to remember.
content:
Create flashcards from this material.

**Topic and exam/goal:** [DETAILS]
**Material:** [PASTE NOTES, TEXT, OR TERMS]
**Format:** [plain Q/A / Anki-ready CSV / cloze deletions]
**Number of cards:** [NUMBER]

Rules:
- One fact or concept per card; questions that test understanding, not just recognition.
- Mix card types: definition, why/how, example, comparison, application.
- Add a memory aid (mnemonic, analogy, or image) for the 5 hardest cards.
- Use only facts from my material.

Return the cards in the requested format.
variables: plain Q/A / Anki-ready CSV / cloze deletions

title: Create scenario-based compliance training questions
description: Writes realistic workplace scenarios with answer options and explanations that test judgment, not memory of policy wording.
content:
Help me create scenario-based questions for compliance training.

**Topic:** [e.g. anti-bribery, data protection, insider trading, harassment, sanctions, information security]
**Audience:** [ROLES, seniority, regions]
**Policy or rule to test:** [PASTE key sections]
**Mistakes we actually see:** [from incidents, audits, or hotline reports - anonymized]
**Number of questions:** [e.g. 10]
**Format:** [multiple choice / branching scenario / discussion prompts for a live session]

For each question give:
1. **Scenario** - 3-5 sentences, set in this audience's real work, with fictional names and realistic pressures (deadlines, a senior person asking, a customer relationship at stake).
2. **Question** - what should you do?
3. **Options** - 4 choices, all plausible; wrong answers should reflect real-world rationalizations, not obviously silly choices.
4. **Correct answer and explanation** - why, citing the policy section, and what to do next (who to contact).
5. **Why the tempting wrong answer is wrong.**

Also:
- Mix difficulty: about 30% straightforward, 50% judgment calls, 20% genuinely gray areas where the right answer is "ask compliance".
- Include at least one scenario about speaking up and one where a manager is involved.
- Avoid stereotypes in names, roles, and regions.
- End with a short list of what learners should remember.
variables: from incidents, audits, or hotline reports - anonymized

title: Define a competency framework
description: Competencies with proficiency levels and observable behaviors.
content:
Role: Act as a capability building lead defining a competency framework for a job family.

Context: Job family and roles it covers: [JOB_FAMILY]. Strategic capabilities the business needs from it: [STRATEGIC_CAPABILITIES]. Existing frameworks or inputs: [EXISTING_INPUTS]. Number of proficiency levels wanted: [LEVELS]. How it will be used (hiring, development, promotion): [USE]. Constraints: [CONSTRAINTS].

Goal: Produce a framework specific enough that two managers would rate the same person similarly and that connects directly to development and progression decisions.

Task: Produce: 6-9 competencies grouped into 2-3 clusters; a one-paragraph definition per competency (observable, not abstract); behavioural anchors at each proficiency level (what a person at that level actually does, with an example); the anchors that typically distinguish adjacent levels; and guidance on evidence sources for assessment.

Constraints: Anchors must describe observable behaviour and outputs, not traits or attitudes. Adjacent levels must be genuinely distinguishable, not just 'more' of the same adjective. Keep the whole framework usable in under ~1200 words. Align verbs to how it will be used.

Examples: Anchor shape: 'Level 3 - Independently leads [X] across teams; anticipates [risk] and adjusts; e.g. redesigned [process] reducing [metric].' Level distinction: 'L2->L3 = shifts from executing within a team to coordinating across teams.'

Format: Sections: Cluster & competency list | Per-competency (definition + level anchors + level distinctions) | Assessment evidence guidance.

Verification: Flag any anchor that is a trait not a behaviour, and any adjacent pair that a rater could not tell apart.

Validation: Apply the framework to one real person you describe: can you place them at a level with evidence, and does the next level give a clear development target? Sharpen where it is fuzzy.

title: Design a course delivered over WhatsApp
description: A messaging-first course plan with bite-size lessons, a sending schedule, engagement tactics, and assessments that work in chat.
content:
Help me design a course that runs entirely over WhatsApp (or a similar messaging app).

**Topic and outcome:** [what learners should be able to do by the end]
**Learners:** [who they are, their devices, data costs, literacy and language]
**Group size and format:** [one-to-one broadcast / community group / small cohorts]
**Length and pace:** [e.g. "3 weeks, one lesson a day"]
**My tools:** [regular app / business app / automation or chatbot tool / none]
**Free or paid:** [and how people sign up]

Plan:
1. **Curriculum:** modules and daily lessons, each with one clear objective.
2. **Lesson format:** what each lesson looks like in chat - a short text, a voice note under 2 minutes, an image or short video, and one task. Keep files small for low-data users.
3. **Schedule:** what goes out when, plus reminders and catch-up messages for people who fall behind.
4. **Engagement:** prompts for replies, peer discussion rules, accountability, and how I'll keep the group from getting noisy.
5. **Assessment and feedback:** quick quizzes, voice or photo submissions, and how I'll give feedback without being overwhelmed.
6. **Operations:** onboarding message, group rules, opt-out handling, moderation, and accessibility.
7. **Privacy:** members' phone numbers are visible in groups - recommend options to protect them and how to get consent.

Return a course overview, a day-by-day schedule table (Day | Objective | Message content | Format | Learner task), the first 3 lessons written out, and the welcome message.
variables: what learners should be able to do by the end
one-to-one broadcast / community group / small cohorts
e.g. "3 weeks, one lesson a day"

title: Design a course or training program
description: Course outline, modules, objectives, activities, and assessments from a learning need.
content:
Role: Act as an instructional designer applying backward design.

Context: Learning need / performance gap: [LEARNING_NEED]. Audience and prior knowledge: [AUDIENCE]. Modality and total duration: [MODALITY_DURATION]. Constraints (tools, SME time, budget): [CONSTRAINTS]. Business outcome it should support: [BUSINESS_OUTCOME].

Task: Produce: 3-5 measurable learning objectives (observable verbs, tied to the performance gap); a module map with each module's objective, key content points, and one active learning method; an assessment plan aligned to each objective (formative and summative); and the SME inputs still needed.

Format: Sections: Objectives | Module map (table) | Assessment plan | SME inputs needed. ~450 words.

Verification: Check every objective is observable and assessable, and that each module and assessment maps to an objective (flag orphans). Fits within the stated duration.

Validation: Test against the performance gap: if a learner completed this, would they actually be able to do the thing on the job? Note the weakest link.

title: Design a project-based learning unit around a real driving question
description: A PBL unit with a driving question, authentic product, milestones, scaffolded lessons, teamwork structures, and assessment.
content:
Help me design a project-based learning unit.

**Subject and level:** [e.g. "7th grade science", "upper-division urban planning"]
**Standards or outcomes to cover:** [LIST]
**Length:** [e.g. "4 weeks, 3 sessions per week"]
**Real-world connections available:** [local issues, partners, community experts, clients]
**Constraints:** [budget, technology, group size, students' independence]

Design:
1. **Driving question:** 3 options that are open-ended, relevant to students, and require the target content to answer. Recommend one.
2. **Final product and audience:** what students create and who outside the class will see it.
3. **Milestones:** 4-6 checkpoints with deliverables and dates, each with a feedback moment (peer critique, teacher conference, expert feedback).
4. **Teaching plan:** the mini-lessons and workshops students need, placed just before they need each skill.
5. **Team structures:** team size, roles, a team contract outline, and how to handle uneven contribution.
6. **Assessment:** what is graded individually vs. as a team, with success criteria tied to the standards.

Watch for the common failure where the project is fun but the content is thin: for each standard, point to the milestone where it is taught and assessed. Return the plan as sections with a calendar table at the end.
variables: local issues, partners, community experts, clients
budget, technology, group size, students' independence

title: Design a training program for new people managers
description: Builds a practical new-manager development program covering core people skills, HR essentials, and practice-based sessions.
content:
Help me design a training program for newly promoted or newly hired people managers.

**Audience:** [number of managers, experience level, in-person or remote]
**Common problems we see with new managers:** [e.g. avoiding feedback, poor documentation, unclear delegation, mishandling sensitive disclosures]
**HR processes they must know:** [e.g. performance reviews, leave requests, hiring, discipline, accommodations]
**Time available:** [e.g. 6 sessions of 90 minutes over 3 months]
**Delivery resources:** [facilitators, budget, LMS]

Design:
1. **Learning outcomes** - what managers will be able to do afterward (observable).
2. **Program outline** - session titles, objectives, and timing. Cover: role shift from peer to manager, 1:1s, feedback, setting expectations, documentation, hiring fairly, handling performance issues, legal basics (what to escalate to HR), team wellbeing, and leading through change.
3. **For each session** - a practice activity (role-play scenario, case study, or real-work assignment), not just content.
4. **"When to call HR" quick-reference card** - situations like harassment disclosures, health issues, leave requests, threats.
5. **Between-session application tasks** and manager-of-manager involvement.
6. **Measurement** - how to evaluate impact (behavior change, team engagement, ER case trends) beyond satisfaction surveys.

Keep it practical and scenario-based, using situations a manager in my organization would actually face.
variables: number of managers, experience level, in-person or remote
e.g. 6 sessions of 90 minutes over 3 months

title: Design a workshop activity or discussion
description: Engaging activities and discussions that achieve a specific learning outcome.
content:
Role: Act as a workshop facilitator designing a single active learning activity.

Context: Learning point the activity must land: [LEARNING_POINT]. Group size and setup: [GROUP_SETUP]. Time available: [TIME]. Materials available: [MATERIALS]. Energy level / point in the day: [CONTEXT].

Task: Design the activity: a one-line purpose, setup, step-by-step participant instructions, timing per step, the facilitator's role during it, 3-4 debrief questions that connect it to the learning point, and a lower-tech or shorter variation.

Format: Sections: Purpose | Setup | Instructions (timed steps) | Facilitator role | Debrief questions | Variation.

title: Design deliberate practice drills for a skill I'm learning
description: Focused drills with clear success criteria, fast feedback, and a way to raise the difficulty as you improve.
content:
Design deliberate practice drills for a skill I'm learning.

**Skill and the sub-skill I'm working on now:** [e.g. "guitar - clean chord changes", "Spanish - past tense in conversation"]
**My current level:** [WHAT I CAN DO NOW, or my latest benchmark result]
**Session length and frequency:** [e.g. "30 minutes, 5 days a week"]
**Feedback I can get:** [e.g. "record myself", "a coach every two weeks", "online community", "answer keys"]
**Tools or materials I have:** [LIST]
**Resources I'm using (optional):** [PASTE FROM STEP 2]

Design principles to follow:
- Each drill targets one narrow sub-skill, just beyond what I can do comfortably.
- Every drill has a measurable success criterion (e.g. "8 out of 10 clean changes at 60 bpm").
- Feedback arrives fast, ideally within the session.
- Repetition with variation, so I don't just memorize one version.
- A clear rule for when to make it harder (e.g. after hitting the criterion in two sessions in a row).
- Avoid drills that feel productive but mostly repeat what I can already do.

Return:
1. 4-6 drills in a table: Drill | Sub-skill it targets | How to do it | Success criterion | How I get feedback | How to make it harder.
2. A sample week showing how to combine drills in my session length, including a short warm-up and a quick review of the previous session.
3. A practice log template: Date | Drill | Reps | Success rate | What went wrong | Next adjustment.

This is step 3 of the "Teach yourself a new skill in 90 days" pack. It works on its own, and can use the resources chosen in step 2.
variables: WHAT I CAN DO NOW, or my latest benchmark result

title: Diagnose my admissions test practice results by question type
description: Accuracy and timing by question type, your biggest point opportunities ranked, and a focus plan for the next two weeks.
content:
Diagnose my GRE, GMAT, LSAT, or similar practice test results by question type.

**Test:** [NAME]
**Practice test source:** [e.g. "official practice test 1" - official tests give the most reliable estimate]
**Section scores and total:** [SCORES]
**Target score:** [PASTE FROM STEP 1, or state it]
**Question-level results:** [FOR EACH QUESTION OR GROUP: question type, right/wrong, time spent - paste the score report export if you have it]
**How it felt:** [e.g. "ran out of time in quant", "guessed a lot on reading"]

Steps:
1. Group results by question type and calculate accuracy and average time for each.
2. Classify wrong answers where possible: didn't know the content, misread, fell for a trap answer, ran out of time, or guessed.
3. Rank point opportunities: how often a question type appears x how far my accuracy is from what my target score requires.
4. Separate quick wins (careless errors, timing) from longer builds (content gaps).
5. Check for timing problems: types where I spend far longer than average for low accuracy.

Return:
- A table: Question type | Questions | Accuracy | Avg time | Main error type | Priority.
- The top 3 point opportunities with why.
- Quick wins I can apply on the next test.
- A two-week focus plan: which question types to drill on which days, and when to take the next practice test.

Work only from the data I give; if the data is too thin for a conclusion, say so. This is step 2 of the "Prepare for a graduate admissions test" pack. It works on its own, and can use the target from step 1.
variables: PASTE FROM STEP 1, or state it
e.g. "ran out of time in quant", "guessed a lot on reading"

title: Explain a concept simply — at any level
description: Clear explanations using analogies and examples, from 'explain like I'm 10' to expert.
content:
Act as an expert teacher who explains complex topics using strong mental models.

**Context**
I am new to [CONCEPT] and want genuine understanding rather than memorization.

**Task**
Explain the concept from intuitive understanding to accurate technical understanding. Start with an analogy, then explain the actual mechanism, show a practical example, clarify misconceptions, and connect it to adjacent concepts.

**Format**
Use:
1. Simple explanation
2. Analogy
3. How it actually works
4. Example
5. Common misconception
6. When it matters
7. Quick test

**Concept:** [PASTE]

title: Explain internet slang, memes, or trends I don't understand
description: Plain-English meaning, origin, how people actually use a term or meme, and whether it is safe to use yourself.
content:
Explain some internet slang, a meme, or an online trend to me.

**Term, phrase, or meme:** [WHAT I SAW - paste it or describe it]
**Where I saw it:** [e.g. "my teenager's group chat", "TikTok comments", "a coworker's Slack message", "a news headline"]
**The exact context:** [the sentence or post it appeared in, if I have it]
**Why I'm asking:** [just curious / want to reply / worried about my kid / thinking about using it at work or in marketing]

For each term, give me:
1. **Meaning in plain English,** including what it means in the context I shared. If it has several meanings, list them and say which one fits.
2. **Where it came from,** briefly.
3. **How it's used:** tone (joking, sarcastic, affectionate, insulting), who tends to use it, and 2 example sentences.
4. **Should I use it?** Whether it would sound natural or awkward coming from me, given my situation.
5. **Flags:** whether it has an offensive, sexual, drug-related, or hateful second meaning, or is linked to harmful challenges. Say so plainly if it does.

Rules:
- Slang changes fast. If you're unsure, or the term may be newer than your knowledge, say so rather than guessing, and suggest how I can check.
- If I'm a parent worried about safety, end with a calm way to bring it up with my child.
- If I'm considering it for marketing, note the risk of sounding forced or out of date.
variables: WHAT I SAW - paste it or describe it
the sentence or post it appeared in, if I have it

title: Find common misconceptions in a class set of student work and plan a reteach
description: Turns a stack of student responses into error patterns, likely misconceptions, student groups, and a targeted reteach lesson.
content:
Help me analyze a class set of student work and plan what to reteach.

**Task or question students answered:** [PASTE IT]
**The correct answer or exemplary response:** [PASTE IT]
**Student responses:** [PASTE, using initials or numbers only - or summarize, e.g. "11 of 28 added denominators"]
**Grade or course level:** [LEVEL]
**Time I have to reteach:** [e.g. "20 minutes tomorrow"]

Analyze:
1. Sort responses into: correct with sound reasoning, correct with weak or lucky reasoning, partially correct, and incorrect.
2. For incorrect and partial responses, name the specific error pattern and the misconception that most likely causes it. Separate careless slips from conceptual gaps.
3. Count how many students show each pattern. Use only the work I provided; don't assume.

Then plan:
- A small-group or whole-class decision based on the counts.
- A reteach activity for each main misconception that targets the faulty idea directly (e.g. a contrasting-cases task, a worked example with an error to find), not a repeat of the original lesson.
- An extension for students who already have it.
- 3 follow-up check questions to confirm the misconception is fixed.

Return a table: Pattern | Likely misconception | # students | Students | Reteach move. Then the reteach plan in steps with timings.

title: Find out whether training will actually fix a performance problem
description: A performance consulting plan to diagnose a training request, uncover the real cause, and recommend training or something better.
content:
Help me respond to a training request by diagnosing whether training is the right fix.

**The request as it was given to me:** [e.g. "Can you run a customer service course for the call center?"]
**Who asked and why now:** [REQUESTER and trigger]
**The business problem or metric:** [e.g. "complaint rate up 20% this quarter"]
**What I know about the people involved:** [roles, tenure, recent changes]
**Deadline or pressure:** [DETAILS]

Use a performance consulting approach (similar to action mapping or Gilbert's Behavior Engineering Model):
1. Restate the business goal as a measurable result.
2. Identify what people need to do differently on the job to reach it.
3. For each behavior, test the likely causes: lack of skill or knowledge, unclear expectations, missing feedback, poor tools or processes, conflicting incentives, workload, or motivation. Only a skill or knowledge gap is fixed by training.

Return:
1. Questions to ask the requester in a 30-minute intake conversation, in order.
2. A short list of data or people I should check before agreeing to build anything.
3. A diagnosis table: Behavior | Likely cause | Evidence needed | Best solution (training, job aid, process fix, manager action, other).
4. A recommendation I can share with the requester, including what training can and cannot achieve here.
5. A polite, non-defensive script for redirecting the request if training is not the answer.

title: Find out why I lost points on a test and fix the gaps
description: An error analysis of your graded test that sorts mistakes by cause and builds a short plan to fix them.
content:
Help me analyze a graded test so I understand why I lost points and don't repeat it.

**Subject and topic:** [e.g. "chemistry - stoichiometry unit test"]
**Questions I got wrong or partly wrong:** [For each: the question, my answer, the correct answer or teacher's comment]
**How I studied:** [WHAT YOU DID, HOW LONG, WHEN]
**Next test or final:** [DATE AND WHAT IT COVERS]

For each missed question, help me classify the cause:
- **Concept gap:** I didn't understand the idea.
- **Procedure error:** I knew the idea but made a mistake in the steps.
- **Careless error:** misread, arithmetic slip, skipped part of the question.
- **Test strategy:** ran out of time, didn't show work, left it blank.
- **Studied the wrong thing:** it wasn't in my notes or practice.

Ask me a short question when you can't tell which cause it was rather than guessing.

Return:
1. A table: Question | What went wrong | Cause | How to fix it.
2. The pattern: which cause cost me the most points.
3. A study plan for the next test that targets those causes (e.g. practice problems for procedure errors, a checklist for careless ones).
4. One question to ask my teacher, if any are still unclear.

Don't redo the test answers for me; explain the idea behind each mistake and let me correct it.
variables: WHAT YOU DID, HOW LONG, WHEN

title: Find the patterns in my practice exam mistakes
description: Your missed questions sorted by cause, with the top fixes, the topics to restudy, and a readiness verdict.
content:
Analyze my practice exam mistakes and find the patterns behind them.

**Exam:** [CERTIFICATION NAME]
**Practice score and passing target:** [e.g. "64%, aiming for 75%+"]
**Results by domain (if available):** [PASTE]
**Missed questions:** [FOR EACH: topic, my answer, correct answer, and why I chose mine - a few words is fine]
**Time used vs. time allowed:** [DETAILS]
**Readiness checklist (optional):** [PASTE FROM STEP 1]

Steps:
1. Classify each miss by cause: knowledge gap, misread the question, fell for a distractor, overthought or changed a correct answer, applied workplace habit instead of the exam's framework, time pressure, or careless error.
2. Count the causes and find the top 3 patterns.
3. Separate content problems (need to study) from test-taking problems (need a technique).
4. Rank topics to restudy by how many points they cost me and their exam weight.

Return:
- A table: Question/topic | Cause | Content or technique | Fix.
- Top 3 patterns, each with a specific fix (e.g. "underline the qualifier: FIRST, BEST, LEAST before reading options").
- Ranked restudy list.
- Updated confidence ratings for my step 1 checklist, if I pasted it.
- A retest plan: what to review and when to take the next practice exam.
- An honest readiness verdict: on track, borderline, or not yet, based only on the data I've given.

This is step 4 of the "Pass a professional certification exam" pack. It works on its own, and can use the practice questions from step 3 or any practice exam.

title: Find the right books for a child
description: Book suggestions matched to a child's age, reading level, interests, and sensitivities, plus how to tell if a book fits.
content:
Help me find books that fit a specific child or group of children.

**Child or group:** [AGE or grade, number of children if a class]
**Reading level:** [e.g. "reads early chapter books independently", "reluctant reader", "level from school if known"]
**How the book will be read:** [read-aloud / independent / classroom / bedtime]
**Interests:** [TOPICS, favorite books or shows]
**Purpose:** [fun, a learning topic, a life event such as a new sibling or moving, building reading confidence]
**Sensitivities or needs:** [e.g. "anxious about scary content", "dyslexia", "grief", "family values on certain topics"]
**Representation I'd like:** [e.g. "characters who look like my child", "different family structures", "disability"]
**Format and budget:** [library, ebook, audiobook, buying]

Give me:
1. 8-12 suggestions in a table: Title | Author | Format (picture book, early reader, chapter book, graphic novel, middle grade) | Why it fits | Content notes | Stretch or comfort read.
2. How to check fit in 2 minutes: the five-finger test or similar for independent reading, and what to look for in content.
3. Ways to keep a reluctant reader going: series, audiobooks, graphic novels, choice.
4. Where to find more: library services, award lists, and librarian recommendations.

Rules: only recommend books you are confident exist and are correctly attributed; if unsure, say so and mark [VERIFY]. Do not guess reading levels; describe them in general terms. Remind me to preview books on sensitive topics before sharing them with the child.
variables: AGE or grade, number of children if a class

title: Gamify a training program with rewards that actually motivate
description: A game-mechanics design for a training program, matched to your learners, that rewards real learning instead of clicks.
content:
Help me add game mechanics and rewards to a training program so learners stay engaged and actually build the skill.

**Program:** [topic, format (e-learning, workshop, blended), length]
**Skill or behavior it must build:** [SPECIFIC SKILL]
**Learners:** [roles, experience, age range, what motivates them, how much time they have]
**Current problem:** [e.g. low completion, people click through, no practice]
**Platform and budget:** [LMS features available, budget for prizes or none]

Design:
1. **Motivation fit:** Which motivators suit these learners (mastery, progress, autonomy, social recognition, competition, tangible rewards), and which could backfire. Note that competitive leaderboards can discourage lower performers.
2. **Core loop:** what learners do, the feedback they get, and how difficulty increases.
3. **Mechanics tied to the skill:** e.g. scenario challenges, levels unlocked by demonstrated mastery, streaks for spaced practice, team quests. Every point or badge must reward evidence of learning or application, not just logins or time spent.
4. **Rewards:** intrinsic and extrinsic options, at no or low cost, and how to avoid rewards replacing interest.
5. **Fairness and inclusion:** opt-out options, accessibility, and no penalties that embarrass people publicly.
6. **Measurement:** how to tell if it worked (skill assessment, behavior on the job, completion, voluntary return).

Return: a one-paragraph concept, a table of mechanics (mechanic, skill it reinforces, how it's earned, risk), and a pilot plan for one cohort.
variables: e.g. low completion, people click through, no practice
LMS features available, budget for prizes or none

title: Generate past-paper-style exam questions with a marking scheme
description: New questions that match your exam's style and mark allocation, with a marking scheme and model answers at the end.
content:
Write new practice questions in the style of my final exam, with a marking scheme.

**Course and topic(s):** [DETAILS]
**Sample past paper questions:** [PASTE 2-3 REAL QUESTIONS SO YOU CAN MATCH THE STYLE, or describe the format]
**Question types and marks:** [e.g. "10-mark short answer", "25-mark essay", "multi-part calculation"]
**Number of questions:** [e.g. 4]
**My notes or ranked topic list (optional):** [PASTE - or the priorities from step 1]

Rules:
- Match the command words (explain, evaluate, compare, calculate), length, and difficulty of the samples.
- Test understanding and application, not just recall, unless the sample questions are recall-based.
- Stay within the topics and material I've given. Flag anything that goes beyond it.
- These are practice questions. Don't present them as likely exam questions.

Return:
1. The questions, with marks and a suggested time per question based on the exam's marks-per-minute.
2. Then, clearly separated, a marking scheme showing where marks are awarded (points, steps, or level descriptors for essays).
3. Then, a model answer or outline for each question.
4. Then, common ways students lose marks on each question.

Put the marking scheme and answers well below the questions so I can attempt them first under timed conditions. This is step 2 of the "Ace your university final exams" pack. It works on its own, and can use the ranked topic list from step 1 to choose topics.
variables: PASTE - or the priorities from step 1

title: Get step-by-step hints on a homework problem without the answer
description: Guided hints that get you unstuck one step at a time, so you solve the problem yourself.
content:
Help me work through a homework problem by giving me hints, not the answer.

**The problem:** [PASTE IT EXACTLY]
**Subject and level:** [e.g. "Algebra 2", "college physics I", "intro chemistry"]
**What I've tried so far:** [YOUR WORK, even if it's wrong]
**Where I'm stuck:** [e.g. "I don't know which formula to use"]

How to help:
1. First, ask me what I think the problem is asking and what I already know.
2. Give one hint at a time, starting small (e.g. "What units does the answer need?"). Wait for my reply before the next hint.
3. If my work has a mistake, point to the line and ask me to check it rather than correcting it.
4. Use a similar practice problem with different numbers if I need to see a method demonstrated.
5. After I reach an answer, ask me how I'd check it (estimate, units, plug back in).

Hint ladder: concept reminder, then which approach to use, then the next step to try, then a worked similar example. Never jump to the final answer for my actual problem, even if I ask; offer the next hint instead.

At the end, give me a 2-line summary of the method so I can use it on the next problem, and one similar practice problem to try on my own.
variables: YOUR WORK, even if it's wrong
e.g. "I don't know which formula to use"

title: Get the key ideas from a book
description: Main ideas, frameworks, examples, and how to apply them — without spoilers if you prefer.
content:
Summarize the key ideas of [BOOK TITLE] by [AUTHOR].

**Why I'm interested:** [GOAL — e.g. deciding whether to read it, applying it at work, revising]
**Depth:** [one page / chapter by chapter]

Include:
1. The core thesis in 2–3 sentences.
2. The main ideas or frameworks, each with the author's best example.
3. What's genuinely useful vs. what's dated or debated.
4. How I could apply it, given my goal.
5. Who should read the full book and who can skip it.

If you're not confident about this specific book's content, say so rather than inventing details. Summaries don't replace the book — I'll support the author if it's useful.

title: Give me work problems to solve before showing the answer
description: Realistic practice problems one at a time, with hints only when you ask and the full solution after your attempt.
content:
Give me practice problems for a work skill and make me solve them before you show the answer.

**Skill or topic:** [e.g. "Excel lookups", "pricing calculations", "writing SQL joins", "prioritizing a backlog"]
**My role and the kind of problems I face:** [CONTEXT]
**My level:** [beginner / intermediate / advanced]
**Number of problems:** [e.g. 5]

Rules:
1. Give one problem at a time, based on a realistic work situation, with all the data I need (use made-up but plausible data and label it as sample data).
2. Then stop and wait for my attempt. Do not show the answer or hints yet.
3. If I type "hint", give the smallest useful nudge. Allow up to 3 hints, each a bit more specific.
4. After my attempt:
   - Say whether it is correct and why.
   - Show a model solution with the reasoning step by step.
   - If my approach was different but valid, say so.
   - Name the specific mistake if I made one, and the rule that prevents it.
5. Make the next problem slightly harder if I got it right, or similar if I did not.

After the last problem, summarize:
- Problems solved without hints, with hints, and missed.
- Patterns in my mistakes.
- One more problem targeting my weakest area.

Start with problem 1.

title: Handle a suspected cheating or AI-misuse case fairly
description: Organizes evidence, plans a fair student conversation, and drafts documentation that follows your institution's process.
content:
Help me handle a suspected academic integrity issue fairly and by the book.

**What I noticed:** [e.g. "two submissions share identical unusual errors", "essay style very different from in-class writing"] (use initials, not names)
**The assignment and its rules:** [PASTE INSTRUCTIONS AND COLLABORATION OR AI POLICY]
**Evidence I have:** [DESCRIBE - drafts, version history, comparisons, sources]
**My institution's process:** [PASTE POLICY OR DESCRIBE - e.g. "faculty must report all cases to the integrity office before deciding any penalty"]
**Student history I'm aware of:** [e.g. "none"]

Help me:
1. Separate what the evidence actually shows from what I'm inferring. List innocent explanations I should rule out (allowed collaboration, shared tutoring, common sources, language support).
2. Note any evidence that is weak, including AI-detector scores, which are not reliable proof on their own.
3. Plan a conversation with the student: an opening that is neutral and not accusatory, open questions (e.g. "Walk me through how you wrote this section"), and what to do if they admit, deny, or get upset.
4. Draft a factual written record of the incident and the conversation.
5. Check my next steps against the policy I pasted, including deadlines and who must be notified.

Do not decide the outcome for me. If the policy requires reporting before talking to the student, say so first. This is general guidance; follow your institution's procedures.
variables: PASTE INSTRUCTIONS AND COLLABORATION OR AI POLICY
DESCRIBE - drafts, version history, comparisons, sources

title: Handle disruptive or disengaged participants in training
description: A practical playbook of facilitator responses for dominating, cynical, silent, distracted, or hostile participants, in person or online.
content:
Help me prepare to handle difficult participant behavior in a training session I facilitate.

**Session:** [TOPIC, LENGTH, FORMAT - in person / virtual / hybrid]
**Group:** [SIZE, ROLES, seniority mix, whether attendance is mandatory]
**Behaviors I expect or have seen:** [e.g. "one senior manager dominates", "cameras off and silent", "cynicism: we've done this before", "side conversations", "challenging my expertise"]
**Sensitivities:** [e.g. "recent layoffs", "topic is controversial"]

For each behavior, give me:
- Likely reasons behind it (e.g. the person feels the session is irrelevant, unsafe, or a waste of their time).
- Prevention: what I can do in the design or opening to make it less likely.
- A light-touch response in the moment (exact words I can use).
- An escalated response if it continues.
- A private conversation script for a break.

Also include:
1. Opening moves that reduce problems: setting agreements, linking to their real challenges, acknowledging mandatory attendance honestly.
2. Virtual-specific techniques: chat, polls, breakouts, named invitations without putting people on the spot.
3. What to do if someone becomes upset or a conversation turns personal or hostile, including when to pause the session.
4. How to handle a question I cannot answer.

Keep responses respectful and non-shaming. If a situation involves harassment, discrimination, or a safety concern, tell me to stop and follow my organization's reporting process.
variables: TOPIC, LENGTH, FORMAT - in person / virtual / hybrid
SIZE, ROLES, seniority mix, whether attendance is mandatory

title: Help my child with homework without doing it for them
description: Coaching questions and a homework routine that build your child's independence instead of handing them answers.
content:
Help me support my child with homework in a way that builds their own skills.

**Child's grade:** [GRADE]
**Subject and assignment:** [PASTE THE TASK OR DESCRIBE IT]
**Where they're stuck:** [e.g. "doesn't know how to start", "gets the steps wrong", "refuses"]
**How I feel about this subject:** [confident / rusty / never learned it this way]

Give me:
1. A quick explanation of the concept for me (the parent), in plain language, including how it is commonly taught today if it differs from older methods.
2. 5-8 coaching questions I can ask, from gentle hints to bigger nudges, that lead my child to the answer without giving it.
3. One similar practice example (not the homework itself) that we can work through together.
4. Signs my child truly understands versus just copying a pattern.
5. A note to the teacher, if needed, explaining where my child got stuck (2-3 sentences).

Also suggest a simple homework routine: time, place, breaks, and what to do when frustration rises. Do not solve the actual assignment questions for me to copy. If the work seems far above my child's level or they struggle across many subjects, suggest raising it with the teacher.
variables: PASTE THE TASK OR DESCRIBE IT
confident / rusty / never learned it this way

title: Learn any topic efficiently
description: A structured mini-course on any topic: roadmap, core concepts, examples, mistakes, and practice.
content:
Act as an expert instructor and learning designer.

**Context**
I want practical working knowledge of [TOPIC]. My current level is [LEVEL], and I can spend [TIME] learning.

**Task**
Teach the essential concepts in the order that will create the most useful mental model. Explain each with an intuitive example, a workplace application, a common mistake, and a short practice activity.

**Format**
Return:
- Learning roadmap
- Core concepts
- Practical examples
- Common mistakes
- Practice exercises
- Mastery check

**Topic:** [PASTE]

title: Learn by being questioned (Socratic tutor)
description: A tutor that asks you one question at a time and only helps as much as you need.
content:
Act as a patient Socratic tutor and expert coach.

**Context**
I want to learn [TOPIC] by thinking through questions rather than receiving a lecture.

**Task**
Ask me one question at a time. Evaluate my response, identify misconceptions, give only the amount of guidance needed, and progressively increase difficulty. Do not reveal the final answer until my attempt has been evaluated.

**Format**
For each turn:
- Question
- Why this question matters
- Wait for my response
Then provide feedback after I respond.

**Topic:** [PASTE]

title: Learn exam vocabulary with context sentences and collocations
description: Turns each word you are studying into a compact card with meaning, a revealing example sentence, collocations, and look-alike traps.
content:
Help me learn vocabulary for an English exam.

**Exam:** [e.g. "IELTS Academic", "TOEFL", "YDT", "SAT", "GRE"]
**My level:** [e.g. "B1", "intermediate"]
**My first language:** [LANGUAGE - used for translations and false-friend warnings]
**Words or phrases to learn:** [LIST]

For each word, use exactly this format:

**Word** (part of speech) - pronunciation guide
- Meaning: a short, plain-English definition for the sense most likely to appear on my exam.
- In my language: [translation]
- Example: one sentence where the meaning is obvious from context alone, written in the style of my exam's reading passages.
- Collocations: 3 common word partners (e.g. "mitigate the risk").
- Word family: related forms (noun, verb, adjective, adverb).
- Synonyms / antonyms: 2 each, noting any difference in strength or formality.
- Watch out: look-alike words, false friends in my language, or a second meaning that could trick me.

After the list:
1. A 10-question check: fill-in-the-blank and choose-the-right-word items using these words in new sentences, with an answer key at the end.
2. A short review schedule (day 1, 3, 7, 14) telling me which words to revisit.

Keep the tone encouraging and brief. If a word has several meanings, focus on the one most common in exam reading and mention the others in one line.
variables: LANGUAGE - used for translations and false-friend warnings

title: Learn from a document or textbook chapter
description: Turns a document into a structured lesson with key ideas, questions, and practice.
content:
Act as a learning designer and subject-matter expert.

**Context**
I need to understand the material below and retain the most useful concepts.

**Task**
Extract the 10 most important concepts, explain each in simple language, connect them to real work, create examples, and test my understanding.

**Format**
Return:
- Key concepts
- Practical application
- Common mistakes
- 10-question quiz
- Answer key hidden under a separate heading

**Document:** [PASTE]

title: Learn to cook a handful of basic meals from scratch
description: A beginner's learning plan of 8-10 foundational meals, the skills each teaches, and a starter kitchen kit.
content:
Teach me to cook, starting from almost nothing.

**My current level:** [e.g. "I can boil pasta and that's it"]
**Kitchen and budget:** [e.g. "shared dorm kitchen, one pan, $40/week for food"]
**Foods I like:** [CUISINES, FAVORITE DISHES]
**Dietary needs:** [e.g. "halal", "vegetarian", "lactose intolerant"]
**Time per week to practice:** [e.g. "3 evenings, 45 minutes each"]

Create:
1. A 4-week plan of 8-10 meals, ordered so each builds a new skill (e.g. knife basics, sautéing, roasting, cooking rice and eggs, a simple sauce, a soup, a one-pan dinner).
2. For each meal: why it's on the list, the skill it teaches, ingredients with amounts and rough cost, steps, and one variation so I don't get bored.
3. A minimal equipment list (must-have vs nice-to-have) and pantry staples to buy once.
4. Kitchen safety basics: knife handling, what to do with a grease fire (lid on, heat off, never water), handwashing and cross-contamination with raw meat, and safe internal temperatures.
5. A short "how to tell it's done" guide and common beginner mistakes.

Write like a patient friend. No jargon without a one-line explanation.
variables: e.g. "I can boil pasta and that's it"
e.g. "shared dorm kitchen, one pan, $40/week for food"

title: Learn to use my smartphone with simple step-by-step lessons
description: A gentle, paced set of short lessons to learn your phone's basics, with practice tasks and no jargon.
content:
Teach me how to use my smartphone, one small lesson at a time.

**My phone:** [MAKE AND MODEL, or "iPhone" / "Android" / "not sure"]
**What I can already do:** [e.g. answer calls, nothing else yet]
**What I want to be able to do:** [e.g. send texts and photos, video call my grandchildren, read email, use maps, check the weather]
**How I learn best:** [e.g. written steps I can print, short daily practice, with my grandson on weekends]
**Things that make it hard:** [optional - e.g. small buttons, eyesight, worried about pressing the wrong thing]

Create a learning plan:
1. Order the skills from easiest to hardest, starting with what I want most.
2. Turn them into 6-10 short lessons, 10-15 minutes each.
3. For each lesson: what I'll learn, numbered steps written very simply, one practice task, and how to undo a mistake or get back to the home screen.
4. Explain any word I might not know (app, icon, swipe, tap, notification) the first time it appears.
5. Add a reassurance tip: what's safe to try, and what to never do (e.g. give my passcode to a caller, tap links in unexpected texts).

Use large, clear headings and keep each step to one action. Menu names differ between phones, so mark anything that may look different on mine as [MAY LOOK DIFFERENT]. Start with Lesson 1 in full, then list the rest so I can ask for the next one when I'm ready.
variables: e.g. answer calls, nothing else yet

title: Make a one-page cheat sheet
description: A compact reference sheet of the essentials on any topic or document.
content:
Act as a knowledge-management expert.

**Context**
I need a compact reference for [TOPIC] that I can use during real work.

**Task**
Compress the topic into the smallest useful amount of information without losing essential concepts, rules, decision points, formulas, examples, or warnings.

**Format**
Create a one-page cheat sheet with:
- Core concepts
- Key rules
- Mental models
- Examples
- Common mistakes
- Decision checklist

**Topic:** [PASTE]

title: Make a practice plan for learning a musical instrument
description: A weekly practice routine with warm-ups, skills, and songs matched to your level, goals, and available time.
content:
Create a practice plan to help me learn an instrument.

**Instrument:** [e.g. "acoustic guitar", "piano", "ukulele", "violin"]
**My level:** [complete beginner / know a few chords or pieces / returning after years]
**Goal in 3 months:** [e.g. "play 5 songs to sing along with", "read simple sheet music", "play at a family party"]
**Music I love:** [ARTISTS OR GENRES]
**Practice time:** [e.g. "20 minutes, 5 days a week"]
**Lessons or resources I use:** [teacher / app / videos / book / none]
**What I find hard:** [e.g. "chord changes", "rhythm", "sore fingers", "staying motivated"]

Give me:
1. A practice session template that fits my time, split into warm-up, technique, new material, and playing for fun, with minutes for each.
2. A 12-week plan, week by week: skill focus, exercises, and a song or piece to work on that suits my level and taste.
3. How to practice well: slow practice, short repeats of the hard bit, using a metronome, and recording myself.
4. Signs I'm ready to move on, and what to do when I plateau.
5. A simple practice log format.

Flag physical warning signs (pain beyond normal fingertip soreness, wrist or shoulder strain) and suggest checking posture with a teacher. Don't overload me; beginners progress best with a few things done often.

title: Make a survival phrase sheet for my trip abroad
description: A pocket-sized phrase sheet with the words you'll actually need, simple pronunciation guides, and polite phrases for the local language.
content:
Make me a pocket phrase sheet for a trip.

**Destination and language:** [COUNTRY and LANGUAGE - include regional variety if relevant]
**My native language:** [LANGUAGE]
**Situations I'll face:** [e.g. restaurants, taxis, hotel, shopping, asking directions, pharmacy, train station]
**Special needs to communicate:** [e.g. a food allergy, vegetarian, traveling with a baby, wheelchair user]
**Days before I leave:** [NUMBER - so you can suggest what to learn first]

Rules:
- Keep it to about 30-40 phrases, grouped by situation. Prioritize polite basics (hello, please, thank you, excuse me, sorry, I don't understand, do you speak [MY LANGUAGE]?).
- For each phrase give: the phrase in my language, the local language, and a simple pronunciation guide written for a speaker of my native language.
- Use the polite or neutral register suitable for strangers, and note when a different form is used with friends.
- Include numbers 1-10, how to ask "how much?", and how to say "help" and "call an ambulance".
- Add 5 phrases I'm likely to HEAR so I can recognize them.

Return a table per situation, then a 7-day mini plan to learn the top 15 phrases. Note that pronunciation guides are approximate and that I should listen to a native-speaker recording to check.
variables: COUNTRY and LANGUAGE - include regional variety if relevant
NUMBER - so you can suggest what to learn first

title: Make training materials accessible and inclusive
description: Audits slides, e-learning, documents, and videos for accessibility barriers and non-inclusive content, with specific fixes.
content:
Review my training materials for accessibility and inclusion.

**Materials:** [PASTE TEXT, SLIDE CONTENT, SCRIPT, OR DESCRIBE THE MODULE]
**Format:** [slides / e-learning / PDF / video / live virtual session]
**Learners:** [WHO, including known needs - e.g. "global, many non-native English speakers", "frontline staff on mobile"]
**Standard we follow:** [e.g. WCAG 2.2 AA, internal policy, or "not sure"]

Check for:
- Visual: color contrast, color used as the only signal, text in images, font size, alt text for meaningful images, slide reading order.
- Audio and video: captions, transcripts, audio description for key visuals, no auto-play.
- Interaction: keyboard navigation, drag-and-drop with no alternative, timed activities, flashing content.
- Cognitive load: reading level, jargon and acronyms, dense screens, unclear instructions, too many steps at once.
- Inclusion: examples, names, and images that reflect a range of people; stereotypes; idioms and culture-specific references that confuse global learners; gendered or ableist language.
- Live sessions: multiple ways to participate (chat, voice, polls), materials shared in advance.

Return:
1. A table: Issue | Where | Who it affects | Fix | Priority (must / should / nice).
2. Rewritten versions of the 5 most problematic passages.
3. Alt text for any images I described.
4. A short checklist I can reuse on future courses.

Note anything you cannot check from text alone (e.g. actual contrast ratios, screen reader behavior) and tell me how to test it.
variables: PASTE TEXT, SLIDE CONTENT, SCRIPT, OR DESCRIBE THE MODULE
slides / e-learning / PDF / video / live virtual session
e.g. WCAG 2.2 AA, internal policy, or "not sure"

title: Map out a college search plan with my teen
description: A shared college-search timeline that splits tasks between teen and parent, sets cost limits early, and keeps the process low-stress.
content:
Help me and my teen plan the college search together.

**Teen's grade and graduation year:** [DETAILS]
**Interests, strengths, and possible fields:** [DETAILS]
**Academic picture:** [grades, course rigor, test plans, if known]
**What matters to them:** [size, distance, programs, campus life]
**Family budget and expectations:** [what we can contribute; open to loans?]
**Location/country:** [DETAILS]
**Other paths on the table:** [community college, gap year, trade school, work]

Give me:
1. A month-by-month timeline from now through decision day, split into: what my teen owns and how I support.
2. A list of questions to research for each college, including net price and aid, not just sticker price.
3. A comparison table template: School | Fit (academic, social) | Net cost after aid | Admission likelihood | Notes.
4. A family money conversation to have early: what we can pay, what we expect from my teen (savings, work, loans), and which schools are off the table on cost, before anyone falls in love with one.
5. Financial-aid steps to look into, kept general and marked [CONFIRM DEADLINES] since dates and forms change each year.
6. How to talk about it without taking over: conversation starters, how to handle disagreement, and protecting my teen's wellbeing during stressful months.

Do not invent admission rates, costs, or deadlines; mark them [CHECK OFFICIAL SOURCE]. For aid and loan decisions, suggest confirming with the school's financial aid office.
variables: grades, course rigor, test plans, if known
what we can contribute; open to loans?
community college, gap year, trade school, work

title: Mark my timed practice exam answer against the marking criteria
description: A criterion-by-criterion mark for a timed practice answer, an estimated band, and what would lift it one level.
content:
Mark a practice exam answer I wrote under timed conditions.

**Question and marks available:** [PASTE]
**Marking scheme or criteria:** [PASTE FROM STEP 2, the course rubric, or describe how exams are marked]
**My answer:** [PASTE EXACTLY AS WRITTEN]
**Time I took vs. time allowed:** [DETAILS]
**Course level:** [e.g. "second-year history"]

How to mark:
1. Go criterion by criterion. Give a mark or level for each and quote the part of my answer that justifies it.
2. Give an estimated overall mark or band, as a range, and say it is an estimate, not an official grade.
3. Check exam-specific habits: Did I answer the exact question asked? Did I plan before writing? Is there a clear argument or method, or just description? Did I use evidence or show working? Was my time split sensible across parts?
4. Point out where I wrote things that earned no marks, so I can save time next attempt.

Return:
- A table: Criterion | Mark or level | Evidence from my answer | How to improve.
- Estimated overall mark range.
- The 3 changes that would lift my answer one band.
- One weak paragraph or step rewritten as an illustration, labeled as such, so I can see the difference; I'll write my own version.
- A 5-minute answer plan I could use for a similar question.

This is for practice and self-improvement only. This is step 3 of the "Ace your university final exams" pack. It works on its own, and can use questions and marking schemes from step 2.

title: Master one admissions test question type with a strategy and drills
description: How a tricky question type works, a step-by-step method, its common traps, and graded practice items with explanations.
content:
Teach me to master one question type on my graduate admissions test.

**Test:** [e.g. "GMAT", "GRE", "LSAT"]
**Question type:** [e.g. "GMAT data sufficiency", "GRE text completion", "LSAT flaw questions"]
**My current accuracy and timing on it:** [PASTE FROM STEP 2, or estimate]
**Mistakes I keep making:** [e.g. "I solve fully instead of checking sufficiency", "I pick answers that are true but don't address the flaw"]

Return:
1. How this question type works: what it is really testing and how the answer choices are built.
2. A step-by-step method I can apply every time, short enough to memorize.
3. The common traps and wrong-answer patterns, with how to spot each.
4. Time targets for this type and when to guess and move on.
5. 8 practice items that get harder as they go, all questions first, then an answer key explaining why each answer is right and why the tempting wrong answers are wrong.
6. How to review my misses so the same mistake doesn't repeat.

Rules:
- Test formats change. If you describe format details (number of questions, timing, section structure), mark them [CONFIRM against the official test site].
- Say clearly that AI-written items may not match the real test's difficulty or style exactly, and recommend official practice questions for my main drilling.

This is step 3 of the "Prepare for a graduate admissions test" pack. It works on its own, and can use the priorities from the step 2 diagnosis.
variables: CONFIRM against the official test site

title: Measure whether training worked
description: Evaluation plan from reaction to behavior change and business impact.
content:
Help me evaluate a training program.

**Program and goal:** [WHAT IT TEACHES / BUSINESS OUTCOME IT SHOULD AFFECT]
**Audience:** [WHO]
**Data available:** [surveys, assessments, performance metrics]

Deliver an evaluation plan across four levels:
1. Reaction — a short post-session survey (5–7 questions).
2. Learning — how to test knowledge or skill gained.
3. Behavior — how to see whether people apply it on the job (manager check-ins, observation, 30/60/90-day follow-ups), plus how to support transfer.
4. Results — business metrics to track and how to isolate the training's effect.

Include a timeline, owners, and a one-page report template.
variables: WHAT IT TEACHES / BUSINESS OUTCOME IT SHOULD AFFECT

title: Observe a trainer and give structured coaching feedback
description: An observation checklist and feedback plan for assessing new or internal facilitators and helping them improve.
content:
Create a facilitator observation tool and help me give coaching feedback to a trainer.

**Context:** [e.g. "certifying internal SMEs as trainers", "new facilitator's first solo session"]
**Session type:** [in person / virtual / hybrid; length; group size]
**What good facilitation looks like in our organization:** [ANY STANDARDS or "suggest them"]
**My observation notes (if I have them already):** [PASTE or "none yet"]

Build an observation checklist covering:
- Opening: purpose, relevance to learners, ground rules, energy.
- Content delivery: accuracy, clarity, examples, pace, timing against the plan.
- Engagement: questions asked (open vs. closed), wait time, inclusion of quiet participants, managing dominant voices.
- Activities: clear instructions, debrief that links back to the job.
- Virtual skills (if relevant): platform fluency, chat and poll use, camera presence.
- Handling challenges: tough questions, off-topic tangents, tech issues.
- Close: summary, action commitments, evaluation.

For each item, give a 3-level rating with observable descriptions (developing / proficient / strong).

Return:
1. The observation checklist as a table.
2. If I gave notes: strengths with specific evidence, the 2-3 highest-impact improvements, and a practice suggestion for each.
3. A structure for the feedback conversation: ask for self-assessment first, then share observations.
4. Criteria for signing off a facilitator as ready to deliver alone.

Base feedback only on observed behavior, not personality.
variables: in person / virtual / hybrid; length; group size

title: Pick a short list of learning resources for my skill and budget
description: A small, vetted set of courses, books, or tools mapped to your focus areas, so you stop collecting and start learning.
content:
Help me choose a small, high-quality set of learning resources for a skill and decide how to use them.

**Skill and focus sub-skills:** [PASTE THE FOCUS LIST FROM STEP 1, or list the 3-4 areas I need most]
**My level:** [BEGINNER / SOME EXPERIENCE / INTERMEDIATE]
**How I learn best:** [e.g. "video then practice", "reading", "learning with others", "hands-on projects"]
**Budget:** [AMOUNT, or "free only"]
**Time per week:** [HOURS]
**Resources I'm already considering (optional):** [NAMES OR LINKS]

Rules:
- Recommend no more than 3-4 core resources: one main path plus a few supplements. Resource hoarding is a common way to stall.
- Judge each option on: covers my focus sub-skills, includes practice with feedback (not just watching), fits my level, and is current.
- Do not invent course names, authors, prices, or links. If you name a specific resource, mark it [CONFIRM it exists, is current, and the price]. Where you are unsure, describe the type of resource to look for and give me search terms instead.
- If I listed resources, evaluate those first and say plainly which to drop.

Return:
1. A table: Resource or resource type | What it covers | Cost | Why it's in the set | How to use it (which parts, in what order).
2. A "not now" list of tempting resources to ignore until later, and why.
3. A plan for the first two weeks that assigns resources to specific sessions.
4. Where to get feedback on my work (communities, peers, a coach, self-check methods).

This is step 2 of the "Teach yourself a new skill in 90 days" pack. It works on its own, but if you have the sub-skill map and benchmark from step 1, paste them in.
variables: CONFIRM it exists, is current, and the price

title: Plan a blended learning unit that mixes in-person and online work
description: A unit plan that decides what happens in class versus online, with activities, platform tasks, and support for students who need it.
content:
Help me plan a blended learning unit.

**Subject, topic, and grade or level:** [e.g. "Grade 7 science, ecosystems"]
**Learning objectives:** [WHAT students should know or be able to do]
**Unit length and schedule:** [e.g. "3 weeks, 4 in-person lessons a week"]
**Blended model:** [station rotation / flipped classroom / flex / not sure]
**Online platform and tools:** [e.g. "Google Classroom, Khan Academy, Padlet"]
**Student access:** [devices and internet at home, school device availability]
**Student needs to address:** [e.g. "wide reading levels", "English learners", "low motivation", "IEP accommodations"]

Give me:
1. A split of what's best done in person (discussion, labs, feedback, group work) versus online (direct instruction video, practice, quizzes, reflection), with the reason for each.
2. A week-by-week plan: in-class activities, online tasks, time estimates, and how each online task feeds the next in-person lesson.
3. Active learning ideas for both settings that build retention and application, not just completion.
4. Differentiation for the needs I listed: scaffolds, choice of tasks, extension work.
5. A plan for students without reliable home access, so no one falls behind.
6. Checks for understanding: quick formative checks in each setting and how I'll use the platform data to group students.
7. Student-facing instructions for the first online task, written at their reading level.

Keep the online workload realistic for the grade, and flag anything that depends on my school's policies on devices or data privacy.
variables: WHAT students should know or be able to do
e.g. "3 weeks, 4 in-person lessons a week"
station rotation / flipped classroom / flex / not sure
devices and internet at home, school device availability

title: Plan a capstone project that proves I learned a new skill
description: A right-sized final project with milestones, a definition of done, and a plan to document and share it.
content:
Help me plan a capstone project that proves I can use a skill I've been learning.

**Skill:** [WHAT]
**My original goal:** [e.g. "run a 20-minute workshop", "build a budget model for a small business"]
**What I can do now:** [CURRENT LEVEL, or paste my latest weekly review from step 4]
**Time available for the project:** [e.g. "3 weeks, 5 hours a week"]
**Who should see the result:** [e.g. "hiring managers", "clients", "my team", "just me"]
**Constraints:** [BUDGET, TOOLS, PRIVACY, ACCESS TO PEOPLE OR DATA]

Steps:
1. Suggest 3 project ideas sized to my time. For each: what it is, which sub-skills it demonstrates, what the finished output looks like, and an optional stretch goal.
2. Recommend one and explain why it best matches my goal and audience.
3. Break it into weekly milestones, each ending with something I can show.
4. Write a definition of done: specific, checkable criteria.
5. Plan how to document the process as I go: a before/after comparison with my day-1 benchmark, key decisions, and mistakes I fixed.

Return:
- The 3 ideas in a short table.
- The recommended project with milestones and definition of done.
- A documentation checklist.
- How to share it with my audience (format and where).
- The top risks (scope creep is the usual one) and how to cut scope if I fall behind.

This is step 5 of the "Teach yourself a new skill in 90 days" pack. It works on its own, and the finished project can feed the "Build a portfolio that gets you hired" pack.
variables: CURRENT LEVEL, or paste my latest weekly review from step 4
BUDGET, TOOLS, PRIVACY, ACCESS TO PEOPLE OR DATA

title: Plan a multi-week unit backward from standards and the final assessment
description: A backward-designed unit plan with goals, a summative task, evidence checkpoints, and a day-by-day lesson sequence.
content:
Help me plan a unit using backward design: start from what students must be able to do, then the evidence, then the lessons.

**Subject, grade or course level:** [e.g. "9th grade biology", "intro macroeconomics, first-year undergrads"]
**Standards or course outcomes to cover:** [PASTE STANDARD CODES/TEXT OR OUTCOMES]
**Unit length:** [e.g. "15 class periods of 50 minutes"]
**What students already know:** [PRIOR UNITS, COMMON GAPS]
**Required materials or texts:** [TEXTBOOK CHAPTERS, LABS, RESOURCES]
**Constraints:** [e.g. "state test in May", "no lab access week 2", "mixed-ability class"]

Work in three stages:
1. **Desired results:** 2-3 enduring understandings, 3-5 essential questions, and what students will know and be able to do. Map each to the standards I gave; do not add standards I did not list.
2. **Evidence:** one summative performance task (with a short student-facing prompt) plus 3-4 formative checkpoints placed through the unit.
3. **Learning plan:** a day-by-day sequence. For each day: objective, key activity, how I'll check understanding, and homework if any.

Checks:
- Every summative skill is taught and practiced before it is assessed.
- Cognitive demand rises across the unit (not all recall, not all analysis on day 1).
- Build in at least one buffer/reteach day and one review day.

Return: the Stage 1-2 content as short lists, then the daily plan as a table: Day | Objective | Activity | Check for understanding | Materials. Flag anything that looks too ambitious for the time available.

title: Plan a phishing simulation campaign and follow-up training
description: Designs an approved phishing test program with realistic scenarios, metrics, and supportive training for people who click.
content:
Help me plan a phishing simulation program for our organization.

**Organization size and departments:** [DETAILS]
**Previous results:** [click rate, report rate - or "first campaign"]
**Simulation tool:** [e.g. "Microsoft Attack Simulation Training", "KnowBe4" - or "not chosen"]
**Threats we actually see:** [e.g. "fake invoices", "MFA fatigue", "payroll change requests"]
**Constraints:** [union or works council rules, legal or HR review required, languages]

Plan:
1. Goals and metrics: report rate (the main one), click rate, credential-entry rate, time to first report. Suggest realistic targets.
2. A 6-month campaign calendar with difficulty increasing over time.
3. Six scenario briefs based on our real threats: pretext, sender type, red flags to include, difficulty level, and target group. Describe them; do not write deployable lures that copy a real outside brand's logo or exact templates unless legal approves.
4. Landing-page "teachable moment" content for people who click: short, kind, and specific.
5. Follow-up training for repeat clickers that supports rather than punishes.
6. Rules of engagement: who must approve, people excluded (e.g. during leave), how results are reported (team level, not public names).

Remind me to get written approval from leadership, HR, and legal before launch, and to avoid scenarios that cause real distress (bonuses, layoffs, health scares).

Return the plan as headed sections with the calendar as a table.
variables: click rate, report rate - or "first campaign"

title: Plan a product training session for a customer's team
description: A session plan for training customer users, built around their real workflows, with exercises and follow-up.
content:
Help me plan a training session for a customer's team.

**Product and features to cover:** [LIST]
**Audience:** [ROLES, NUMBER OF PEOPLE, experience with the product - e.g. "new admins", "end users who've had accounts for 3 months but rarely log in"]
**Their real workflows or use cases:** [e.g. "weekly reporting to managers", "handling inbound requests"]
**Format and length:** [live virtual / in person / recorded; e.g. 60 minutes]
**What they should be able to do afterward:** [OUTCOMES]
**Common mistakes or support tickets from this customer:** [DETAILS]

Give me:
1. 3-4 learning objectives written as things they'll be able to do.
2. A minute-by-minute agenda that alternates short demos with hands-on practice. No more than 10 minutes of demo before they try something.
3. Exercises based on their actual workflows, with the expected result for each.
4. Questions to check understanding and keep people engaged on a video call.
5. A one-page quick reference guide outline they can keep.
6. Follow-up: a recap email, how to measure whether behavior changed (usage data to check after 2 weeks), and when to offer a refresher.

Prioritize the workflows they'll use weekly over a complete feature tour.
variables: live virtual / in person / recorded; e.g. 60 minutes

title: Plan a response to a recurring behavior problem in my classroom
description: A function-based plan for persistent disruptive behavior, with prevention, response steps, tracking, and family communication.
content:
Help me plan a response to a recurring behavior issue in my classroom.

**Grade level:** [GRADE]
**The behavior, described observably:** [e.g. "leaves seat and talks to peers during independent work, 4-6 times per period" - not "is disrespectful"]
**When and where it happens most:** [time of day, activity, setting]
**What usually happens right before:** [triggers]
**What usually happens right after:** [how I and peers respond]
**What I've already tried and results:** [STRATEGIES]
**Supports in place:** [e.g. IEP/504 behavior plan, counselor involvement] (no names)

Help me:
1. Form a hypothesis about the function of the behavior (attention, escape/avoidance, sensory, access to something) based on the patterns I described, and explain why. Say if the information is too thin to tell.
2. Suggest prevention strategies (changes to the task, environment, or routine) that address that function.
3. Identify a replacement behavior that meets the same need appropriately, and how to teach it.
4. Give a calm, consistent response sequence for when it happens.
5. Create a simple 2-week tracking sheet (frequency or ABC log).
6. Draft a short, positive first message to the family.

Keep strategies practical for one teacher with a full class. If the behavior involves harm to self or others, or there is an existing behavior intervention plan, tell me to involve the school's support team and follow that plan first.
variables: e.g. IEP/504 behavior plan, counselor involvement

title: Plan a train-the-trainer program
description: A program to prepare internal experts to deliver a course consistently: selection, practice teaching, materials, certification, and quality checks.
content:
Help me plan a train-the-trainer program so internal people can deliver a course or training consistently.

**Course they will deliver:** [topic, length, format - in person / virtual / blended]
**Learners they will teach:** [roles, number, locations, languages]
**Who the trainers are:** [e.g. "experienced supervisors with no teaching experience", "subject matter experts"]
**Number of trainers and timeline:** [DETAILS]
**Materials we already have:** [slides, facilitator guide, activities, assessments]
**Constraints:** [budget, time away from regular work, tools]

Give me:
1. **Trainer selection criteria:** subject knowledge, communication, credibility, and availability, and how to assess them.
2. **Program outline:** sessions covering the course content itself, how adults learn, facilitation skills (asking questions, managing discussion, handling difficult participants), running each activity, virtual delivery skills if relevant, and assessing learners.
3. **Practice teaching:** each trainer delivers sections of the real course and gets feedback using a simple observation rubric. Include the rubric.
4. **Trainer toolkit:** what goes in it - facilitator guide with timings, slide notes, activity instructions, FAQs and tricky questions with answers, and a setup checklist.
5. **Certification:** what a trainer must show before teaching alone, and co-delivery with an experienced trainer first.
6. **Keeping quality consistent:** learner feedback, periodic observation, a trainer community or check-in, and how to update materials across all trainers.
7. **Timeline** from selection to first solo delivery.

Keep it practical for trainers who have full-time jobs.
variables: topic, length, format - in person / virtual / blended
budget, time away from regular work, tools

title: Plan annual HIPAA and OSHA training for clinic staff
description: A role-based yearly compliance training plan covering privacy, security, bloodborne pathogens, and hazard communication, with tracking and documentation.
content:
Help me build our clinic's annual compliance training plan.

**Clinic type and services:** [e.g. "primary care with in-house lab and vaccines", "dental practice", "dermatology with procedures"]
**Staff roles and headcount:** [e.g. providers 6, MAs 8, front desk 5, billing 3, remote staff 2]
**Topics required or already covered:** [e.g. HIPAA privacy and security, OSHA bloodborne pathogens, hazard communication, fire safety, emergency preparedness, fraud waste and abuse, harassment prevention]
**Recent incidents or audit findings:** [e.g. phishing click, needlestick, misdirected fax]
**Time and format available:** [e.g. 30 minutes per month, staff meeting slots, online modules]
**How we track completion today:** [DETAILS]

Give me:
1. A topic-by-role matrix showing who needs what: e.g. bloodborne pathogens for anyone with occupational exposure, security awareness for everyone with system access, Medicare fraud, waste, and abuse for billing and providers where applicable. Mark any requirement I should verify as [CONFIRM REQUIREMENT].
2. A 12-month calendar spreading topics into short sessions, with new-hire training within their first weeks and refreshers tied to real incidents.
3. For each topic: 3-5 learning objectives, a realistic clinic scenario to discuss (e.g. a family member asks for a patient's results at the front desk), and a short knowledge check.
4. Documentation to keep: sign-in sheets or completion records, content version, trainer, date, and retention period [CONFIRM].
5. How to measure whether training worked (e.g. phishing test results, incident trends, audit checks).

Return the matrix, calendar, and topic outlines. Check state-specific training requirements with our compliance lead.
variables: e.g. phishing click, needlestick, misdirected fax

title: Plan coaching sessions for a client with a specific challenge
description: Fresh, tailored coaching techniques and a session plan matched to a person's learning style, goals, and obstacles.
content:
Help me plan how to coach someone.

**Who I'm coaching:** [individual or group; role, age range, or level]
**Coaching context:** [e.g. executive, career, sports, sales, life coaching, teacher mentoring]
**Their goal:** [WHAT they want to achieve and by when]
**The challenge:** [e.g. "low confidence", "procrastination", "plateaued performance", "resistant to feedback"]
**How they learn and respond best:** [e.g. "needs data", "learns by doing", "shuts down with direct criticism"]
**What I've tried so far:** [approaches and results]
**Session format:** [frequency, length, in person or remote]

Give me:
1. My read of what may be underneath the challenge, as hypotheses to test, not conclusions.
