2. 6-8 techniques or exercises suited to this person, each with: what it is, why it fits their style, how to run it, and a sign it's working.
3. 10 powerful open questions for our next sessions.
4. A 4-session plan with a goal for each session, activities, and between-session practice.
5. How to track progress (simple measures we both agree on).
6. What to avoid with this person, given what I've described.

Keep it practical and respectful of their autonomy. If what I describe sounds like a mental health issue (e.g. depression, trauma, burnout with physical symptoms), say so and suggest I encourage them to see a qualified professional alongside coaching.
variables: individual or group; role, age range, or level
WHAT they want to achieve and by when
frequency, length, in person or remote

title: Plan continuing education to keep professional licenses current
description: A license-by-license plan to track and meet continuing education requirements for CPAs, engineers, and architects at my firm.
content:
Help me plan continuing education for the licensed professionals at my firm so no one falls out of compliance.

**License types held:** [e.g. "CPA", "Professional Engineer (PE)", "registered architect", "professional association membership requiring learning units"]
**Jurisdictions:** [states or countries where each person is licensed - many hold several]
**Staff list:** [name or ID, licenses, jurisdictions, renewal dates, hours earned so far this cycle]
**Requirements I've confirmed:** [PASTE - total hours, cycle length, required subjects such as ethics, regulatory review, health-safety-welfare, or technical hours, carryover rules]
**Firm priorities for skills:** [e.g. "new lease standard", "data analytics", "mass timber design", "AI tools"]
**Budget and format preferences:** [in-house sessions, webinars, conferences, self-study]

Produce:
1. A tracker table: person | license | jurisdiction | cycle end | hours required | hours earned | required subject hours still needed | at risk (Y/N).
2. A list of people at risk in the next 6 months, ordered by deadline.
3. A firm-wide learning calendar that covers common requirements (such as ethics) through group sessions to save cost, and maps firm skill priorities to eligible courses.
4. Rules for documentation: certificates, attendance records, and how long to keep them in case of a licensing board audit.
5. Tips for people licensed in multiple jurisdictions, such as courses that count in more than one place.

Only use requirements I've confirmed; anything I haven't confirmed should be marked [CHECK WITH LICENSING BOARD] - do not fill in hour requirements from memory, as they vary by jurisdiction and change often.

title: Plan how to make training stick on the job
description: A before, during, and after plan that helps trainees apply new skills at work, with roles for managers and ways to measure it.
content:
Help me design a learning-transfer plan so people apply what they learn in training to their actual work.

**Training program:** [TOPIC and format]
**Learners:** [roles, experience]
**The work situation where they should use it:** [specific task or challenge, e.g. "handling pricing objections on renewal calls"]
**What usually gets in the way:** [e.g. no time to practice, managers don't reinforce, old habits, tools don't support it]
**Who can help:** [managers, peer coaches, L&D, team leads]

Use the main drivers of transfer: learner motivation and confidence, relevance of the content to real tasks, opportunity to use the skill soon, and support from managers and peers.

Return:
1. **Before training:** how to set expectations (manager pre-conversation, a real goal or work problem each learner brings).
2. **During training:** practice on real cases, action plans, and anticipating obstacles (if-then plans).
3. **After training (first 90 days):** spaced reminders, on-the-job assignments, check-ins, job aids, and peer practice, laid out week by week.
4. **Manager toolkit:** a short script for the pre- and post-training conversations and what to observe.
5. **Barrier fixes:** for each barrier I listed, a specific countermeasure.
6. **Measurement:** behaviors to observe, who observes them, and when; one business metric to watch.

Keep it practical for busy managers: their total time commitment should be under 30 minutes a month per learner.
variables: managers, peer coaches, L&D, team leads

title: Plan how to teach the key vocabulary for a unit
description: Selects the academic vocabulary that matters most for a unit and plans explicit teaching, practice, and review.
content:
Help me plan vocabulary instruction for an upcoming unit.

**Subject, grade, and unit:** [e.g. "5th grade science, ecosystems"]
**Texts and materials students will read:** [LIST OR PASTE EXCERPTS]
**Words I'm considering:** [LIST, or ask you to pull candidates from the text]
**Students' language needs:** [e.g. "a third are English learners", "strong readers but weak academic writing"]
**Time available per day for vocabulary:** [MINUTES]

Do the following:
1. Sort the words into: general academic words used across subjects (e.g. "analyze", "evidence"), domain-specific terms for this unit, and words not worth direct teaching. Pick 8-12 to teach explicitly and explain the choices.
2. For each chosen word: a student-friendly definition, an example sentence connected to the unit, a non-example, a visual or gesture idea, and related word forms (e.g. "predict, prediction, predictable").
3. Plan a teaching routine for introducing words (under 5 minutes per word).
4. Plan 5 practice activities across the unit that get students using the words in speaking and writing, not just matching definitions.
5. Add sentence frames for discussion and writing.
6. Include a quick review schedule and a short end-of-unit check that asks students to use the words in context.

Keep definitions accurate for the subject; mark any term where a simplified definition might create a misconception.
variables: LIST, or ask you to pull candidates from the text

title: Plan my final week before a certification exam
description: A day-by-day last-week plan, a one-page memory sheet from your notes, and an exam-day checklist and strategy.
content:
Plan my final week before a certification exam.

**Certification:** [NAME]
**Exam date, time, and format:** [e.g. "Friday 9am, online proctored, 180 questions, 230 minutes"]
**Latest practice scores:** [SCORES AND DATES]
**Remaining weak spots:** [PASTE FROM STEP 4, or list them]
**Must-know facts, formulas, or frameworks:** [PASTE MY NOTES]
**Hours available each day this week:** [DETAILS]

Return:
1. A day-by-day plan: targeted review of weak spots early in the week, one final full practice exam 3-4 days out, light review only the day before, and no new material in the last 48 hours.
2. A one-page memory sheet built only from the notes I pasted: key facts, formulas, process orders, and easily confused pairs. Mark anything that looks wrong or incomplete with [CHECK].
3. An exam-day checklist: ID requirements, arrival or check-in time, and, for online proctoring, the system check, room setup, and allowed items. Mark each with [CONFIRM with the exam provider's current rules].
4. An in-exam strategy: time checkpoints, when to flag and move on, how to use review time, and guessing rules (confirm whether wrong answers are penalized).
5. A short plan for nerves: what to do the night before, the morning of, and if I blank on a question.
6. If I don't pass: how to read the score report and plan a retake (check the provider's retake waiting period and fees).

This is step 5 of the "Pass a professional certification exam" pack. It works on its own, and can use the mistake analysis from step 4.
variables: PASTE FROM STEP 4, or list them
CONFIRM with the exam provider's current rules

title: Plan my SAT or ACT prep from a practice test score
description: A study plan built from your practice test results, targeting the sections and question types that will raise your score most.
content:
Help me build an SAT or ACT prep plan based on my practice test results.

**Test:** [SAT / ACT], test date: [DATE]
**Practice test scores:** [total and section scores, which official practice test]
**Question types I missed most:** [e.g. "linear equations, comma rules, inference questions", or paste the score report breakdown]
**Target score and why:** [e.g. "1350 to be in the middle range for my list"]
**Time available per week:** [HOURS]
**Accommodations, if any:** [e.g. extended time]

Do this:
1. Find where the most points are available: question types I miss often that are common on the test and learnable.
2. Separate content gaps (didn't know the rule) from timing issues and careless errors, and suggest a fix for each.
3. Build a week-by-week plan until the test: targeted practice, timed sections, full practice tests every 2-3 weeks, and a review routine for every missed question (why I missed it, the rule, a similar problem).
4. Include pacing strategy for each section and the week-before and test-day plan.
5. Recommend free, official practice materials first.

Return the gap analysis, a weekly plan table (Week | Focus | Practice | Checkpoint), pacing tips, and the test-day checklist.

Don't promise a score increase. Remind me to check current test format and dates on the official site and to compare with my colleges' testing policies, since many are test-optional.
variables: total and section scores, which official practice test
e.g. "1350 to be in the middle range for my list"

title: Plan ongoing assessment for a blended or online class
description: A practical mix of checks for understanding, tools, and tracking that shows how each student is progressing toward a learning goal.
content:
Help me plan how to assess and track student learning in my blended or online class.

**Subject, level, and class size:** [DETAILS]
**Learning objective(s) to track:** [e.g. "solve two-step equations", "write an argument with evidence"]
**Format:** [how time is split between in-person, live online, and self-paced]
**Tools available:** [e.g. LMS, quiz tools, shared docs, discussion boards]
**Constraints:** [grading time, device access, students with accommodations]

Give me:
1. **Assessment map** - for each objective: what mastery looks like, 2-3 formative checks (exit tickets, short quizzes, polls, recorded explanations, peer review), and one summative task.
2. **How to use technology well** - which checks to auto-grade, which need my judgment, and how to make online checks harder to game (application questions, explain-your-reasoning, varied versions).
3. **Tracking system** - a simple gradebook or mastery tracker layout (columns, scale such as not yet / approaching / met), and how often to update it.
4. **Acting on the data** - what to do when a student or group is behind: reteach, small groups, extra practice; and how to flag students who aren't engaging online.
5. **Feedback loop** - how students see their own progress and what they do next.
6. **Fairness and access** - options for students with limited devices or connectivity and with accommodations.

Keep the workload realistic: estimate my weekly grading time and suggest cuts if it's too high.
variables: e.g. LMS, quiz tools, shared docs, discussion boards
grading time, device access, students with accommodations

title: Plan post-training nudges that make learning stick
description: A spaced reinforcement sequence of short practice prompts, reminders, and challenges sent in the weeks after a training session.
content:
Plan a reinforcement campaign to send learners after a training program.

**Program and objectives:** [DETAILS]
**Key behaviors to apply on the job:** [LIST]
**Learners and their work rhythm:** [e.g. "nurses on rotating shifts", "remote sales reps"]
**Channel:** [email, Slack/Teams, LMS app, SMS]
**Duration:** [e.g. "6 weeks after the workshop"]
**Manager involvement:** [yes / no]

Design rules:
- Use spaced retrieval: ask learners to recall and apply, not just re-read. Space nudges out with longer gaps over time.
- Mix nudge types: scenario question, quick reflection, on-the-job challenge, peer share, success story, myth vs. fact.
- Each nudge takes under 2 minutes and links to one behavior.
- Write like a colleague, not a marketing email. Make opting into replies easy.
- Include at least one nudge that asks what is getting in the way of applying the learning.

Return:
1. A schedule table: Day | Behavior | Nudge type | Message (ready to send) | Response or action requested.
2. Answer and explanation for every question nudge (sent the next day or on reply).
3. A note on how to adjust if engagement drops.
4. What to measure: response rates, answer accuracy over time, self-reported application, and manager observations.
variables: e.g. "nurses on rotating shifts", "remote sales reps"

title: Plan several ways to teach a concept my students keep getting wrong
description: Teaching moves for a stubborn concept: analogies with their limits, a board visual, misconceptions to confront, a demo, and check questions.
content:
Help me explain a concept my students struggle with.

**Concept:** [e.g. "photosynthesis vs. respiration", "statistical significance", "the subjunctive mood"]
**Level:** [GRADE OR COURSE]
**What students already understand:** [PRIOR KNOWLEDGE]
**Where they get stuck:** [e.g. "they think p < 0.05 means the result is important"]
**Students' interests or context:** [optional - e.g. "many play sports", "rural community"]

Give me:
1. **A plain-language explanation** in 3-5 sentences at my students' level.
2. **2 analogies**, each with a note on where the analogy breaks down so I can say so.
3. **A visual or diagram idea** I can sketch on the board, described step by step.
4. **A concrete example and a non-example** that show the boundary of the concept.
5. **The misconceptions** behind where students get stuck, and a short way to confront each one.
6. **A quick demonstration or activity** (under 10 minutes) that lets students experience the idea.
7. **3 check questions** from easy to hard, with answers.

Rules:
- Keep it accurate for the level; simplify without saying anything that will need to be unlearned later. Flag any simplification that is technically incomplete.
- Avoid analogies that rely on cultural knowledge some students may not share, or offer an alternative.
variables: e.g. "they think p < 0.05 means the result is important"

title: Plan structured literacy tutoring for a student with dyslexia
description: A one-on-one reading intervention plan built on explicit, systematic phonics, with session routines and progress checks.
content:
Help me plan one-on-one reading tutoring for a student with dyslexia, based on structured literacy.

**Student:** [age, grade, language(s) spoken at home]
**What I know about their reading:** [assessment results if any, e.g. phonological awareness, decoding, oral reading fluency, spelling; specific errors I see]
**Strengths and interests:** [WHAT MOTIVATES THEM]
**Schedule:** [sessions per week, minutes per session, number of weeks]
**My role:** [parent / teacher / tutor / specialist]
**Materials I have:** [decodable books, letter tiles, a specific program, none]

Create:
1. **Starting point:** which skills to check first and simple informal checks I can use, in this order: phonological and phonemic awareness, letter-sound knowledge, decoding, encoding (spelling), fluency, vocabulary, comprehension.
2. **Scope and sequence:** the order to teach sound-spelling patterns and syllable types, starting from what the student already knows.
3. **Session template:** a timed routine — review, phonemic awareness warm-up, explicit new concept, guided practice, decodable text reading, dictation, and a short success to end on. Include multisensory options.
4. **Sample lesson:** one complete session for the student's current level.
5. **Progress monitoring:** what to measure (e.g. accuracy on taught patterns, words correct per minute), how often, and when to move on or reteach.
6. **Motivation and confidence:** how to keep sessions encouraging.
7. **Home and classroom support:** simple accommodations like audiobooks and extra time.

This plan supports, but does not replace, a formal evaluation. If the student has not been assessed, suggest asking the school or a qualified specialist for one.
variables: age, grade, language(s) spoken at home
sessions per week, minutes per session, number of weeks
decodable books, letter tiles, a specific program, none

title: Practice a new language with a patient tutor
description: Conversation practice with gentle corrections, vocabulary, and grammar at your level.
content:
Be my language tutor for [LANGUAGE].

**My level:** [beginner / A2 / B1 / B2 / C1]
**My native language:** [LANGUAGE]
**Goal:** [travel / work / exam / conversation]
**Topics I enjoy:** [LIST]

How we'll practice:
- Hold a conversation with me in [LANGUAGE] at my level. Keep your replies short so I talk more.
- After each of my messages: show a corrected version of what I wrote, explain the 1–2 most important mistakes briefly (in my native language if I'm a beginner), then continue the conversation.
- Introduce 3–5 useful new words or phrases per session, and reuse them later.
- Every 10 exchanges, give me a quick summary of my recurring mistakes.

Start by asking me a simple question about my day.

title: Practice a real conversation through role-play
description: Rehearse sales calls, feedback, negotiations, or difficult talks with an AI playing the other person.
content:
Act as an expert workplace simulation coach.

**Context**
I need to practice [SKILL] in a realistic professional situation.

**Task**
Create a scenario with realistic constraints and stakeholder responses. Let me respond before evaluating me. Score my response against clear criteria and provide coaching.

**Format**
Start with:
- Scenario
- My objective
- Constraints
- Stakeholder context
Then wait for my response.
After I respond, provide:
- Evaluation
- What worked
- What to improve
- Better response example

**Skill:** [PASTE]

title: Prepare for an exam
description: A study schedule, practice questions from your syllabus or past papers, and a revision strategy.
content:
Help me prepare for an exam.

**Exam and subject:** [NAME]
**Date and time available to study:** [DATE / HOURS PER DAY]
**Syllabus or topics:** [PASTE]
**Past papers or sample questions (optional):** [PASTE]
**Where I'm strong and weak:** [SELF-ASSESSMENT]

Deliver:
1. Topic priorities — weight by exam importance (from past papers if provided) and my weakness.
2. A day-by-day study schedule with spaced review and full practice tests before the exam.
3. Exam patterns — question types and topics that come up repeatedly.
4. 10 practice questions on my weakest topic, with answers and explanations after I attempt them.
5. Exam-day strategy — time allocation and question order.

Quiz me when I'm ready: one question at a time, and track what I get wrong.

title: Prepare questions to bring to office hours
description: A short list of focused questions and what to bring, so a 10-minute office hours visit actually helps.
content:
Help me prepare for office hours with my professor or teacher so I get real help in a short visit.

**Course and current topic:** [e.g. "Intro Stats - hypothesis testing"]
**What I'm confused about:** [DESCRIBE IN YOUR OWN WORDS, even if messy]
**What I've already tried:** [re-read notes, watched videos, attempted problems]
**Specific problems or passages:** [PASTE OR LIST]
**Other goals for the visit:** [e.g. "ask about research opportunities", "introduce myself", "talk about my grade"]
**Time I'll likely have:** [e.g. "10 minutes, there's usually a line"]

Do this:
1. Turn my confusion into 3-5 specific questions, ordered from most to least important. Replace vague questions ("I don't get chapter 4") with precise ones ("Why do we use n-1 instead of n here?").
2. For each question, tell me what to bring or have open (my attempt, the problem, my notes).
3. Suggest one question that shows how I'm thinking, so they can spot my misunderstanding.
4. Give me a 2-sentence way to introduce myself if this is my first visit.
5. Suggest a quick way to take notes during the conversation and a follow-up step afterward.

Return: the prioritized question list, what to bring, the introduction, and a 3-item after-the-visit checklist. Keep it brief enough to read on my phone while I wait.
variables: DESCRIBE IN YOUR OWN WORDS, even if messy
re-read notes, watched videos, attempted problems
e.g. "10 minutes, there's usually a line"

title: Prepare SME interview questions to capture expert know-how
description: A structured interview plan that pulls the real decisions, mistakes, and shortcuts out of a subject matter expert, not just theory.
content:
Help me prepare to interview a subject matter expert (SME) so I can build training from what they know.

**Topic or task:** [WHAT THE TRAINING COVERS]
**SME's role:** [e.g. "senior claims adjuster, 12 years"]
**Learners:** [WHO WILL TAKE THE TRAINING and their experience level]
**Time I have with the SME:** [e.g. "two 45-minute sessions"]
**What I already have:** [existing docs, slides, SOPs, or "nothing"]

Build an interview plan that:
- Focuses on what people must DO, not everything the SME knows.
- Uses cognitive task analysis techniques: walk me through a real recent case, critical decision points, cues they notice, what a novice would miss.
- Surfaces the most common and most costly mistakes, and why people make them.
- Separates "must know" from "nice to know" and "can look up".
- Captures real stories and examples I can turn into scenarios.

Return:
1. A one-paragraph pre-interview note to send the SME (purpose, time, what to bring).
2. Interview questions grouped by phase: warm-up, task walkthrough, decisions and judgment, mistakes and edge cases, wrap-up. Mark the 8 must-ask questions.
3. Follow-up probes for when answers are vague ("It depends" - on what?).
4. A note-taking template: Task step | Decision or cue | Common error | Example or story | Must/Should/Could know.
5. Tips for keeping a talkative SME on track and for validating content afterward.
variables: WHO WILL TAKE THE TRAINING and their experience level

title: Quiz me on a work topic and pinpoint my knowledge gaps
description: An adaptive quiz, one question at a time, followed by a gap report showing what you know, what you half know, and what to study.
content:
Test my understanding of a topic and tell me exactly where my gaps are.

**Topic:** [TOPIC]
**Material to base questions on (optional):** [PASTE NOTES, DOCUMENT, OR COURSE CONTENT]
**My role and why I need this:** [CONTEXT]
**Level I am aiming for:** [working knowledge / confident practitioner / can teach others]

How to run it:
1. Ask 10-12 questions, one at a time, and wait for my answer before the next.
2. Mix question types: explain in my own words, apply to a work situation, spot the error, compare two ideas, and predict what happens.
3. Adapt: if I answer well, go harder; if I struggle, probe the same idea from another angle before moving on.
4. After each answer, give one line of feedback: correct, partly correct, or incorrect, and why. Do not give long lectures mid-quiz.
5. Ask me to rate my confidence (1-5) on each answer, so we can spot overconfidence.

At the end, return a gap report:
- **Solid** - ideas I clearly understand.
- **Shaky** - partly right, or right with low confidence.
- **Gaps** - wrong or missing, including any misconceptions.
- **Blind spots** - wrong answers I was confident about (highest priority).
- A table: Concept | Status | Evidence from my answer | What to review | Practice task.
- The 3 things to study first.

If I provided material, base questions and answers on it and do not add outside facts without labeling them.
variables: PASTE NOTES, DOCUMENT, OR COURSE CONTENT
working knowledge / confident practitioner / can teach others

title: Redesign a lecture with active learning for a large class
description: Breaks a lecture into short segments with active-learning activities that work in a large room and fit the time.
content:
Help me add active learning to one of my lectures.

**Course and topic:** [e.g. "intro chemistry, acid-base equilibria"]
**Class size and room:** [e.g. "220 students, tiered lecture hall, fixed seats"]
**Session length:** [MINUTES]
**Learning outcomes for this session:** [LIST]
**Current lecture outline or slides:** [PASTE OUTLINE]
**Tools available:** [polling app, LMS, whiteboards, TAs in the room]

Redesign the session:
1. Split the content into segments of 10-15 minutes, each tied to an outcome.
2. Between segments, insert an activity that fits a large fixed-seat room, such as think-pair-share, peer instruction with a concept question, a minute paper, a worked-example completion, or a prediction before a demo. For each, give the exact prompt, timing, and how I'll bring the room back.
3. Write 2 concept questions for peer instruction with distractors based on common misconceptions.
4. Cut or move content to pre-class reading if the time doesn't fit, and tell me what you moved.
5. Add a plan for low participation in the first activity (how to set norms and keep it low-stakes).

Return a minute-by-minute run sheet: Time | Segment or activity | What I do | What students do | Outcome. Keep at least 30% of the session for student activity.
variables: e.g. "220 students, tiered lecture hall, fixed seats"
polling app, LMS, whiteboards, TAs in the room

title: Redesign an assignment so it still measures learning in the age of AI
description: Rethinks an assignment so it shows genuine student understanding, using process evidence, personal context, and in-class components.
content:
Help me redesign an assignment so it still measures what students actually learned now that AI tools are widely available.

**Current assignment:** [PASTE PROMPT AND RUBRIC]
**Course and level:** [LEVEL]
**What it is meant to assess:** [SKILLS OR OUTCOMES]
**My AI policy for this assignment:** [e.g. "not allowed", "allowed for brainstorming with disclosure", "required and documented"]
**Constraints:** [class size, grading time, online vs. in person]

Do the following:
1. Test it honestly: explain how a student could complete the current version with AI with little learning, and which outcomes are most at risk.
2. Propose 3 redesign options, mixing approaches such as: staged process with drafts and reflections, connection to class-specific material or local data, personal experience, in-class or oral components, critiquing or improving an AI output, or a short follow-up conversation.
3. For the option you recommend: rewrite the student prompt, list the deliverables at each stage, and update the rubric so it rewards the thinking I care about.
4. Estimate the added grading time and suggest how to keep it manageable.
5. Write a short student-facing explanation of why the assignment is designed this way.

Don't suggest relying on AI-detection tools as evidence; they are unreliable. Keep accessibility in mind (oral components need alternatives for students with accommodations).
variables: class size, grading time, online vs. in person

title: Remember what I learned with a spaced-review plan
description: A spaced-repetition schedule with recall and application tasks so new knowledge sticks.
content:
Act as a learning-science-informed instructional designer.

**Context**
I have learned [TOPIC] but want to retain and apply it over time.

**Task**
Create a spaced retrieval plan using increasingly difficult recall and application tasks. Prioritize active recall, practical application, and error correction over passive rereading.

**Format**
Use:
| Time | Recall task | Application task | Success criterion |
Schedule: Day 1, 3, 7, 14, 30.

**Topic:** [PASTE]

title: Review an e-learning draft against instructional design best practices
description: A structured quality review of a draft course or storyboard covering alignment, cognitive load, practice, feedback, and usability.
content:
Review my draft e-learning module or storyboard before it goes to development or launch.

**Objectives:** [LIST]
**Learners:** [WHO and their context]
**Draft:** [PASTE STORYBOARD, SCRIPT, OR SCREEN-BY-SCREEN TEXT]
**Constraints:** [length limit, authoring tool, stakeholder must-haves]

Review against these criteria:
1. Alignment: does every section serve an objective, and does every objective get practice and assessment?
2. Relevance: does it open with why it matters to the learner and use realistic job examples?
3. Cognitive load: chunk size, text density, unnecessary detail, redundant narration and on-screen text, decorative visuals that distract.
4. Practice: are learners making decisions and applying content, or just clicking next and answering recall questions?
5. Feedback: is it explanatory and tied to consequences?
6. Navigation and usability: clear instructions, consistent controls, progress indicators, no forced locking without reason.
7. Tone and language: plain, consistent, inclusive, learner-focused.
8. Accessibility basics.

Return:
1. An overall verdict and the 3 biggest problems to fix first.
2. A table: Screen or section | Issue | Criterion | Suggested fix | Severity.
3. Rewrites for the 3 weakest screens.
4. Content that could be cut or moved to a job aid.

Do not alter technical facts; flag doubtful content as [CONFIRM WITH SME].
variables: PASTE STORYBOARD, SCRIPT, OR SCREEN-BY-SCREEN TEXT
length limit, authoring tool, stakeholder must-haves

title: Review my weekly learning progress and adjust the plan
description: A short weekly check-in that spots plateaus, finds your bottleneck, and sets next week's practice.
content:
Run a weekly review of my progress on a skill I'm learning and help me adjust the plan.

**Skill and 90-day goal:** [DETAILS]
**My current plan or drills:** [PASTE FROM STEP 3, or describe what I'm doing each session]
**This week's practice log:** [PASTE - sessions done, drills, success rates, notes]
**Benchmark or test results so far:** [SCORES OR OBSERVATIONS, with dates]
**What felt hard / easy:** [NOTES]
**What got in the way:** [TIME, ENERGY, MOTIVATION, OTHER]

Analyze:
1. Planned vs. actual practice time, and whether the plan is realistic for my life.
2. Which sub-skills improved and what the evidence is.
3. Plateau vs. normal dip: same errors and a flat success rate for 2+ weeks suggest a plateau; a short dip after raising difficulty is normal.
4. Whether I am drifting toward practicing what's comfortable instead of what's hard.
5. The single biggest bottleneck right now.

Return:
- A three-sentence summary of the week.
- What's working (keep doing).
- The one bottleneck and why it matters.
- No more than 3 changes for next week (keep / adjust / drop).
- Next week's session plan.
- Two short reflection questions for me to answer before the next review.

Keep it brief and practical. If I missed sessions, focus on an easy restart, not on guilt. This is step 4 of the "Teach yourself a new skill in 90 days" pack. It works on its own, and can use the drills and log from step 3.
variables: PASTE FROM STEP 3, or describe what I'm doing each session
PASTE - sessions done, drills, success rates, notes

title: Rewrite a text at several reading levels for my students
description: Adapts a reading passage into leveled versions that keep the content and key vocabulary, with comprehension questions.
content:
Rewrite a reading passage at different levels so all my students can access the same content.

**Original text:** [PASTE IT - only content I'm allowed to adapt for classroom use]
**Grade level of my class:** [GRADE]
**Levels needed:** [e.g. "2nd-3rd grade, 5th grade, 7th grade" or Lexile ranges]
**Content and vocabulary that must stay:** [KEY CONCEPTS AND TERMS]
**Purpose:** [e.g. "background for a science lab", "shared discussion tomorrow"]

For each level:
1. Rewrite the passage, keeping every key concept and fact. Do not add new facts or change meaning.
2. Adjust sentence length, syntax, and vocabulary to the level, but keep the key terms and define them in context or in a short glossary.
3. Keep the same headings and structure so students can discuss across levels.
4. Write 3 comprehension questions at that level: one literal, one inferential, and one connecting to the purpose.

Then add:
- A shared discussion question every level can answer.
- A note on which details were simplified, so I can check accuracy.

Readability estimates are approximate; tell me to check with my school's leveling tool if exact levels matter. Return each version under a clear heading with an approximate word count.
variables: e.g. "2nd-3rd grade, 5th grade, 7th grade" or Lexile ranges

title: Rewrite quiz questions to test application, not recall
description: Reviews my existing assessment items for common writing flaws and rewrites them as scenario-based questions with useful feedback.
content:
Review and improve my existing quiz or assessment questions.

**Learning objectives they should measure:** [PASTE OBJECTIVES]
**Learners:** [WHO and their job context]
**The questions (with answer options and correct answers):** [PASTE QUESTIONS]
**Stakes:** [knowledge check / graded / certification]

For each question, check for these item-writing flaws:
- Tests trivia or recall when the objective requires a decision or application.
- Answer can be guessed from cues: longest option, grammatical mismatch, repeated words from the stem, "all of the above".
- Implausible distractors no real learner would pick.
- Negative stems ("Which is NOT...") without a good reason.
- Ambiguity: more than one defensible answer, or depends on context not given.
- Not linked to any objective.

Then rewrite weak items as short workplace scenarios where the learner must choose what to do. Distractors should reflect real mistakes people make on the job.

Return:
1. A table: Question # | Objective it maps to | Flaws found | Keep / Revise / Cut.
2. Rewritten questions with the correct answer marked.
3. Feedback for every option: why it is right or wrong, written to the learner in 1-2 sentences.
4. Objectives with no question measuring them, and a suggested item for each.

Do not change the technical facts in my content. If a correct answer looks wrong or outdated, mark it [CONFIRM WITH SME] instead of changing it.

title: Run a learning needs analysis
description: Identifies what a role or team needs to learn — and what isn't a training problem.
content:
Role: Act as a capability building lead conducting a learning needs analysis.

Context: Team or role in scope: [SCOPE]. Business goal and the performance it depends on: [GOAL_PERFORMANCE]. Evidence of the current gap (metrics, manager input, observations): [EVIDENCE]. What has been tried: [PRIOR]. Constraints: [CONSTRAINTS].

Task: Produce: the specific performance gaps (current vs required, with evidence); a root-cause read for each (skill / knowledge / motivation / environment / process) - be explicit that not all gaps are training problems; recommended interventions split into learning and non-learning (process, tools, incentives, management); and a prioritised plan by impact and feasibility.

Format: Sections: Performance gaps | Root causes | Interventions (learning / non-learning) | Priorities (table). ~450 words.

Verification: Flag every gap where the evidence is thin, and every case where training is unlikely to fix the real cause.

Validation: Challenge as a sceptical business sponsor: which recommended item would actually change the metric, and which is training for its own sake? Cut the latter.

title: Run a workplace simulation that gets harder as I improve
description: An interactive role-play of a realistic work situation that raises the difficulty each round and scores how you handled it.
content:
Run an interactive workplace simulation so I can practice a skill.

**Skill to practice:** [e.g. "handling an angry client", "pushing back on a senior stakeholder", "triaging an incident", "negotiating a renewal"]
**My role and setting:** [DETAILS - industry, team, who I deal with]
**My current level:** [new to this / some experience / experienced]
**What a good outcome looks like:** [CRITERIA]

How to run it:
1. Set the scene in 3-5 sentences: who is involved, what is at stake, and what I know. Then play the other people realistically, including incomplete information and emotions.
2. Let me respond in my own words. Do not coach me during a round.
3. After each round, step out of the role and give feedback:
   - What worked.
   - What to change, with a better example line.
   - A score from 1-5 against my success criteria.
4. Run 4 rounds, each harder than the last. Increase difficulty by adding time pressure, conflicting goals, a difficult personality, missing data, or a twist mid-conversation.
5. If I score 2 or below, repeat the same difficulty with a new scenario before moving up.

At the end, return:
- A table: Round | Scenario | Score | Main strength | Main fix.
- My 3 most important habits to build.
- One scenario to try again next week.

Keep scenarios realistic for my industry. Start with round 1 now.
variables: DETAILS - industry, team, who I deal with
new to this / some experience / experienced

title: Set a target score and test date for my graduate admissions test
description: A target score grounded in your programs' published data, a test date that leaves room for a retake, and a weekly prep load.
content:
Help me set a target score and choose a test date for my graduate admissions test.

**Test:** [e.g. "GRE", "GMAT", "LSAT", "MCAT"]
**Programs I'm applying to:** [LIST]
**Their published score data:** [PASTE MEDIANS OR RANGES FROM EACH PROGRAM'S OFFICIAL CLASS PROFILE]
**Application deadlines:** [DATES]
**Diagnostic or past score (if any):** [SCORE AND DATE, or "none yet"]
**Hours per week I can study:** [DETAILS]
**Other parts of my application:** [e.g. "strong GPA", "limited work experience"]

Rules:
- Use only the score data I paste. Do not guess program medians or ranges. If I haven't provided them, tell me where to find them (each program's class profile or admissions page).
- Suggest aiming at or above the median of my target programs, adjusted for the strength of the rest of my application.
- Check whether any program is test-optional or accepts an alternative test, based on what I paste, and mark it [CONFIRM on the program's site].

Return:
1. A target score, plus a minimum acceptable score, with the reasoning.
2. A recommended test date that leaves time for one retake before my earliest deadline, including score reporting time [CONFIRM with the testing organization].
3. The gap between my current and target score, and a realistic weekly study load and total prep length for that gap (state the uncertainty).
4. A short list of first actions this week: take an official diagnostic, register, gather materials.

This is step 1 of the "Prepare for a graduate admissions test" pack. The target and timeline feed step 2 (diagnosing a practice test).

title: Set up a note-taking system that works for my classes
description: A note-taking method matched to each of your classes, with a template and a quick after-class review routine.
content:
Help me set up a note-taking system that actually helps me learn and study.

**My classes and how they're taught:** [e.g. "Biology - fast slides, lots of terms", "History - discussion-based", "Calculus - board problems"]
**How I take notes now:** [laptop, tablet, paper; what I do with them afterward]
**Problems I have:** [e.g. "I write everything and miss the point", "I can't keep up", "I never look at them again"]
**Learning needs or accommodations:** [optional, e.g. note-taker, recordings allowed]

Do this:
1. Recommend a method for each class type and explain why: Cornell notes, outline, mapping, charting (tables) for comparisons, or worked-example notes for math and science.
2. Weigh handwriting vs. typing for each class, and how to avoid distractions if typing.
3. Give me a template for my main method.
4. Show how to catch the important points: cues professors give (repetition, "this will be on the exam", what's written on the board).
5. Build a short after-class routine (10-15 minutes within 24 hours): fill gaps, write questions, summarize in 2-3 sentences.
6. Explain how to turn notes into study material later (self-quizzing from the cue column).

Return: a table (Class | Method | Why), the template, the after-class routine, and a weekly review habit. Keep it simple enough to start next class.
variables: laptop, tablet, paper; what I do with them afterward

title: Set up classroom routines and procedures for the first weeks of school
description: A plan for teaching the key routines that make a class run smoothly, with scripts, practice, and reinforcement.
content:
Help me plan the routines and procedures I'll teach in the first weeks of school.

**Grade level and subject:** [e.g. "kindergarten" or "10th grade English, 5 sections"]
**Class size and room setup:** [e.g. "28 students, tables of 4"]
**Schedule:** [e.g. "50-minute periods", "self-contained day"]
**My biggest pain points last year:** [e.g. "chaotic transitions", "bathroom requests", "students not starting work"]
**School-wide expectations to align with:** [e.g. PBIS matrix, hall pass system]

Do the following:
1. List the 8-12 routines that matter most for my setting (e.g. entering, starting work, getting help, transitions, turning in work, technology, dismissal), ranked by impact.
2. For each, write: the step-by-step procedure in student-friendly words, a short script for introducing it, how students will practice it, and what I'll say when it goes well or poorly.
3. Create a rollout schedule for the first 2-3 weeks: which routines to teach on which days, and when to re-practice.
4. Suggest how to post or display each routine (anchor chart, slide, visual cues for younger students or English learners).

Keep procedures short (3-5 steps). Make reinforcement positive and specific. Return the routines as a table: Routine | Steps | How to teach | How to practice | Day introduced.
variables: e.g. PBIS matrix, hall pass system

title: Start a student-run study group or learning community
description: Roles, meeting formats, accountability habits, and a launch plan for a peer learning group that keeps going without a teacher running it.
content:
Help me set up a student-run study group or learning community.

**Who it's for:** [e.g. "first-year engineering students", "high school juniors taking AP Biology", "adult coding learners"]
**Shared goal:** [e.g. "pass the course final", "build projects together", "read and discuss one book a month"]
**Expected size:** [NUMBER]
**Format:** [in person / online / hybrid; how often]
**Support available:** [teacher sponsor, room booking, budget, platform]
**What has gone wrong in past groups:** [e.g. "people stop showing up", "one person does all the work"]

Give me:
1. A one-paragraph charter: purpose, who can join, and what members commit to.
2. Rotating roles (e.g. facilitator, timekeeper, note-taker, question-setter) with a one-line job description each and a rotation plan.
3. Three meeting formats with timed agendas, matched to the goal (e.g. teach-back, problem-solving sprint, practice quiz, peer review of work).
4. Accountability that motivates without shaming: goal check-ins, progress tracking, and what happens when someone falls behind.
5. Ground rules for respectful discussion, inclusion, and academic honesty (share understanding, not answers on graded work).
6. A shared resource system: notes, question bank, and how to keep it organized.
7. A launch plan for the first 4 weeks, and how to hand leadership to new members so it outlasts the founders.
8. Signs the group is working, and a quick monthly health check.

Keep it simple enough to run with 1-2 hours of organizing per month.
variables: in person / online / hybrid; how often
teacher sponsor, room booking, budget, platform
e.g. "people stop showing up", "one person does all the work"

title: Storyboard an e-learning module
description: Screen-by-screen storyboard and script for an e-learning module.
content:
Role: Act as an instructional designer scripting a self-paced e-learning module.

Context: Module objective: [OBJECTIVE]. Content source / SME notes: [CONTENT]. Audience and reading level: [AUDIENCE]. Runtime target: [RUNTIME]. Authoring tool and interaction types available: [TOOL_INTERACTIONS]. Accessibility requirements: [ACCESSIBILITY]. Brand/style notes: [STYLE].

Task: Produce a storyboard: for each screen give the purpose, on-screen text (concise), narration script (conversational, matched to on-screen text), visual/media direction, and the interaction or knowledge check. Include an intro screen with the objective and a summary screen. Keep to the runtime.

Format: A screen-by-screen table: Screen # | Purpose | On-screen text | Narration | Visual | Interaction.

Verification: Flag any screen where narration just reads the on-screen text, any check not tied to the objective, and any media that would fail the accessibility requirements.

Validation: Review as a learner clicking through: is each screen doing one job, and does the module hold attention for its runtime? Cut or merge weak screens.

title: Teach me a work topic using examples from my own role
description: Explains a topic at beginner, intermediate, and advanced levels using situations from your job, with a quick check at each level.
content:
Teach me a topic using examples from my actual job.

**Topic:** [e.g. "discounted cash flow", "API rate limits", "change management"]
**My role and what I work on:** [DETAILS - e.g. "procurement manager negotiating software contracts"]
**What I already know:** [NOTHING / SOME BASICS / USED IT A BIT]
**Why I need it now:** [e.g. "a meeting next week", "new project"]
**Time I have:** [e.g. 15 minutes]

Teach it in three levels, each built on examples from my role:
1. **Beginner** - what it is and why it matters to my work, one plain analogy, one example from my day-to-day.
2. **Intermediate** - how it actually works, the key terms I will hear, and a worked example using a realistic situation from my job.
3. **Advanced** - edge cases, trade-offs, common mistakes experienced people still make, and how experts reason about it.

After each level, ask me one question to check understanding and wait for my answer before moving on. If my answer shows a gap, re-explain that part a different way.

Finish with:
- A one-paragraph summary I could repeat in a meeting.
- 5 terms with plain definitions.
- 3 questions I could ask a colleague who knows this well.
- One small way to use this at work this week.

If the topic depends on my company's specific rules, numbers, or systems, say so and tell me what to confirm internally rather than guessing.
variables: NOTHING / SOME BASICS / USED IT A BIT

title: Train store associates on clienteling and add-on selling
description: A short floor-ready training session with a service sequence, model language, role-plays, and coaching targets that raise UPT without pushiness.
content:
Create a training session that teaches my store associates clienteling and add-on selling.

**Store type and products:** [e.g. "specialty apparel", "home goods", "beauty"]
**Current metrics and goals:** [ATV, UPT, conversion - current and target]
**Tools available:** [clienteling app, customer profiles, loyalty program, text and email consent capture]
**Associates' experience:** [NEW / MIXED / EXPERIENCED]
**Commission or incentives:** [YES/NO - affects the risk of pushy selling]
**Session length and format:** [e.g. "45 minutes before opening, standing"]

Include:
1. Learning goals: what associates will do differently on the floor.
2. A simple service sequence: greet, discover needs with open questions, recommend, complete the outfit or solution with add-ons that genuinely fit, close, and follow up.
3. Model language for each step, plus phrases to avoid because they feel pushy.
4. Clienteling basics: what to record in a customer profile (sizes, preferences, past purchases, upcoming occasions), and how to follow up, only with the customer's documented consent to be contacted.
5. Three role-play scenarios, each with a brief for the person playing the shopper and an observer checklist (e.g. a "just looking" browser, a gift shopper on a budget, a returning regular).
6. Practice targets for the next two weeks and how the manager will coach on the floor.
7. A five-question quiz with answers.

Add-ons must solve the customer's need. Associates should never misrepresent products, prices, or promotions.
variables: ATV, UPT, conversion - current and target
YES/NO - affects the risk of pushy selling

title: Turn a certification exam outline into a weighted readiness checklist
description: Each exam domain and objective scored by weight and your confidence, so you study where the points are.
content:
Turn my certification's official exam outline into a weighted readiness checklist.

**Certification:** [NAME and exam code/version - e.g. "PMP", "AWS Solutions Architect Associate", "CPA - FAR section"]
**Official exam outline:** [PASTE THE DOMAINS, OBJECTIVES, AND WEIGHTINGS FROM THE OFFICIAL EXAM GUIDE]
**My background:** [RELEVANT EXPERIENCE AND TRAINING]
**Exam date:** [DATE, or "not booked yet"]

Rules:
- Use only the outline I paste. If I haven't pasted one, ask me for it rather than guessing domains or weightings; outlines change between exam versions.
- List every objective, then ask me to rate my confidence on each from 1 (never heard of it) to 5 (could teach it). If I've already given ratings, use them.
- Calculate a priority score for each objective: domain weight x (5 - my confidence).

Return:
1. A table: Domain | Weight | Objective | My confidence (1-5) | Priority score | Notes (e.g. "hands-on practice needed", "memorization").
2. My top 5 priorities, with the kind of study each needs (concept, hands-on, memorization, scenario practice).
3. Strengths to maintain with light review only.
4. A suggested split of my total study hours by domain.
5. Objectives where experience at work may mislead me because the exam expects the official framework's answer.

This is step 1 of the "Pass a professional certification exam" pack. The priorities feed step 2 (the study calendar).

title: Turn a compliance policy into engaging mandatory training
description: Converts a dry policy into scenario-driven compliance training that changes behavior and still meets audit requirements.
content:
Help me turn a compliance policy into mandatory training people will actually learn from.

**Policy or regulation:** [PASTE OR SUMMARIZE - e.g. anti-bribery, data privacy, harassment prevention, safety]
**Who must complete it and how often:** [ROLES, annual / onboarding]
**Required elements from legal, compliance, or the regulator:** [e.g. specific topics, minimum duration, attestation, records]
**Real risks and past incidents (anonymized):** [WHAT ACTUALLY GOES WRONG HERE]
**Format and length limit:** [e.g. "25-minute e-learning"]

Design approach:
- Start from the 3-5 behaviors that matter most, not a tour of the whole policy.
- Use realistic gray-area scenarios from these learners' jobs, where the right choice is not obvious.
- Let experienced learners test out of sections they already know, where the requirements allow it.
- Make "how to report or ask for help" concrete: who, how, and what happens next.
- Keep a clear audit trail: completion, assessment score, policy acknowledgment.

Return:
1. A module outline: Section | Key behavior | Scenario | Assessment question | Minutes.
2. Two scenarios written in full with choices and consequences.
3. A plain-language summary of the policy for learners (under 200 words).
4. An attestation statement draft.
5. A checklist mapping each required element to where it is covered.

This is general information. Have legal or compliance review all content and requirements for my jurisdiction before launch. Do not invent legal requirements; mark gaps [CONFIRM WITH COMPLIANCE].
variables: e.g. specific topics, minimum duration, attestation, records

title: Turn a course I finished into on-the-job practice
description: Converts course notes or modules into weekly practice assignments on your real work, so the training changes how you work.
content:
Help me turn what I learned in a course into practice on my actual job.

**Course name and topic:** [DETAILS]
**Course content:** [PASTE MODULE TITLES, NOTES, KEY SLIDES, OR TAKEAWAYS]
**My role and current projects:** [DETAILS]
**What I hoped to change in my work after this course:** [GOAL]
**Time I can spend on practice each week:** [HOURS]
**Who could give me feedback:** [manager, peer, mentor, none]

Steps:
1. Pull out the 5-8 ideas or techniques from the course that are most usable in my role. Skip anything that does not apply, and say why.
2. For each, design an on-the-job assignment using my real work: what to do, when it naturally comes up, and what output it produces.
3. Sequence the assignments over 4-6 weeks, starting with the easiest wins.

Return:
1. A table: Week | Technique from the course | Assignment on my real work | Output | How I will know it worked.
2. A short reflection template to fill in after each assignment (what I tried, what happened, what I will change).
3. How to involve my feedback person: what to ask them and when.
4. A 30-day check: signs the course is changing how I work, and what to do if it is not.

Stick to what the course content says. If my notes are incomplete or a technique is unclear, flag it rather than filling it in.
variables: PASTE MODULE TITLES, NOTES, KEY SLIDES, OR TAKEAWAYS

title: Turn a lecture or transcript into study notes
description: Structured notes, key terms, summaries, and review questions from lectures, videos, or readings.
content:
Turn this lecture, video, or reading into study notes.

**Course and level:** [DETAILS]
**Material:** [PASTE TRANSCRIPT OR TEXT]
**What I'll use the notes for:** [exam / quick review / deep understanding]

Create:
1. **Overview** — the main topic and 3–5 key takeaways.
2. **Structured notes** following the order of the material: headings, concise bullets, and definitions in bold.
3. **Key terms** — a glossary.
4. **Examples and formulas** exactly as given.
5. **Connections** — how ideas link to each other.
6. **Review questions** — 5–10 questions, answers at the end.

Stay faithful to the source: don't add facts that weren't in the material, and mark anything unclear or inaudible as [UNCLEAR].

title: Turn a long work document into a step-by-step learning path
description: Converts a policy, manual, playbook, or spec into short, sequenced lessons with practice and checks.
content:
Turn this document into a learning path I can work through step by step.

**Document:** [PASTE TEXT - e.g. a policy, process manual, product spec, playbook, or standard]
**Who is learning:** [me / a new hire / my team - and their role]
**What they need to be able to do afterward:** [e.g. "handle refund requests without escalating"]
**Time available:** [e.g. "30 minutes a day for one week"]

Steps:
1. Identify the 5-10 core ideas or procedures in the document, and the parts that are reference material (to look up, not memorize).
2. Put them in a learning order: foundations first, then procedures, then exceptions and edge cases.
3. Group them into short modules that fit the time available.

For each module return:
- Learning goal (what the learner can do after it).
- The relevant section of the document, cited by heading or page.
- A plain-language explanation (under 120 words).
- One practice task or scenario from real work.
- 3 check questions, with answers in a separate section at the end.

Also return:
1. A one-page overview of the path (modules, time, goals).
2. A quick-reference sheet of the things people look up most.
3. A final scenario that combines several modules.
4. Any parts of the document that are unclear, contradictory, or out of date, so I can confirm them with the owner.

Use only what is in the document. Do not add rules, numbers, or steps that are not there; mark gaps as [CONFIRM WITH OWNER].
variables: me / a new hire / my team - and their role
e.g. "30 minutes a day for one week"

title: Turn a technical document into theory notes and MATLAB code
description: Section-by-section explanations of the theory in a paper or chapter, with clear MATLAB code that implements each part.
content:
Help me understand a technical document and implement it in MATLAB, one section at a time.

**Document:** [PASTE THE TEXT or describe the paper/chapter and its sections]
**My level:** [e.g. "second-year electrical engineering student", "comfortable with linear algebra, new to DSP"]
**MATLAB version and toolboxes I have:** [e.g. "R2024a, Signal Processing Toolbox" / "base MATLAB only"]
**What I need it for:** [coursework / lab report / reproducing results / my own learning]

For each section of the document:
1. **Theory in plain words:** what the section is doing and why, the key equations with every symbol defined, and any assumptions.
2. **MATLAB code:** a short, runnable script or function that implements the section. Use clear variable names that match the document's notation, comment each step, and avoid toolbox functions I don't have (or show a base-MATLAB alternative).
3. **Code walkthrough:** how each block maps to the equations, what the output should look like, and a quick sanity check (a known input with a known answer, a plot, or a dimension check).
4. **Common mistakes:** indexing (MATLAB starts at 1), element-wise vs. matrix operators (.* vs *), units, and sign conventions.

Rules:
- If the document is ambiguous or skips a step, say so and state the assumption you made.
- Do not invent parameter values or results; mark anything I must supply as [ADD VALUE].
- Keep the code simple enough for me to explain it myself.

End with a list of the sections in order, what each script produces, and how to run them together.
variables: PASTE THE TEXT or describe the paper/chapter and its sections
e.g. "R2024a, Signal Processing Toolbox" / "base MATLAB only"

title: Turn my course syllabus into a ranked list of final exam topics
description: A topic map that ranks what to revise by exam signals and your confidence, so you spend time where marks are.
content:
Turn my course syllabus into a ranked list of topics to revise for the final exam.

**Course:** [NAME AND LEVEL]
**Syllabus or learning outcomes:** [PASTE]
**Exam format:** [e.g. "3 hours, 4 essay questions from 8", "60 multiple choice + 3 problems", open or closed book]
**Exam weight in my grade:** [e.g. "40%"]
**What the instructor emphasized:** [e.g. "said week 7 will definitely come up", review session notes]
**Past paper topics (if I have them):** [LIST OR PASTE]
**My confidence by topic (optional):** [STRONG / OK / WEAK]

Rules:
- Rank topics only from the signals I give: stated learning outcomes, instructor emphasis, past papers, and time spent in class. Do not guess what will be on the exam.
- Point out topics that connect several others, since they tend to support many questions.
- If the format lets me choose questions, tell me how many topics I can safely skip, and the risk of doing so.

Return:
1. A table: Topic | Weeks or lectures | Exam signals | My confidence | Priority (high / medium / low) | Type of revision needed (understand, memorize, practice problems, essay planning).
2. My top priorities in revision order.
3. Topics to cover lightly and why.
4. Questions to ask my instructor or TA to confirm the exam scope.

This is step 1 of the "Ace your university final exams" pack. The ranked list feeds step 2 (practice questions) and step 4 (revision timetable).

title: Turn my mistakes at work into lessons and a practice plan
description: Analyzes what went wrong without blame, finds the pattern behind your mistakes, and builds habits and practice to prevent repeats.
content:
Help me turn my recent mistakes at work into lessons I actually learn from.

**The mistakes (what happened, when, and the impact):** [DESCRIBE 1-5 MISTAKES - e.g. "sent a report with last month's numbers", "missed a dependency in a project plan"]
**What I was trying to do at the time:** [CONTEXT]
**Feedback I received, if any:** [PASTE OR DESCRIBE]
**What has already been fixed:** [ACTIONS TAKEN]

For each mistake:
1. Separate what happened from my story about it. State the facts neutrally.
2. Identify the type: knowledge gap (did not know), skill gap (knew but could not execute), process gap (no check in place), attention or overload, or judgment call that turned out wrong.
3. Find the root cause by asking "why" until we reach something I can change.

Then look across all mistakes for a pattern (e.g. rushing at deadlines, skipping review, unclear requirements).

Return:
1. A table: Mistake | Type | Root cause | Lesson in one sentence.
2. The pattern, if there is one.
3. Prevention: a checklist step, habit, or process change for each root cause.
4. A short practice plan for any knowledge or skill gaps (2-3 exercises using realistic work situations).
5. If useful, a brief, non-defensive note I could send to my manager or team about what I learned and what I changed.

Tone: honest but not harsh. Mistakes are information. Do not minimize real impact, and do not catastrophize.

title: Turn one assignment into three tiers for different readiness levels
description: Rewrites a single task into supported, on-level, and extension versions that all hit the same learning goal.
content:
Help me differentiate one assignment into three tiers so every student works on the same goal at the right level of challenge.

**The original assignment:** [PASTE IT]
**Learning goal everyone must reach:** [e.g. "compare two fractions with unlike denominators and justify"]
**Grade level:** [GRADE]
**Who is in the room:** [e.g. "6 students below grade level in reading, 4 ready for extension, 2 with IEP accommodations for chunked tasks"] (no names)
**Time available:** [MINUTES]

Create:
1. **Tier 1 (supported):** same goal, with scaffolds such as worked examples, sentence frames, visuals, fewer steps per chunk, or manipulatives. Do not lower the goal itself.
2. **Tier 2 (on level):** the core task, tightened if needed.
3. **Tier 3 (extension):** more depth or complexity (transfer, justification, open-ended), not just more problems.

For each tier, give the student-facing instructions and the materials needed.

Then add:
- How to assign tiers quickly (e.g. a 3-question pre-check) and let students move between tiers.
- A shared closing activity where all tiers come back together.
- One way to make the tiers not look ranked to students (neutral names, choice boards).

Check that all three versions can be assessed against the same success criteria, and list those criteria at the end.

title: Turn theory into practice at work
description: Converts a concept or framework into concrete actions in your job.
content:
Act as an applied learning expert.

**Context**
I understand the concept below but struggle to apply it consistently at work.

**Task**
Translate the concept into practical workplace behavior. Give realistic examples, one advanced application, one common mistake, and a simple checklist for daily use.

**Format**
Return:
- Concept in one sentence
- 5 workplace applications
- Common mistake
- Advanced use
- Practical checklist

**Concept:** [PASTE]

title: Understand a philosopher's ideas, from big picture to critique
description: A structured study guide to one philosopher: core ideas, key terms, how they answer life's big questions, criticisms, and what to read first.
content:
Help me understand a philosopher's thinking in depth.

**Philosopher:** [NAME - e.g. "Spinoza", "Simone de Beauvoir", "Nietzsche"]
**My background:** [e.g. "no philosophy background", "undergrad student", "read some Plato"]
**Why I'm studying them:** [course, exam, personal interest, a specific question]
**Depth:** [quick overview / study guide / deep dive]

Work through these phases in order:
1. The big picture: what problem or target they were responding to, the historical context and influences, and their 4-5 core ideas in plain language.
2. Key terms: a glossary of their specialist vocabulary, with what each term means in their usage (not everyday usage).
3. How the system fits together: their views on knowledge, reality, ethics, and politics, and how one leads to another.
4. Personal existence: what their philosophy says about how to live, freedom, meaning, suffering, and death, with one everyday example for each.
5. Critical evaluation: the strongest objections from other thinkers, where the ideas are weakest, and how defenders respond.
6. Legacy: who they influenced and where their ideas show up today.
7. Primary texts: the 3-5 most important works, which to read first, and which sections matter most.

Rules:
- Quote only short, well-known lines, and say which work they come from. If you aren't sure of a quotation or attribution, paraphrase and say so.
- Separate what the philosopher said from common interpretations and from your own summary.
- End with 5 discussion questions and a 5-question self-check quiz with answers.
variables: course, exam, personal interest, a specific question
quick overview / study guide / deep dive

title: Understand the music theory behind a song I love
description: A friendly breakdown of a song's key, chords, rhythm, and structure, explained in plain words.
content:
Explain the music theory behind a song I love, in plain language.

**Song and artist:** [TITLE - ARTIST]
**What I know already:** [e.g. "nothing", "basic chords on guitar", "I read treble clef"]
**What I want to understand:** [e.g. "why the chorus feels so uplifting", "how to play it", "how the bridge changes mood"]
**The chords or notes, if I have them:** [PASTE CHORDS OR TAB, or leave blank]

Explain:
1. Song structure: sections (intro, verse, chorus, bridge) and how they repeat.
2. Key and chords: the key, the main chord progression, and each chord's job (home, tension, release), using Roman numerals with plain-English meaning.
3. What creates the feeling: specific moves like a borrowed chord, key change, rhythm shift, or melody leap, and why they affect the listener.
4. Rhythm and groove: time signature, tempo feel, and anything unusual.
5. One small exercise to try on my instrument (or by ear) to hear the key idea for myself.
6. Two other songs that use a similar trick, for me to look up.

Important: if you're not sure of the exact chords or key from memory, say so and work from the chords I paste, or tell me how to check by ear. Do not reproduce the song's lyrics; refer to sections by name.
variables: PASTE CHORDS OR TAB, or leave blank

title: Update an old ESL lesson or unit to make it engaging and level-appropriate
description: Revises outdated ESL course material for a target CEFR level, with refreshed texts, clearer instructions, and new practice activities.
content:
Help me update an existing ESL lesson or unit.

**Material:** [PASTE the text, exercises, and instructions - or describe each section if it's a PDF]
**Learners:** [age group, first language(s), context - e.g. "adult immigrants", "teens in Brazil", "business English"]
**Target level:** [CEFR level, e.g. A2, B1]
**Lesson length and format:** [e.g. "90 min in person", "self-study online"]
**What feels outdated or isn't working:** [e.g. "old references", "too much grammar, no speaking", "instructions confuse students"]
**Must keep:** [grammar point, vocabulary set, or exam alignment]

Please:
1. **Diagnose** the current material: level fit (vocabulary, sentence length, grammar), dated content, unclear instructions, and the balance of reading, writing, listening, and speaking.
2. **Rewrite the texts** at the target level, with current, culturally inclusive topics and the same target language.
3. **Rewrite instructions** so they are short, imperative, and easy for a learner at that level to follow, with one example per task.
4. **Add practice** that moves from controlled to freer use - e.g. gap-fill, then information gap, then a short role-play or personal task.
5. **Add a warm-up and a quick check** (exit ticket or 5 self-check questions with answers).

Return the revised lesson in order, with timings, plus a table: Original section | What changed | Why. Write all new texts yourself - don't copy passages from published coursebooks.
variables: grammar point, vocabulary set, or exam alignment

title: Work through an engineering or math calculation step by step
description: A fully worked solution with every formula, intermediate value, and a check, so you can follow and repeat it.
content:
Work through this calculation step by step so I can follow and repeat it.

**Problem:** [PASTE THE PROBLEM — e.g. "compute the MDCT of x(n) = [1, 2, 3, 4]", "find the beam deflection at midspan"]
**Given values and units:** [VALUES]
**Course or context:** [e.g. "signals and systems", "statics", "thermodynamics"]
**Method required, if any:** [e.g. "use the definition, not a library function"]
**My level:** [what I already know]

Structure the answer:
1. **Identify:** what is being asked, the knowns, unknowns, and any sizes or parameters (e.g. N, 2N, boundary conditions).
2. **Formula:** the governing equation with every symbol defined, and why it applies.
3. **Substitution:** plug in values one step at a time. When there are many repeated terms (sums, matrices, cosine or sine values), show them in a table so nothing is hidden.
4. **Result:** the final answer with units and sensible rounding.
5. **Check:** a sanity test — dimensions, a limiting case, symmetry, an estimate, or a short code snippet I can run to verify.
6. **Watch out for:** the two or three mistakes students most often make on this type of problem.

Rules:
- Do not skip algebra or arithmetic steps.
- If the problem is ambiguous (conventions, normalization, index starting point), state the assumption and show how the answer would change.
- Then give me a similar practice problem with the answer only, so I can test myself.
variables: e.g. "use the definition, not a library function"

title: Write a Bible study or sermon outline with discussion questions
description: A clear, engaging study outline with discussion questions, scripture references to verify, applications, and a closing appeal.
content:
Help me prepare a Bible study or sermon outline.

**Topic or passage:** [e.g. "the fear of God", "Psalm 23", "forgiveness"]
**Format:** [small-group study / sermon / youth lesson / slide deck]
**Audience:** [e.g. "general congregation", "new believers", "teens"]
**Length:** [minutes or number of slides]
**Tradition and translation:** [e.g. denomination; preferred Bible translation]
**Other sources I want to draw on (optional):** [commentaries or authors I will quote from my own copies]

Create:
1. A lesson title and one-sentence main idea.
2. An opening question or story that connects to everyday life.
3. A question-and-answer flow of 6-10 questions, each answered with scripture references and a short plain-language explanation.
4. Two or three practical applications for this week.
5. A closing appeal and prayer prompt.
6. Small-group discussion questions (if relevant).
7. If I asked for slides: a slide-by-slide outline with a short heading and no more than 30 words per slide.

Accuracy rules:
- Give scripture as book, chapter, and verse references. Only quote verse text if you are confident it matches my translation, and mark every quote [VERIFY IN MY BIBLE].
- Do not invent quotes, page numbers, or citations from other authors. Leave [ADD QUOTE AND PAGE] placeholders for me to fill from sources I have.
- Note where Christian traditions interpret the passage differently, so I can teach it consistently with my own.
variables: small-group study / sermon / youth lesson / slide deck
commentaries or authors I will quote from my own copies

title: Write a course syllabus students will actually read
description: A clear, student-friendly syllabus with outcomes, grading, schedule, and policies, plus a one-page quick-start version.
content:
Help me write a syllabus for my course.

**Course title, level, and format:** [e.g. "PSYC 210, sophomore, in person, 3 credits"]
**Learning outcomes:** [PASTE OR DESCRIBE]
**Major assessments and weights:** [e.g. "3 exams 45%, project 30%, weekly quizzes 15%, participation 10%"]
**Schedule:** [TERM DATES, MEETING DAYS, KEY DEADLINES]
**Policies I want:** [late work, attendance, regrades, AI use, communication response time]
**Required institutional statements:** [PASTE - accessibility, academic integrity, Title IX, etc.]
**Tone I want:** [warm / straightforward / formal]

Write the syllabus with these sections: welcome and why this course matters, how to reach me, learning outcomes, materials, how the course works week to week, assessments and grading (with a table), policies, support resources, and a week-by-week schedule.

Rules:
- Use plain language and second person ("you will"). Explain the reason behind each policy in one sentence.
- Put deadlines and point values in tables, not paragraphs.
- Keep institutional statements word-for-word as I pasted them; if one is missing, insert [ADD REQUIRED STATEMENT] rather than writing your own.
- Make the late-work and regrade policies specific enough to apply consistently.

Also return a one-page "Start here" summary and 5 syllabus quiz questions I can give in week 1.
variables: TERM DATES, MEETING DAYS, KEY DEADLINES
PASTE - accessibility, academic integrity, Title IX, etc.

title: Write a facilitator guide and session run sheet
description: Everything a facilitator needs to deliver a session: timing, scripts, activities, and materials.
content:
Role: Act as a corporate trainer preparing to facilitate a live session.

Context: Session topic and objectives: [TOPIC_OBJECTIVES]. Audience, size and room/virtual setup: [AUDIENCE_SETUP]. Total time and any fixed breaks: [TIME]. Content and slides available: [MATERIALS]. Facilitator experience level: [FACILITATOR_LEVEL]. Known tricky moments: [TRICKY_MOMENTS].

Task: Produce a run sheet: each segment with start time, duration, objective, what the facilitator says / does (brief script), the activity and its instructions, materials needed, and transition. Add an opening and close, timing checkpoints, and a contingency plan for running long or low energy.

Format: A table: Time | Duration | Segment | Facilitator actions | Activity | Materials. Plus opening, close, and contingencies.

Verification: Check the durations sum to the available time including breaks; flag any activity whose instructions are unclear or that needs materials not listed.

Validation: Walk it as a first-time facilitator: could they run this without guessing? Add detail where they would stall.

title: Write a monthly safety meeting talk for drivers
description: A short, practical safety talk on one topic, using real incidents and seasonal risks, with discussion questions and a sign-off sheet.
content:
Write a driver safety meeting talk for me.

**Topic:** [e.g. "rear-end collisions", "winter driving", "backing in tight docks", "distracted driving", "load securement", "fatigue", "pedestrians in urban delivery"]
**Why now:** [recent incidents, near misses, inspection violations, season, new rule]
**Our recent examples:** [BRIEF, ANONYMIZED DETAILS - or "none"]
**Drivers attending:** [long haul / local / delivery van, new or experienced, languages]
**Format and length:** [e.g. "10-minute in-person talk at the terminal", "video call", "printed handout"]
**Company rules to reinforce:** [e.g. "no handheld phone use", "get out and look before backing", "following distance of 7 seconds"]

Requirements:
- Open with a real or realistic scenario drivers recognize, not statistics.
- Cover 3 practical behaviors drivers can use on their next shift.
- Explain why each one matters in terms of consequences drivers care about: injury, losing their license, out-of-service orders, a crash on their record.
- Speak to drivers as professionals; no lecturing or blame.
- Include 3 discussion questions that get drivers to share their own experience.

Return:
1. The talk script with speaker notes.
2. A one-page handout with key points.
3. A 3-question quiz to confirm understanding.
4. A sign-in sheet layout to record attendance.

Do not invent crash statistics; if you use any, mark them [ADD SOURCE]. Keep incident examples anonymous.

title: Write a role-play or scenario simulation for training
description: Realistic practice scenarios with roles, branches, and debrief questions.
content:
Role: Act as a corporate trainer designing a scenario-based role-play.

Context: Skill being practised: [SKILL]. Realistic context / setting: [SETTING]. Roles involved: [ROLES]. Learner level: [LEVEL]. Time available: [TIME]. Common mistakes learners make: [COMMON_MISTAKES]. Observation criteria: [OBSERVATION_CRITERIA].

Task: Produce: a scenario brief; a role card for each role (goal, information they hold, constraints); 2-3 decision points, each with options and realistic consequences that branch the scenario; an observer checklist tied to the criteria; and a debrief guide (what happened / why / what to do differently).

Format: Sections: Brief | Role cards | Decision points (option -> consequence) | Observer checklist | Debrief guide.

Verification: Ensure each role card only reveals what that role would know, and each decision point has a genuinely different consequence per option. Flag any that railroads to one outcome.

Validation: Play it through making the common mistakes: does the scenario surface them and does the debrief address them well? Adjust the weak decision point.

title: Write a toolbox talk on a specific jobsite hazard
description: A 10-minute safety talk tied to today's work, with real-world scenarios, crew questions, and a sign-in record.
content:
Write a toolbox talk for my crew.

**Hazard or topic:** [e.g. "ladder use near open edges", "trench cave-ins", "lockout/tagout on panels", "silica dust from cutting", "heat illness"]
**Today's work that makes it relevant:** [TASKS AND LOCATION]
**Crew:** [TRADE, SIZE, EXPERIENCE MIX, LANGUAGES SPOKEN]
**Recent near miss or incident to reference:** [DESCRIBE WITHOUT NAMES - or "none"]
**Company rules or equipment on site:** [e.g. "harness required above 6 ft", "trench box on site"]

Write a talk that takes about 10 minutes to deliver, with:
1. Why this matters today, in two or three sentences tied to the actual task.
2. How people get hurt doing this work: 3 realistic scenarios.
3. The controls, in order: eliminate, engineer, administrative, PPE. Be specific to the equipment I listed.
4. A stop-work reminder: what conditions mean stop and who to tell.
5. 3 questions to ask the crew that require more than a yes/no answer.
6. A one-line takeaway.
7. A sign-in block: date, topic, presenter, crew names and signatures.

Rules:
- Plain spoken language at a 6th-8th grade reading level; short sentences that work when read aloud.
- If you mention an OSHA standard, name it only if you are confident of the reference, and tell me to verify it. Do not invent regulation numbers or statistics.
- If my crew speaks more than one language, add a short version of the key points in that language and recommend a fluent speaker check it.
- Remind me that this supports, but does not replace, required training and a competent person's judgment.
variables: TRADE, SIZE, EXPERIENCE MIX, LANGUAGES SPOKEN
e.g. "harness required above 6 ft", "trench box on site"

title: Write an instructional design document for stakeholder sign-off
