majority vote, consensus, committee vs. all members
dues, grants, bank account, who can sign

title: Draft a contract amendment that changes only what we agreed
description: Produces a clean amendment that references the original agreement precisely, changes the agreed terms, and leaves everything else intact.
content:
Draft an amendment to an existing contract.

**Original agreement:** [title, parties with full legal names, date, and any prior amendments]
**Relevant sections of the original:** [PASTE the exact text being changed]
**What the parties agreed to change:** [e.g. "extend the term to Dec. 31, 2027", "increase fees by 5%", "add a new service"]
**Effective date of the change:** [DATE, or "on signature"]
**Governing law:** [as in the original]
**Signatories:** [names and titles, if known]

Draft the amendment with:
- Title, parties, and recitals identifying the original agreement and prior amendments
- Defined terms consistent with the original ("capitalized terms have the meaning given in the Agreement")
- Each change stated precisely: "Section 4.2 is deleted and replaced with..." or "The following is added as Section 9.5..." - never vague phrases like "the parties agree to update pricing"
- An effective-date clause
- A "no other changes" / ratification clause and an order-of-precedence clause
- Counterparts and electronic signature clause, and signature blocks

Before the draft, list:
- Knock-on effects: other sections, schedules, or defined terms that the change affects and may also need updating
- Anything that may need consents, notices, or approvals (e.g. assignment, change of control, board approval)

Use [CONFIRM] for any party name, date, or section number I have not given you; do not guess. This is a draft only; a qualified lawyer must check it against the full original agreement before signature.
variables: PASTE the exact text being changed

title: Draft a contract from a term sheet
description: A first-pass commercial contract built from agreed terms, for lawyer review.
content:
Role: Act as a contracts manager preparing a first-pass draft of a commercial agreement for legal review.

Context: Agreement type: [AGREEMENT_TYPE]. Parties and roles: [PARTIES]. Agreed commercial terms (term sheet): [TERM_SHEET]. Our contracting playbook positions and fallbacks: [PLAYBOOK]. Governing law and any regulatory overlay: [LAW_REGULATORY]. Deal-specific risks: [DEAL_RISKS]. Template or precedent to base it on: [PRECEDENT].

Goal: Produce a clean first draft that reflects the term sheet and our preferred positions, so legal review is about judgement calls, not fixing structure.

Task: Draft the agreement section by section from the precedent: reflect every term-sheet point; use our preferred playbook position for each key clause and note the agreed fallback in a comment; insert placeholders for anything not yet agreed; and produce (a) a list of open points needing instruction, (b) a list of clauses that must have qualified legal review before sending.

Constraints: This is a drafting aid, not legal advice. Do not state legal conclusions or opine on enforceability. Do not invent commercial terms - use [TO BE CONFIRMED]. Keep defined terms consistent. Flag any clause where the playbook is silent.

Examples: Clause note shape: 'Limitation of liability - drafted at our preferred cap ([X]); playbook fallback is [Y]; do not go below [Z] without GC approval.'

Format: A drafted agreement with numbered clauses and inline [COMMENTS], followed by: Open points | Clauses requiring legal review.

Verification: Cross-check every term-sheet item appears in the draft; list any that do not. Flag every placeholder and every deviation from the precedent.

Validation: Have a qualified lawyer review before this is sent to a counterparty - this draft must not leave the building without that review. Note the three clauses most likely to be negotiated.

title: Draft a data protection impact assessment (DPIA)
description: A DPIA draft for a new system or process handling personal data.
content:
Role: Act as a data protection officer drafting a DPIA for review.

Context: Processing activity and its purpose: [ACTIVITY_PURPOSE]. Data categories, subjects and volumes (including any special-category data): [DATA_SUBJECTS]. Data flows, systems, recipients and any transfers: [FLOWS]. Legal basis relied on: [LEGAL_BASIS]. Retention: [RETENTION]. Stakeholders consulted: [CONSULTED]. Applicable framework: [FRAMEWORK] (e.g. UK GDPR).

Goal: Produce a DPIA draft that a DPO and legal can finalise: a clear description, a real necessity/proportionality analysis, and risks with mitigations that reduce them to an acceptable level.

Task: Draft: (1) a systematic description of the processing and the data flows; (2) the necessity and proportionality assessment against the purpose and legal basis, including whether a less intrusive option exists; (3) a risk assessment to data subjects (each risk: source, likelihood, severity, overall) covering unauthorised access, excessive collection, loss of control, re-identification, function creep, transfers; (4) mitigations per risk and the residual risk; (5) the consultation record and the sign-off / residual-risk decisions needed.

Constraints: This is a draft for the DPO and legal to complete and approve - not a final assessment and not legal advice. Do not assert that the legal basis is valid - present the analysis. Do not minimise special-category or vulnerable-subject risks. Flag any transfer needing a transfer mechanism.

Examples: Risk row: 'Risk: re-identification of pseudonymised records via [dataset]. Source: linkage. Likelihood: medium. Severity: high. Mitigation: [k-anonymity / access controls / DPA clause]. Residual: low-medium.'

Format: Sections: Processing description & flows | Necessity & proportionality | Risk assessment (table) | Mitigations & residual risk | Consultation & sign-offs needed. ~800 words.

Verification: Check every data category, flow and recipient in the description also appears in the risk assessment; flag missing legal-basis or transfer analysis.

Validation: The DPO and legal must review and approve before processing proceeds. Pressure-test the necessity analysis: would a regulator accept that a less intrusive alternative was truly considered? Strengthen if not.

title: Draft a gift acceptance policy for non-cash gifts
description: A board-ready policy defining which gifts you accept, who decides, and how to handle stock, real estate, crypto, and in-kind donations.
content:
Draft a gift acceptance policy for my nonprofit.

**Organization size and staffing:** [budget, finance staff capacity]
**Gifts we already receive:** [cash, stock, DAF grants, IRA distributions, in-kind goods, vehicles, real estate, crypto, bequests]
**Gifts we are being offered or expect:** [e.g. a donated building, artwork, a business interest]
**Who approves gifts today:** [executive director, finance committee, board]
**Values concerns:** [donors or industries we would not accept from, naming concerns]

The policy should cover:
1. Purpose and guiding principles: mission alignment, donor intent, and the right to decline.
2. Gift types, each with an acceptance rule and approval level: readily accepted, accepted with review, and generally declined.
3. Special review for high-risk gifts: real estate (environmental review, title, carrying costs), closely held stock, restricted gifts we cannot fulfill, gifts with ongoing costs, and gifts that create conflicts of interest or reputational risk.
4. Valuation and IRS responsibilities: we do not appraise gifts for donors; donors are responsible for qualified appraisals where required; our duties to sign Form 8283 and to file Form 8282 if we sell certain property within three years. [CONFIRM current thresholds with our CPA.]
5. Liquidation policy (e.g. selling stock promptly).
6. Naming and recognition rules, including what happens if a pledge is unpaid or a donor's conduct becomes a concern.
7. Confidentiality and anonymous gifts.
8. Review cycle.

Return the policy in numbered sections (2-4 pages) and a one-page decision flowchart in text. This is general information, not legal or tax advice; have counsel review before board adoption and adapt for laws outside the US.
variables: e.g. a donated building, artwork, a business interest
CONFIRM current thresholds with our CPA.

title: Draft a litigation hold notice employees will actually follow
description: Writes a clear preservation notice telling custodians exactly what to keep, where it lives, and what not to do.
content:
Draft a litigation hold (legal hold) notice for employees.

**Matter (described neutrally):** [e.g. "a contract dispute with a former supplier" - avoid details that waive privilege or prejudge the case]
**Relevant time period:** [START DATE to present]
**Subjects and keywords the hold covers:** [TOPICS, projects, people, products]
**Custodians receiving it:** [roles or names]
**Where relevant data lives:** [e.g. email, Slack/Teams, shared drives, CRM, phones, paper files, personal devices used for work]
**Jurisdiction / forum:** [if known]
**Legal contact:** [NAME, email]

The notice must:
- Open with a plain statement that this is a legal requirement and overrides normal deletion and retention schedules
- Say exactly what to preserve, with concrete examples, including drafts, chats, texts, voicemails, and files on personal devices or accounts used for work
- Say what NOT to do: delete, edit, move, wipe devices, or turn on auto-delete; do not discuss the matter outside legal
- Explain that the hold lasts until legal releases it in writing
- Ask for written acknowledgment by a deadline
- Be under one page, plain language, no legal jargon

Also give me:
1. A short IT instruction list (suspend auto-deletion, preserve departing employees' accounts, back up mailboxes).
2. A custodian tracking table: Custodian | Date sent | Acknowledged | Interview done | Data collected.
3. A reminder notice to send every [INTERVAL].

Preservation duties vary by jurisdiction; a qualified lawyer must confirm scope and timing before this is issued.

title: Draft a policy for a supported living or care service
description: A structured policy for a supported living or home care provider that maps to the regulations and standards that apply.
content:
Help me draft a policy for my supported living or care service.

**Country and region:** [e.g. "England", "Scotland", "Ontario", "California" — regulators and laws differ]
**Regulator:** [e.g. "Care Quality Commission (CQC)", or "not sure"]
**Service type:** [supported living / domiciliary care / residential / mixed]
**People we support:** [e.g. "adults with learning disabilities and autistic adults", "older adults", "mental health needs"]
**Policy needed:** [e.g. "overall supported living policy", "safeguarding", "medication support", "consent and mental capacity", "complaints"]
**Our current practice:** [how we actually do this today, staffing, and any recent inspection feedback]

Draft the policy with:
1. **Purpose and scope:** who it applies to and when.
2. **Legal and regulatory basis:** the laws, regulations, and standards that apply in my region (for England, typically the Health and Social Care Act 2008 regulations, the Care Act 2014, and the Mental Capacity Act 2005). List them and mark each as [CONFIRM CURRENT VERSION].
3. **Principles:** person-centered support, choice and control, dignity, independence, and positive risk-taking.
4. **Procedures:** step-by-step responsibilities for staff and managers, including assessment, support planning, review, and record keeping.
5. **Safeguarding and escalation:** what staff do if they suspect abuse or neglect, and who they contact.
6. **Consent and capacity:** how decisions are made when someone may lack capacity.
7. **Training and competence** required.
8. **Monitoring and audit:** how we check the policy is followed.
9. **Review date and version control.**

Write in plain language staff can follow. Do not invent regulation numbers or quote standards I haven't provided; mark them [ADD REFERENCE]. Have the final policy reviewed by a care compliance specialist or legal adviser before use, and check it against current guidance from my regulator.
variables: supported living / domiciliary care / residential / mixed

title: Draft a response to a regulator's information request
description: Plans and drafts an accurate, well-organized response to a regulator's request or exam finding, with an evidence index and review checklist.
content:
Help me prepare a response to a regulator.

**Regulator and type of request:** [e.g. information request, exam finding, inquiry letter, matter requiring attention]
**The request text:** [PASTE each question or finding exactly]
**Deadline:** [DATE]
**Facts and documents we have:** [SUMMARY or PASTE]
**Actions already taken or planned:** [REMEDIATION with dates and owners]
**Sensitivities:** [e.g. related litigation, ongoing internal investigation, prior commitments to this regulator]

Give me:
1. **Response plan** - each request item, owner, source documents, internal deadline, and reviewer.
2. **Draft response** - a cover letter, then answers numbered to match the request exactly. Each answer: direct answer first, then supporting detail, then a reference to the attached evidence.
3. **Remediation commitments** (for findings) - specific, owned, dated, and achievable. Flag any date that looks unrealistic.
4. **Evidence index** - table: Exhibit #, Description, Responds to item #, Source, Confidentiality marking.
5. **Pre-submission checklist** - accuracy verified by the business owner, consistency with prior submissions, no over-promising, legal review, confidentiality requests, sign-off.

Rules:
- Answer what was asked, accurately and completely; do not volunteer speculation.
- Never state something as fact unless I provided it; mark gaps [CONFIRM WITH OWNER].
- Respectful, factual tone; no defensiveness or minimizing.
- Legal counsel should review before anything is sent.
variables: PASTE each question or finding exactly

title: Draft a risk appetite statement leadership can use
description: Writes a risk appetite statement with a qualitative stance and measurable limits for each risk category, ready for leadership review.
content:
Help me draft a risk appetite statement.

**Organization type and size:** [e.g. mid-size insurer, SaaS company, hospital, nonprofit]
**Strategy and objectives:** [what leadership is trying to achieve over the next 3 years]
**Risk categories we use:** [e.g. strategic, financial, operational, compliance, cyber, reputational, people]
**Leadership's views (from interviews or a workshop):** [PASTE notes]
**Regulatory expectations:** [any required elements, or "none"]
**Existing limits or metrics:** [PASTE]

Produce:
1. **Overall statement** - 3-5 sentences on how much risk the organization is willing to take in pursuit of its strategy.
2. **By category** - for each: appetite level (averse / minimal / cautious / open / seeking), a qualitative statement, and 1-3 measurable tolerances or limits. Where I gave no data, write the metric with [SET LIMIT] rather than inventing a number.
3. **Zero-tolerance areas** stated explicitly (e.g. knowing regulatory breaches, bribery, safety).
4. **Tensions** - where my leadership notes conflict (e.g. aggressive growth plus minimal operational risk) with questions to resolve them.
5. **Governance** - who owns it, how breaches of tolerance are escalated, how often it is reviewed.
6. **Cascade guidance** - how business units should translate it into their own limits.

Plain language a new board member could understand. This is a draft for leadership and board deliberation, not a final position.
variables: e.g. mid-size insurer, SaaS company, hospital, nonprofit
what leadership is trying to achieve over the next 3 years

title: Draft an engagement letter with a clear scope of representation
description: An engagement letter that defines exactly what the firm will and will not do, the fee terms, and client responsibilities, written in plain English.
content:
Draft an engagement letter for a new client of my law firm.

**Client:** [NAME and whether individual or entity - and who at the entity we represent]
**Matter:** [DESCRIPTION]
**Work included:** [SPECIFIC TASKS]
**Work excluded:** [e.g. "appeals", "tax advice", "collection of any judgment"]
**Fee arrangement:** [hourly rates by timekeeper / flat fee / contingency percentage and how costs are handled / hybrid]
**Retainer or advance deposit:** [AMOUNT, whether it goes to trust, evergreen or not]
**Billing and payment terms:** [INVOICE FREQUENCY, DUE DATE, LATE TERMS]
**State whose rules apply:** [STATE]

Include sections for: who the client is (and is not, e.g. officers or family members); scope and exclusions; staffing; fees, costs, and how the retainer is held and applied; billing increments; client responsibilities (honesty, cooperation, timely payment); communication; no guarantee of outcome; conflicts disclosures or waivers if any [ADD IF NEEDED]; termination and withdrawal; file retention and destruction period; and signature blocks.

Rules:
- Plain English, short paragraphs, defined terms only when needed.
- For a contingency fee, include the items many states require in writing: the percentage at each stage, whether costs come off before or after the fee, and which expenses the client pays regardless of outcome.
- Mark any state-specific requirement I should verify as [CONFIRM - STATE RULE], e.g. fee dispute arbitration notices or required statements.

title: Draft an ethics (IRB) application for research with people
description: Prepares the core sections of an ethics or IRB application, including risks, consent, data protection, and plain-language participant materials.
content:
Help me draft my research ethics (IRB/REC) application.

**Institution and form sections required:** [PASTE the headings or questions]

**What participants will do:** [tasks, interviews, surveys, interventions, time required]

2. A risk assessment: physical, psychological, social, legal, and privacy risks, with likelihood and mitigation for each.
3. Consent process: how and when consent is obtained, right to withdraw (and until when data can be withdrawn), and any assent for minors.
4. Data protection: identifiability, security, retention, and sharing.
5. A participant information sheet and consent form at a reading level around grade 8.

Return each section under the institution's headings. Flag answers that depend on local policy or law (e.g. GDPR, HIPAA, mandatory reporting) as [CHECK with ethics office]. Do not describe approvals or procedures I have not confirmed.

identifiable data, sensitive topics, recordings, linkage

title: Draft an uptime SLA with service credits for my SaaS product
description: A customer-facing service level agreement with a measurable uptime target, exclusions, credit table, and claim process.
content:
Draft a service level agreement (SLA) for my SaaS product.

**Product and plans covered:** [e.g. "Enterprise plan only"]
**Uptime target we can actually meet:** [e.g. 99.9% monthly] **and our last 12 months of actual uptime:** [DATA or "unknown"]
**How we measure availability:** [status page, synthetic checks, error rates - what we have today]
**Planned maintenance practice:** [windows, notice period]
**Support response targets, if included:** [by severity]
**Credit appetite:** [e.g. "credits capped at 25% of monthly fees"]

Include:
1. Definitions: availability, downtime, monthly uptime percentage (show the formula), scheduled maintenance, severity levels.
2. Exclusions: customer-caused issues, third-party services, force majeure, beta features, scheduled maintenance with notice.
3. A service credit table tied to uptime bands, with a cap.
4. Claim process: how and within how many days to request credits, what evidence is needed.
5. Credits as the sole remedy, plus an optional termination right for repeated failures (flag it as a negotiation lever).
6. Support response and resolution targets by severity, if I gave them.

Also give me:
- The allowed downtime per month and per year for my target (e.g. 99.9% is about 43 minutes a month).
- A warning if my target is higher than my history supports.
- Monitoring and reporting I need in place before publishing this.

Use plain language. Mark anything I have not confirmed as [CONFIRM]. This is general information - have a lawyer review it against my master agreement before use.

title: Draft board resolutions or a written consent
description: Drafts recitals and resolutions for a board or shareholder approval, with authorizations, conditions, and a checklist of supporting steps.

Draft board resolutions (or a unanimous written consent) for a corporate approval.

title: Draft legal correspondence
description: Standard legal letters and responses in the right tone and structure.
content:
Role: Act as a paralegal drafting routine legal correspondence for a lawyer to review.

Context: Type of correspondence and recipient: [TYPE_RECIPIENT]. Purpose and the outcome we want: [PURPOSE_OUTCOME]. Key facts and dates: [FACTS]. Points that must be made: [MUST_MAKE]. Points to avoid conceding or stating: [AVOID]. Tone required: [TONE]. Deadline referenced: [DEADLINE].

Task: Draft the letter/email: appropriate opening, a clear statement of purpose, the facts and points in a logical order, the action requested and by when, and a professional close. Insert [PLACEHOLDER] for anything not supplied. Note where a lawyer must review before sending.

Format: A ready-to-review draft, followed by a short 'review flags' list.

title: Edit a company or stock write-up so it isn't investment advice
description: A compliance edit of a market report or company analysis that strips recommendations, certainty, and promotional tone, with a log of every change.
content:
Review this write-up about a listed company and edit it so it is neutral, factual, and does not read as investment advice.

**Text to review:** [PASTE report, newsletter, post, or summary]
**Where it will be published and to whom:** [e.g. company blog, newsletter to retail readers, internal research]
**Jurisdiction or regulator:** [e.g. US SEC/FINRA, UK FCA, EU, other]

Check and fix:
1. **Title** - present, neutral, descriptive; no implied recommendation or forecast.
2. **Investment advice** - remove explicit or implied buy/sell/hold language, "opportunity", "undervalued", "must-own", and suggestions about when to act.
3. **Certainty and tone** - replace definite predictions with conditional wording; remove hype, urgency, and persuasive framing.
4. **Prohibited content** - price targets, return projections, timing advice, and unsupported claims of superiority over competitors.
5. **Facts and sources** - every number has a source and date; separate reported facts from opinion; flag anything unsourced as [SOURCE NEEDED].
6. **Balance** - material risks and uncertainties are mentioned alongside positives.
7. **Disclosures** - whether a disclaimer and conflict-of-interest statement (e.g. holdings) are needed.

Return:
- The revised text.
- A change log table: original wording, issue, revised wording.
- Remaining items for a compliance officer to decide.

This is an editorial check, not legal sign-off. Rules differ by jurisdiction and publisher; have a qualified compliance or legal professional approve the final version.
variables: PASTE report, newsletter, post, or summary
e.g. US SEC/FINRA, UK FCA, EU, other

title: Evaluate a settlement offer with a simple decision tree
description: Compares a settlement offer to the expected value of continuing, including costs, timing, and non-money factors, to support a recommendation.
content:
Help me evaluate a settlement offer against the alternative of continuing the dispute.

**Dispute summary:** [SHORT]
**Our side:** [claimant / defendant]
**Offer on the table:** [amount and key terms - payment timing, confidentiality, admissions, releases, non-money terms]
**Our estimates (from the legal team):**
- Probability of winning on liability: [%]
- Likely damages range if we win / lose: [AMOUNTS]
- Remaining legal costs through trial and appeal: [AMOUNT]
- Time to final outcome: [MONTHS]
- Chance of collecting a judgment: [% - relevant if claimant]
- Fee shifting or costs risk: [DETAILS]
**Non-money factors:** [e.g. precedent for other claims, publicity, relationship, management time, insurance coverage]

Do this:
1. Build a simple decision tree with each branch, its probability, and net outcome after costs.
2. Calculate the expected value of continuing and compare it to the offer; show the arithmetic.
3. Run a sensitivity check: how the answer changes if the win probability moves by plus or minus 15 points, or costs run 30% over.
4. Weigh the non-money factors separately; do not force them into a number.
5. List settlement terms worth negotiating beyond the amount (release scope, confidentiality, no admission, payment schedule, tax treatment [CONFIRM WITH TAX ADVISOR]).
6. Suggest a counteroffer range and the reasoning.

Use only the estimates I give; mark any missing input as [ESTIMATE NEEDED]. This is decision support, not legal advice; the responsible lawyer and the decision-maker must make the final call.

title: Evaluate how severe a control deficiency is
description: Works through likelihood, magnitude, and compensating controls to classify a deficiency and document a defensible conclusion.
content:
Help me evaluate the severity of a control deficiency.

**The control and what went wrong:** [DESCRIPTION, number of exceptions, sample size]
**Account, process, or obligation affected:** [e.g. revenue, payroll, AML monitoring]
**Exposure:** [dollar volume through the control, or number of customers/transactions affected]
**Was an actual error or breach found?** [YES - details / NO]
**Other controls that might catch the same issue:** [COMPENSATING CONTROLS and whether they were tested]
**Framework we use:** [e.g. SOX deficiency / significant deficiency / material weakness; or our internal rating scale - PASTE]
**Materiality or tolerance thresholds:** [if applicable]

Walk through:
1. **Is it a design or operating deficiency?** And why.
2. **Likelihood** that the control would fail to prevent or detect an error or breach - consider the nature of the risk, susceptibility to fraud, subjectivity, and how the failure happened.
3. **Magnitude** of the potential error or harm - the realistic maximum, not just what was found.
4. **Compensating controls** - do they operate at a precision that would actually catch the issue? What evidence supports that?
5. **Aggregation** - questions to ask about other deficiencies in the same area that could combine.
6. **Proposed classification** under my framework, with the reasoning a reviewer or external auditor would expect.
7. **Documentation memo** - a 200-word draft conclusion I can adapt.

Flag every assumption as [CONFIRM]. This supports my professional judgment; final classification should be agreed with my audit lead and, for SOX, the external auditor.
variables: DESCRIPTION, number of exceptions, sample size
COMPENSATING CONTROLS and whether they were tested

title: Explain the reasons for a credit denial in an adverse action notice
description: Clear, specific, compliant principal-reason statements for a declined or counter-offered credit application.
content:
Help me write the statement of reasons for an adverse action notice on a credit application.

**Product:** [consumer or business credit - e.g. "credit card", "auto loan", "small business line"]
**Action taken:** [declined / approved on different terms (counteroffer) / account closed or limit reduced]
**Decision factors from our underwriting or model:** [LIST the actual factors in order of importance - e.g. "debt-to-income 52%, policy max 43%"]
**Was a credit report or score used?** [yes/no; bureau name; score and key factors if provided]
**Jurisdiction:** [e.g. "US" plus state]

Do this:
1. Turn the factors into up to four principal reasons written in specific, plain language (for US consumer credit, the reasons must reflect the actual factors - avoid vague phrases like "internal standards" or "insufficient score").
2. Check each reason against prohibited bases and flag any factor that could be or act as a proxy for a protected characteristic (e.g. age, marital status, receipt of public assistance, ZIP code).
3. List the other elements the notice typically needs for this situation - e.g. the creditor's details, the ECOA anti-discrimination notice and regulator, and, if a consumer report was used, the credit reporting agency details, the score disclosure, and the applicant's right to a free report and to dispute - as a checklist marked [CONFIRM with our template].
4. Flag if the counteroffer scenario changes what must be sent.

Do not invent reasons that are not in my list. This is general information, not legal advice; have compliance or counsel confirm the final notice against current regulations and our approved templates.
variables: yes/no; bureau name; score and key factors if provided

title: Explain to customers how my product's AI features use their data
description: A clear, accurate AI data-use FAQ and trust page section that answers what procurement and security teams actually ask.
content:
Help me write a customer-facing explanation of how my product's AI features use customer data.

**AI features:** [what each feature does]
**Model providers and hosting:** [vendors, regions, whether data leaves our cloud]
**Training and retention facts:** [Is customer data used to train our models or vendor models? How long are prompts and outputs retained? Zero-retention agreements? - only confirmed facts]
**Customer controls:** [opt-out, admin toggles, per-workspace settings, data deletion]
**Contract terms:** [what our DPA and terms say about AI and sub-processors]
**Common customer questions so far:** [PASTE or summarize]

Write:
1. A one-paragraph summary a buyer can paste into a vendor review.
2. An FAQ covering: Is my data used for training? Who can see it? Where is it processed and stored? How long is it kept? Which sub-processors are involved? Can admins turn AI off? How are outputs checked for accuracy? What happens to data when we cancel?
3. A short in-product notice for the first time a user tries an AI feature.
4. A gap list: any question I could not answer from the facts given, marked [CONFIRM WITH ENGINEERING OR LEGAL].

Rules:
- Only state facts I provided. Never imply guarantees ("100% secure", "never wrong").
- Match the wording to our contract and DPA; flag any mismatch.
- Note where rules such as GDPR, the EU AI Act, or sector rules for our customers may require more disclosure.
- Plain language, no marketing spin.

This is general information - have legal review the final text before publishing.
variables: vendors, regions, whether data leaves our cloud
opt-out, admin toggles, per-workspace settings, data deletion
what our DPA and terms say about AI and sub-processors

title: Extract key terms from contracts into a tracker
description: Pulls renewal dates, notice periods, caps, and other key terms from each contract into consistent rows for a contract register.
content:
Extract the key terms from these contracts into rows for my contract tracker.

**Contracts:** [PASTE one or more contracts, separated clearly, or the relevant sections]
**Fields I track:** [use the defaults below, or list your own]
**Date format:** [e.g. YYYY-MM-DD]

Default fields:
- Contract name, counterparty (full legal name), our contracting entity
- Contract type, effective date, initial term, expiry date
- Renewal mechanism (auto / manual), renewal term, notice deadline to stop renewal (calculate the actual date)
- Termination for convenience: who, notice period
- Fees and payment terms, price increase mechanism
- Liability cap and carve-outs (short)
- Indemnities (who indemnifies whom, for what)
- Assignment / change-of-control restrictions
- Exclusivity, non-compete, non-solicit, most-favored-customer terms
- Data protection terms or DPA (yes/no, reference)
- Governing law and dispute forum
- Notice address and method
- Unusual or non-standard terms worth knowing

Rules:
- Quote the section number for every field you fill.
- If a term is not in the text, write "Not found" - never infer or guess.
- If a term is ambiguous, write the field as [REVIEW] and explain in a note.
- Show your working for any calculated date.

Return: a table (one row per contract) that I can paste into a spreadsheet, then a list of [REVIEW] items and any renewal or notice deadlines in the next 90 days. Extraction errors are possible; a lawyer or paralegal should spot-check against the source documents.
variables: use the defaults below, or list your own

title: Extract shareholder and ownership details from company documents
description: Structured shareholder data from registers or registry extracts, with totals checks, ownership-threshold flags, and follow-up questions.
content:
Extract shareholder and ownership information from a company document into structured data.

**Document:** [PASTE text from a shareholder register, company registry extract, cap table, or annual return]
**Purpose:** [e.g. "KYC onboarding", "due diligence", "beneficial ownership check"]
**Ownership threshold to flag:** [e.g. "25%", "10%"]
**Output format:** [JSON / table]

Rules:
- Extract only what the document states. If a field is missing or unreadable, use null. Never guess names, numbers, or dates.
- Keep names exactly as written, including legal suffixes (Ltd, GmbH, LLC).
- Distinguish individuals from legal entities. For entities, capture the registration number and registry where shown.
- If share amounts and percentages don't reconcile, keep both and flag the conflict.
- If the document is partial, corrupted, or not a shareholder record, say so instead of forcing output.

For each shareholder return: shareholder_name, type (individual or entity), registration_number_and_registry, address, date_of_birth (individuals, only if shown), nationality_or_jurisdiction, share_class, number_of_shares, share_percentage, voting_rights_if_different, date_acquired, source_location (page or section).

Then add:
1. **Totals check:** do the percentages add up to 100%? List any gap.
2. **Flags:** shareholders at or above my threshold; entities whose own owners must be traced to identify the ultimate beneficial owners; nominee or trustee arrangements; inconsistencies.
3. **Follow-up:** questions or documents to request.

If I chose JSON, return valid JSON only inside one code block, followed by the checks and flags.

Use the personal data only for the stated purpose and in line with my organization's data protection rules.

title: Flag defamation and privacy risks in an article before publishing
description: A pre-publication read that highlights risky statements about people or companies, why they are risky, and safer edits to discuss with a lawyer.
content:
Do a pre-publication risk read of my article.

**The draft:** [PASTE THE ARTICLE]
**Jurisdiction(s) where it will be published or read:** [e.g. US, UK, EU, India - risk differs a lot by country]
**Evidence for each allegation:** [DOCUMENTS, recordings, on-record sources, anonymous sources]
**Right of reply:** [who was contacted for comment, when, and what they said]
**Images and personal details used:** [photos, names, addresses, health or criminal details, minors]

Go through the draft and flag:
- Statements of fact that could harm a person's or company's reputation, and whether my evidence supports each as written.
- Implied meanings, headlines, captions, and photo pairings that say more than the text.
- Opinion presented as fact, or fact presented as opinion.
- Allegations without a fair chance to respond, or responses not fairly reflected.
- Privacy issues: private information, identification of minors, victims, or bystanders, and whether public interest justifies it.
- Reporting on legal proceedings that could prejudice a case or break a reporting restriction.
- Quotes or documents that might reveal a confidential source.

Return a table: passage | risk type | risk level (high/medium/low) | why | evidence needed | suggested safer wording. Then list the questions to take to our lawyer and the edits to make first.

This is general information to help me prepare, not legal advice. Have a qualified media lawyer review anything rated high before publishing.
variables: e.g. US, UK, EU, India - risk differs a lot by country
DOCUMENTS, recordings, on-record sources, anonymous sources
who was contacted for comment, when, and what they said
photos, names, addresses, health or criminal details, minors

title: Get my site ready for a customer or regulatory inspection

Help me prepare my site for an upcoming inspection or audit.

**Type of inspection:** [e.g. "customer supplier audit", "ISO 9001 surveillance audit", "health and safety inspection", "food safety audit"]

**Date and duration:** [DETAILS]
**Areas they will likely see:** [e.g. receiving, production, storage, offices, records]
**Known weak spots or past findings:** [OPEN ITEMS]

Give me:
1. A readiness checklist grouped by area: what an inspector typically checks, what "good" looks like, and who owns it.
2. A document and evidence list: records, training logs, procedures, calibration or maintenance records, corrective actions - and how far back they usually look.
3. A plan for open past findings: show status and evidence of closure, or an honest plan if not yet closed.
4. A 2-week countdown with daily priorities.
5. A briefing for staff: how to answer questions honestly, say "I'll find out" when unsure, and never guess or alter records.
6. The walk-through route and who escorts the inspector.

Requirements differ by standard, regulator, and location; confirm the specific criteria with the auditing body or a qualified compliance advisor. Never suggest hiding problems or backdating documents.

e.g. receiving, production, storage, offices, records

title: Handle a data subject access request from start to finish
description: Gives a step-by-step plan, search checklist, exemption review, and response letter for responding to a personal data access request on time.
content:
Help me handle a data subject access request (DSAR).

**Request (paste or summarize):** [TEXT]
**Date received:** [DATE]
**Requester's relationship to us:** [customer / employee / ex-employee / other]
**Applicable law:** [e.g. GDPR, UK GDPR, CCPA/CPRA, other]
**Context:** [e.g. "ex-employee in a dispute with us", "routine customer request"]
**Our systems that may hold their data:** [e.g. CRM, HR system, email, support tickets, backups, vendors]

Give me:
1. **Timeline** - the response deadline and any extension option under the law I named, marked [CONFIRM DEADLINE], with internal milestones.
2. **Identity verification** - proportionate steps, without asking for more data than needed.
3. **Clarifying scope** - whether and how I can ask the requester to narrow the request, without delaying the clock improperly.
4. **Search plan** - systems, custodians, search terms, and date ranges, as a checklist with owners.
5. **Review checklist** - third-party personal data to redact, privileged material, other possible exemptions to consider [CONFIRM EXEMPTION APPLIES], and whether a dispute or litigation affects how I handle it.
6. **Supplementary information** to include (purposes, recipients, retention, source, rights, transfers).
7. **Response letter** - clear, polite, and complete, with placeholders for the data provided.
8. **Record of handling** - a log template for accountability.

Do not state statutory deadlines or exemptions as settled; flag them for confirmation. A qualified privacy lawyer must review before responding, especially if the request is linked to a dispute.
variables: e.g. GDPR, UK GDPR, CCPA/CPRA, other
e.g. CRM, HR system, email, support tickets, backups, vendors

title: Map the steps to apply for a business license or regulatory permit
description: A step-by-step application roadmap with the regulator, documents, eligibility checks, likely costs, and timeline to confirm.
content:
Help me understand how to apply for a license or permit my business needs.

**License or permit:** [e.g. "food establishment permit", "liquor license", "contractor license", "home-based business permit" - or "not sure which I need"]
**Country, state, and city:** [LOCATION]
**Business and activity:** [WHAT I'll be doing, business structure, ownership]
**Timeline:** [when I want to start operating]
**What I already have:** [registration, premises, documents]

Give me:
1. **Which licenses are likely involved** - the main one plus any related registrations (e.g. business registration, tax ID, zoning, health, fire, or professional or equipment approvals).
2. **The regulator(s)** responsible for each, and what each one decides.
3. **Eligibility checks** - ownership or residency rules, minimum capital, qualifications, premises or technical requirements.
4. **Step-by-step process** - from pre-application to approval, including inspections, public notices, or hearings if typical.
5. **Document checklist** - each document, who provides it, and tips to avoid rejection.
6. **Costs and timeline** - categories of fees and typical stages. Do not state specific amounts or processing times unless you are confident; mark them [CONFIRM WITH REGULATOR].
7. **Common reasons applications are delayed or refused.**
8. **Questions to ask the regulator or a local lawyer.**

Rules and fees change often and differ by location. This is general information - confirm every requirement on the regulator's official website and consider a local lawyer or licensing consultant for complex or high-value licenses.
variables: WHAT I'll be doing, business structure, ownership
when I want to start operating

title: Plan data breach notifications and draft the notices
description: Assesses risk of harm from a personal data breach, maps who must be told and by when, and drafts regulator and individual notices.
content:
Help me assess a personal data breach and plan notifications.

**What happened:** [facts known so far - how discovered, when, systems affected, whether data was accessed, exfiltrated, encrypted, or lost]
**When we became aware:** [DATE and TIME]
**Data involved:** [categories, including any sensitive, financial, health, or ID data; whether encrypted]
**Individuals affected:** [types, approximate numbers, countries or states of residence]
**Our role:** [controller / processor; vendor involved?]
**Containment status:** [DETAILS]
**Contracts with notification duties:** [e.g. customer DPAs requiring notice within X hours]
**Insurance:** [cyber policy? notice requirements?]

Give me:
1. **Facts vs. unknowns** - two lists; what we must find out next and from whom.
2. **Risk to individuals** - likelihood and severity of harm (identity theft, fraud, discrimination, distress), with reasoning.
3. **Notification map** - a table: Who (regulators, individuals, customers/controllers, insurers, banks, law enforcement) | Trigger | Deadline from awareness | Status. Mark every legal deadline [CONFIRM UNDER APPLICABLE LAW] - do not state them as fact.
4. **Privilege steps** - routing forensic work through counsel where appropriate [CONFIRM WITH COUNSEL].
5. **Draft notices** - a regulator notification (nature of the breach, categories and approximate numbers, likely consequences, measures taken, contact point) and a plain-English notice to affected individuals (what happened, what data, what we are doing, what they should do, how to reach us), with placeholders. No minimizing language ("no evidence of misuse") unless the facts support it.
6. **Holding statement** - 3-4 factual sentences for customer-facing teams if asked before notices go out.
7. **Incident log** - template recording decisions and their reasons.

Keep public statements factual; do not speculate about cause or attacker. Breach rules vary by jurisdiction and deadlines can be short; a qualified lawyer must confirm notification decisions immediately.
variables: types, approximate numbers, countries or states of residence
e.g. customer DPAs requiring notice within X hours

title: Plan the response to a public records or FOIA request
description: A search plan, exemption review, fee estimate, and response letter for a public records request, built around your statutory deadlines.
content:
Help me plan and draft our response to a public records request.

**Governing law:** [e.g. "federal FOIA", "state public records act", "local open records ordinance"]
**Request text:** [PASTE the request exactly as received]
**Date received and statutory deadline:** [DATES, plus any extension allowed]
**Requester type, if relevant to fees:** [e.g. "media", "commercial", "individual"]
**Where records may live:** [email, shared drives, case systems, texts, paper files]
**Sensitive content I expect:** [e.g. "personnel records", "law enforcement investigation", "attorney advice", "personal data of residents"]

Work through it in this order:
1. Restate the request as a list of distinct record categories. Flag any part that is unclear or overly broad and draft a short clarification email to the requester.
2. Build a search plan: custodians, systems, date range, and search terms for each category.
3. List the exemptions that could plausibly apply under the law I named, what each requires, and what kind of record would trigger it. Describe them generally and mark each [CONFIRM WITH COUNSEL]; do not cite section numbers unless I provide them.
4. Note where redaction rather than withholding is required, and what a withholding log or index should record.
5. Outline a fee estimate approach and whether a fee waiver request needs a decision.
6. Draft the response letter: records released, records withheld or redacted with the basis, appeal rights and deadline, and contact person.

Rules: never invent statute citations, deadlines, or fee amounts; use [ADD] markers. Remind me that withholding decisions should be reviewed by our records officer or legal counsel.
variables: PASTE the request exactly as received
email, shared drives, case systems, texts, paper files

title: Prepare a deposition outline for a witness
description: Builds a topic-by-topic examination outline with goals, questions, exhibits, and admissions to lock in.
content:
Help me prepare a deposition outline.

**Witness:** [name, role, relationship to the parties, friendly or adverse]
**Case summary and claims/defenses:** [SHORT]
**What I need from this witness:** [e.g. "admit receipt of the notice", "establish timeline", "lock in lack of knowledge"]
**Key documents / exhibits:** [LIST with IDs and one-line descriptions]
**Known facts and prior statements by this witness:** [SUMMARY]
**Time available:** [e.g. "7 hours"]
**Jurisdiction / rules:** [court and any limits]

Build the outline:
1. **Goals** - 3-5 specific admissions or facts to lock in, ranked.
2. **Preliminaries** - background, preparation for the deposition, documents reviewed, who they spoke with.
3. **Topic modules** - for each topic: purpose, exhibits to use, and a sequence of short, single-fact questions moving from open ("what happened") to closed ("you received this on March 3, correct?").
4. **Exhibit plan** - when to introduce each exhibit and the foundation questions needed.
5. **Lock-in questions** - exhausting the witness's knowledge ("anything else?", "anyone else?").
6. **Risk areas** - topics that could hurt us, and whether to avoid or address them.
7. **Time budget** per topic.

Keep questions short and non-compound. Do not invent facts or document contents; mark gaps [CONFIRM FROM FILE]. This is a preparation aid; the examining lawyer must review it against the record and applicable rules.
variables: name, role, relationship to the parties, friendly or adverse
LIST with IDs and one-line descriptions

title: Prepare a hearing prep sheet with likely judge questions
description: Condenses a motion or hearing into a one-page argument map, the toughest likely questions, and short answers.
content:
Help me prepare for a court hearing or oral argument.

**Hearing type and what is being decided:** [e.g. "motion to dismiss", "preliminary injunction", "case management conference"]
**Our position and the relief we want:** [SHORT]
**Our main arguments:** [LIST or PASTE brief summary]
**Other side's main arguments:** [LIST or PASTE]
**Key authorities each side relies on:** [names and citations as they appear in the briefs]
**Key facts and record cites:** [LIST]
**Time allotted:** [MINUTES]
**What I know about the judge's approach:** [OPTIONAL]

Return:
1. **Opening (60-90 seconds)** - what we want and the 2-3 reasons the court should grant it.
2. **Argument map** - each point with the one fact and one authority that best supports it.
3. **Hardest questions** - 10 questions the judge is likely to ask, especially on our weak points, each with a 2-3 sentence answer and the record or brief cite to point to.
4. **Concessions** - what we can safely concede and what we must never concede.
5. **Rebuttal points** for each of the other side's strongest arguments.
6. **Fallback ask** if the court will not give us everything (e.g. narrower relief, leave to amend).
7. **One-page cheat sheet** of key cites, dates, and record pages.

Use only authorities I have given you; never add or describe case law from memory. Flag any authority whose holding I should re-check with [VERIFY]. A qualified lawyer must confirm all citations and positions before the hearing.
variables: names and citations as they appear in the briefs

title: Prepare a signature pack with a summary of what's being signed
description: A cover sheet that tells my executive what each document is, what they're committing to, and what to check before signing.
content:
Help me prepare a signature and approval pack for my executive.

**Documents in the pack:** [for each: title, type (contract, NDA, purchase order, policy, letter, board resolution), counterparty, who prepared it, who already approved it]
**Key details from each:** [PASTE THE RELEVANT CLAUSES, AMOUNTS, DATES, OR THE COVER EMAIL]
**Approval rules:** [e.g. "contracts over $50k need legal sign-off", "CFO approves all POs first"]
**Deadline:** [WHEN IT MUST BE SIGNED]

Create a cover sheet with, for each document:
1. What it is, in one plain sentence.
2. What signing commits the company or my executive to: value, term, renewal, key obligations - only from what I've provided.
3. Approvals already obtained vs. required by our rules - flag any gaps.
4. Points to check: blanks not filled in, dates or names that don't match, missing pages or schedules, wrong legal entity, signature blocks in the wrong name.
5. Signing method (wet ink, e-signature platform, witness or notarization needed) - mark [CONFIRM].
6. Deadline and who to return it to.

Order the documents by urgency. This cover sheet summarizes; it isn't legal review. Anything unusual or high-value should go to legal before my executive signs, and I'll say so on the sheet.

title: Prepare an import shipment so it clears customs without delays
description: A document checklist, candidate tariff classification reasoning, and broker questions so an import clears without delays or penalties.
content:
Help me prepare for importing a product so it clears customs smoothly.

**Product description:** [WHAT IT IS, WHAT IT'S MADE OF (% BY MATERIAL), WHAT IT DOES, HOW IT'S USED]
**Country of origin and where it's manufactured or substantially transformed:** [DETAILS]
**Importing country:** [COUNTRY]
**Shipment details:** [VALUE, QUANTITY, MODE, INCOTERM]
**Special features:** [BATTERIES, CHEMICALS, FOOD CONTACT, WIRELESS, DUAL-USE, WOOD PACKAGING]

This is general information, not a binding classification or legal advice. Mark every tariff code and duty rate [CONFIRM WITH BROKER], and recommend a binding ruling where the classification is uncertain. Do not invent rates or rules.

Also give me a list of questions to send my customs broker.

title: Prepare my trucking company for a DOT compliance audit
description: A gap checklist and document plan covering driver files, hours of service, maintenance, drug and alcohol testing, and insurance before an audit.
content:
Help me get my fleet ready for a safety compliance audit.

title: Respond to a patient's request for their medical records

title: Respond to a shipper's cargo loss or damage claim

content:
Help me assess and respond to a cargo claim.

**What they say happened:** [loss, shortage, damage, temperature, delay]

**Contract and liability terms:** [carrier agreement, tariff liability limits, released value on BOL, broker-carrier contract, cargo insurance limits]
**Governing rules:** [e.g. "US interstate - Carmack", "CMR in Europe", "Montreal Convention for air", or [CONFIRM]]
**Evidence we have:** [photos, seal numbers, load and unload method (shipper load and count?), reefer download, driver statement, inspection report]

Assess:
1. Was the claim filed on time and with the required documents (claim letter, invoice, BOL, delivery receipt, proof of loss amount)?
2. Was the freight in good condition at pickup, and was damage noted at delivery?
3. Possible defenses: shipper's packaging, shipper load and count, inherent vice, act of God, released value limits.
4. Is the amount correct (invoice value vs. selling price, salvage value, freight charges)?
5. Does it go to our cargo insurer and what is our deductible exposure?

- A missing-document request list.

title: Review a client's contractor agreement for freelancer risks

content:
Review a contract a client has sent me as a freelancer or consultant, focusing on the risks that matter most for independent contractors.

**Fee and payment terms I agreed verbally:** [DETAILS]

**My priorities:** [e.g. getting paid on time, keeping rights to my tools and templates, portfolio use]

Check and explain in plain English:
1. Payment: due dates, conditions on approval, whether withheld payments are possible, and kill fees if they cancel.
2. Intellectual property: when ownership transfers (ideally on full payment), whether it captures my pre-existing tools, templates, and know-how, and my right to show the work in my portfolio.
3. Scope and acceptance: vague scope, unlimited revisions, or acceptance at the client's sole discretion.
4. Liability and indemnity: uncapped liability, indemnities that are out of proportion to my fee, and insurance requirements.
5. Non-compete and non-solicitation clauses that could stop me working in my field.
6. Termination: notice, payment for work done, and what I must hand over.
7. Contractor status wording that conflicts with how the work will actually be done.

For each issue: quote the clause, explain the risk, rate it (high/medium/low), and suggest alternative wording I could propose.

This is general information, not legal advice. Recommend I have a qualified lawyer in my jurisdiction review it before signing, especially for high-risk clauses.

title: Review a contract and flag risky clauses
description: A risk-ranked issues list, suggested redlines, and questions before you sign.
content:
Role: Act as legal counsel reviewing a counterparty's contract draft.

Context: Contract and its purpose: [CONTRACT_PURPOSE]. The counterparty draft (paste or summary by clause): [DRAFT]. Our playbook / acceptable positions: [PLAYBOOK]. Our risk appetite and must-nots: [RISK_APPETITE]. Deal context and leverage: [DEAL_CONTEXT]. Governing law: [LAW].

Goal: Give the deal team a clear, prioritised view of where this contract exposes us and what to push back on.

Task: Produce: (1) a risk-ranked issues list - clause reference, the issue in plain English, the business impact if unchanged, our playbook position, and a suggested redline or fallback; (2) the 3-5 points that are deal-blockers vs negotiable; (3) missing protections we would normally expect; (4) questions for the business before we respond.

Constraints: Identify issues and positions; do not give a legal opinion on enforceability or litigation outcome. Base risk ratings on our stated appetite. Do not assume facts not in the draft - flag ambiguities instead. Quote clause references, not long extracts.

Examples: Issue row: 'Cl. 11.2 Indemnity - uncapped and covers indirect loss. Impact: unlimited exposure on [scenario]. Playbook: mutual, capped at fees. Suggested: cap at 12 months' fees, carve back indirect loss.'

Format: Sections: Risk-ranked issues (table) | Deal-blockers vs negotiable | Missing protections | Questions for the business.

Verification: Check each issue cites a real clause in the draft and each rating matches the stated risk appetite; flag clauses you could not fully assess.

Validation: A qualified lawyer must confirm the positions before redlines go back. Sanity-check the top 3 issues against the deal leverage: are we pushing where we can actually win?

title: Review a data processing agreement against GDPR Article 28

title: Review documents for due diligence red flags
description: A due diligence document review with red flags and follow-up questions.
content:
Role: Act as legal counsel conducting legal due diligence on a target for a transaction.

Context: Transaction type and rationale: [TRANSACTION]. Area(s) of DD in scope (e.g. material contracts, litigation, IP, employment, compliance): [DD_SCOPE]. Documents provided (index): [DOC_INDEX]. Deal issues that especially matter: [KEY_CONCERNS]. Materiality threshold: [MATERIALITY]. Governing law: [LAW].

Goal: Give the deal team a clear view of the legal red flags in the reviewed documents, ranked by how much they should affect the deal, and the follow-ups needed.

Task: Produce: (1) findings by category - what the documents show, with the document reference; (2) for each material finding: the issue, the risk and potential deal impact (price, indemnity, condition, walk-away), and the severity; (3) change-of-control, consent, termination and assignment issues triggered by the transaction; (4) gaps - expected documents not provided; (5) a prioritised Q&A list for the target and disclosure-schedule points.

Constraints: Report only what the provided documents show; do not infer facts or opine on the merits of litigation. Reference documents by index number. Distinguish confirmed issues from items needing clarification. Not legal advice - for the deal team and supervising partner.

Examples: Finding row: 'Material contract [Doc 4.2] - customer accounting for [X]% of revenue; change-of-control termination right on 30 days' notice. Impact: revenue at risk post-close; seek consent as a condition or price adjustment. Severity: high.'

Format: Sections: Findings by category | Material findings (table) | Change-of-control / consents | Document gaps | Q&A list for target. ~800 words.

Verification: Check every finding cites a provided document and every change-of-control trigger is supported by an actual clause; list documents in the index not yet reviewed.

Validation: The supervising partner must review before the report goes to the client. Pressure-test the severity ratings against the deal concerns: are the top 3 flags really the ones that would change the deal?

Review my drivers' hours-of-service data and tell me what's going wrong.

**Rules we operate under:** [e.g. "US FMCSA property-carrying 11/14 with 60/70-hour limits", "EU drivers' hours", "Canada cycle 1", short-haul exemption yes/no]
**Log data:** [PASTE ELD EXPORT OR SUMMARY - driver, date, on-duty, driving, off-duty, sleeper berth, violations flagged]
**Period covered:** [DATES]
**Type of work:** [long haul, regional, local, team drivers]
**What I suspect:** [e.g. "one terminal keeps running out of hours", "too many edits"]

Analyze:
1. Violations by type (driving limit, duty window, break, cycle, form and manner) and by driver, terminal, and dispatcher.
2. Risky patterns that are legal but tiring: back-to-back maximum days, overnight driving swings, short resets, frequent split-sleeper use.
3. Red flags for log falsification: personal conveyance overuse, unassigned driving, edits after the fact, gaps that do not match fuel or GPS data.
4. Root causes on our side: unrealistic appointment times, detention at shippers, poor load planning, pay structure pushing drivers.

Return:
- A summary table: Issue | Count | Drivers or lanes affected | Likely cause.
- Which drivers need coaching versus which problems are dispatch or customer problems.
- 5 process changes to cut violations next month.
- A short, non-accusatory script for a coaching conversation with a driver.

Only use numbers from my data. Flag where you need more data as [ADD]. This is general guidance; confirm rule interpretations with a compliance specialist.
variables: long haul, regional, local, team drivers

title: Review marketing material for compliance issues before it goes out
description: Checks ads, web copy, or sales collateral for misleading claims, missing disclosures, and regulated wording, with suggested fixes.
content:
Help me review marketing material for compliance issues.

**Material:** [PASTE copy, or describe images, video, and placement]
**Product or service:** [WHAT is being promoted]
**Channel and audience:** [e.g. social ad to consumers, investor deck, email to existing customers, website]
**Where it will run:** [COUNTRIES/STATES]
**Sector rules and internal guidelines that apply:** [e.g. financial promotion rules, health claims, testimonial rules, our brand and disclosure standards - PASTE]
**Substantiation available:** [data, studies, or sources behind the claims]

Check for:
1. **Claims** - every factual, comparative, or superlative claim ("best", "guaranteed", "risk-free", "fastest", "clinically proven"), and whether substantiation exists.
2. **Balance** - benefits shown with equal prominence to risks, costs, and limitations where required.
3. **Disclosures** - required fees, terms, conditions, risk warnings; placement and legibility.
4. **Testimonials, endorsements, and influencers** - typicality, disclosure of paid relationships.
5. **Pricing and offers** - "from" prices, free trials, auto-renewal terms, expiry dates.
6. **Targeting** - vulnerable audiences, minors, and channel restrictions.

Return a table: Text or element, Issue, Rule or guideline concerned, Severity, Suggested compliant rewrite. Then a short overall verdict: approve / approve with changes / reject.

Mark claims needing evidence [SUBSTANTIATE]. Do not state that a specific law applies unless I provided it - mark [CONFIRM WITH LEGAL]. This is a first-pass review, not legal sign-off.
variables: PASTE copy, or describe images, video, and placement
data, studies, or sources behind the claims

title: Review my hiring process for bias and compliance risks
description: A review of job ads, screening, interviews, and decisions for bias and common legal risks, with practical fixes.
content:
Review my hiring process for bias and compliance risks.

**Country / state where we hire:** [LOCATIONS]
**Materials to review:** [PASTE job ad, screening questions, interview questions, scorecard, rejection templates]
**Process description:** [steps, who decides, tools used - e.g. AI resume screening, assessments, video interviews]
**Company size:** [employees - this can change which laws apply]
**Concerns:** [anything specific]

Check for:
1. Job ads: gendered or age-coded wording, unnecessary requirements (degrees, years, physical demands), missing pay ranges where pay-transparency laws apply.
2. Screening: knockout questions that may screen out protected groups, salary-history questions where banned, criminal-history timing rules, work-authorization questions phrased improperly.
3. Interviews: unstructured questions, illegal or risky questions, inconsistent criteria between candidates.
4. Tools: automated or AI screening that may need bias audits, notices, or candidate consent.
5. Decisions and records: documentation of reasons, record retention, data privacy, and accommodation requests.

Output: a table with Issue | Where found | Risk (High / Medium / Low) | Why it matters | Fix. Then rewrite any problem questions.

This is general information, not legal advice - laws differ by location and change often. Mark items to confirm with an employment lawyer as [VERIFY].
variables: employees - this can change which laws apply

title: Review open-source licenses in our software for compliance risk
description: Sorts dependencies by license type, flags copyleft and distribution triggers, and lists the notices and actions engineering must take.
content:
Help me review the open-source licenses used in one of our products.

**Dependency list:** [PASTE - component, version, license as reported by the scanner or package manager]
**Product type and how it is delivered:** [e.g. "SaaS only, no code distributed", "mobile app", "on-prem software shipped to customers", "embedded device"]
**How components are used:** [linked / modified / bundled / dev-tooling only - if known]
**Our commercial model and customer commitments:** [e.g. "customer contracts promise no copyleft code"]
**Company OSS policy:** [PASTE, or "none"]

Do this:
1. Group components by license family: permissive (e.g. MIT, BSD, Apache-2.0), weak copyleft (e.g. LGPL, MPL), strong copyleft (e.g. GPL), network copyleft (e.g. AGPL), source-available or non-OSI licenses, and unknown/missing licenses.
2. For each group, explain in plain English what triggers obligations (distribution, network use, modification, linking) given our delivery model.
3. Flag high-risk items: strong or network copyleft in distributed or networked code, licenses with field-of-use or commercial restrictions, unknown licenses, license conflicts, and dual-licensed components where we must choose.
4. List obligations: attribution notices, license texts, NOTICE files, source-code offers, change notices.
5. Note dev-only or build-time tools that are likely lower risk [CONFIRM WITH ENGINEERING].

Return: a table (Component | License | Use | Risk | Obligation | Action), a prioritized remediation list, and a one-paragraph summary for leadership. Scanner output can be wrong; a qualified lawyer must confirm license interpretations before relying on them.
variables: linked / modified / bundled / dev-tooling only - if known
e.g. "customer contracts promise no copyleft code"

title: Review outside counsel invoices against our billing guidelines
description: Checks law firm bills for guideline breaches, block billing, staffing issues, and budget overruns, and drafts questions for the firm.
content:
Review an outside counsel invoice against our billing guidelines.

**Invoice line items:** [PASTE - date, timekeeper, role, hours, rate, narrative, amount; plus expenses]
**Our billing guidelines:** [PASTE key rules - e.g. rates, increments, staffing limits, non-billable items, expense rules, approval for research over X hours]
**Matter and agreed budget / fee arrangement:** [e.g. "budget $80k for phase 1, $52k billed to date"]
**Approved timekeepers and rates:** [LIST]

Check for:
- Rates above agreed rates or unapproved timekeepers
- Block billing (several tasks in one entry with one time figure) and vague narratives ("review documents", "attention to matter")
- Billing increments that break the guidelines
- Duplicate entries or several people attending the same call or meeting without justification
- Senior lawyers doing junior or administrative work; clerical tasks billed as legal work
- Excessive time for routine tasks, or research without approval
- Time spent on billing, conflicts, onboarding new team members, or fixing the firm's own errors
- Non-compliant expenses (meals, overhead, markups, travel class)
- Spend against budget and the remaining runway

Return:
1. A table: Entry | Issue | Guideline rule | Amount questioned | Suggested action (accept / query / reduce / reject).
2. Totals: billed, questioned, recommended adjustment.
3. Budget status and forecast if the current pace continues.
4. A polite, specific email to the relationship partner raising the issues.

Flag judgment calls rather than assuming bad faith. The responsible lawyer must approve any reductions.
variables: e.g. "budget $80k for phase 1, $52k billed to date"

title: Rewrite a compliance policy so employees can actually follow it
description: Turns a dense compliance policy into clear rules, decision points, and examples, with a mapping so no requirement is lost.
content:
Help me rewrite a compliance policy so the people it applies to can understand and follow it.

**Current policy text:** [PASTE]
**Who it applies to:** [e.g. all employees, sales team, traders, procurement]
**Regulation or standard behind it:** [e.g. anti-bribery law, data protection law, insider trading rules - or "internal only"]
**Where people get it wrong today:** [COMMON MISTAKES, audit findings, or questions you get]
**Our policy template sections:** [PASTE or "use a standard structure"]

Produce:
1. **The rewritten policy** - purpose (2 sentences), who it applies to, then the rules as "You must" and "You must not" statements, decision points (thresholds, approvals, who to ask), what happens if it is breached, and contacts.
2. **"Is this allowed?" examples** - 5 realistic scenarios from this audience's daily work, with the answer and the reason.
3. **One-page quick guide** for the intranet.
4. **Requirement mapping table** - columns: Original clause, Where it now appears, Change made (kept / clarified / merged / removed). Every original requirement must be accounted for.
5. **Issues found** - contradictions, undefined terms, missing owners, approval thresholds with no stated amount.

Rules:
- Do not weaken or drop any obligation. If something is unclear in the original, flag it [NEEDS POLICY OWNER DECISION] instead of interpreting it.
- Plain language, active voice, short sentences.
- Have legal or compliance leadership approve the final text.
variables: e.g. all employees, sales team, traders, procurement
COMMON MISTAKES, audit findings, or questions you get

title: Run a fraud risk assessment for a business process
description: Brainstorms realistic fraud schemes for a process, assesses them against existing controls, and recommends prevention and detection fixes.
content:
Help me run a fraud risk assessment for a business process.

**Process:** [e.g. procurement, payroll, expenses, revenue recognition, inventory, customer refunds]
**How it works:** [KEY steps, roles, systems, approval limits]
**Existing controls:** [LIST]
**Pressures and incentives:** [e.g. aggressive targets, bonus structures, cost cuts, staff turnover]
**Past incidents or allegations:** [SUMMARY or "none known"]

Work through:
1. **Fraud schemes** - 8-12 realistic schemes for this process across asset misappropriation, corruption, and financial reporting fraud. For each: who could commit it (role), how, and how they would conceal it. Include collusion and management override scenarios.
2. **Fraud triangle** - for the main schemes, the likely pressure, opportunity, and rationalization.
3. **Assessment table** - columns: Scheme, Perpetrator role, Likelihood, Impact, Existing controls, Would controls prevent or detect it?, Residual risk.
4. **Control gaps** - especially segregation of duties, master data changes, manual overrides, and controls performed by the same person they are meant to check.
5. **Recommendations** - preventive and detective controls, including data analytics tests to run on the full population.
6. **Red flags** for managers and staff in this process.

Keep it practical, and do not accuse anyone: this assesses where fraud could happen, not who did it. If I describe a suspected live fraud, tell me to preserve evidence and involve legal before investigating.
variables: KEY steps, roles, systems, approval limits

title: Run a HIPAA security risk assessment for a small practice
description: A structured security risk analysis covering where ePHI lives, threats, likelihood and impact ratings, and a documented remediation plan.
content:
Help me conduct and document a HIPAA Security Rule risk analysis for our practice.

**Practice size and locations:** [e.g. "9 staff, 1 office, some remote billing staff"]
**Systems that hold or touch ePHI:** [EHR/PM, email, texting, fax, imaging, cloud storage, billing service, patient portal, personal phones]
**Devices:** [workstations, laptops, tablets, medical devices on the network]
**Current safeguards:** [e.g. MFA, encryption, backups, antivirus, access reviews, training, locked server closet]
**Vendors with ePHI access:** [LIST - and whether we have signed BAAs]
**Last assessment and known incidents:** [DATE / DETAILS or "none"]

Work through:
1. An inventory of where ePHI is created, received, stored, and sent, including paper-to-digital points like scanning and fax.
2. For each asset: threats and vulnerabilities (e.g. phishing, ransomware, lost device, former employee access, unpatched systems), current controls, likelihood (low/medium/high), impact (low/medium/high), and risk level.
3. Gaps against the administrative, physical, and technical safeguards, noting which are "required" versus "addressable" and that addressable items still need a documented decision.
4. A remediation plan prioritized by risk, with owner, cost range as [ESTIMATE], and target date.

Return the risk register as a table, then the remediation plan, then a list of policies and documentation we should have on file. Do not assume a control exists unless I said so; mark unknowns as [CONFIRM]. This is a working draft; have it reviewed by our privacy/security officer or a qualified HIPAA consultant.
variables: e.g. "9 staff, 1 office, some remote billing staff"
LIST - and whether we have signed BAAs

title: Run a preliminary trademark check on a proposed brand name
description: Assesses a proposed name for distinctiveness and obvious conflict risks and gives a search plan before formal clearance.
content:
Help me do a preliminary trademark assessment of a proposed brand name before we order a full clearance search.

**Proposed name / logo / tagline:** [MARK]
**Goods and services it will cover:** [DETAILS]
**Markets and countries:** [LIST]
**Launch timing and how much we will invest in it:** [DETAILS]
**Results of any searches I have done:** [PASTE register hits, web results, domain/social handle availability - or "none yet"]
**Our existing marks:** [LIST]

Do this:
1. **Distinctiveness** - place the mark on the spectrum (generic, descriptive, suggestive, arbitrary, fanciful) and explain; flag descriptive or laudatory elements, geographic terms, surnames, or meanings in other languages for the target markets.
2. **Likely trademark classes** for the goods and services [CONFIRM CLASSIFICATION].
3. **Conflict risk** - using only the search results I pasted, assess similarity in look, sound, meaning, and overall impression, plus relatedness of goods and services. Do not claim any mark exists or does not exist beyond what I gave you.
4. **Search plan** - registers and databases to search, variants to search (spelling, phonetic, translations, plurals), and common-law/unregistered use to check.
5. **Risk rating** - Low / Medium / High with reasons, and what would change it.
6. **Options** - modifications that would improve registrability, and fallback names to test.
7. **Next steps** - formal search, filing strategy, priority dates.

This is a screening aid only, not a clearance opinion; a qualified trademark lawyer must conduct and review a full search before adoption or filing.

title: Run a user access review and flag risky permissions
description: Compares who has access against job need and flags excess rights, orphaned accounts, and segregation-of-duties conflicts.
content:
Help me run a user access review for one system.

**System:** [e.g. "ERP", "AWS production", "file shares", "Salesforce"]
**Access export:** [PASTE: user, role or group, permissions, last login, account status]
**HR roster or job titles:** [PASTE current employees with department and title]
**Role definitions or expected access:** [what each job should have - or "infer and mark as assumption"]
**Rules that apply:** [e.g. "SOX: no one can create and approve vendors", "least privilege policy"]

Check for:
1. Orphaned accounts: users not on the HR roster (leavers, contractors past end date).
2. Dormant accounts: no login in [NUMBER] days.
3. Privilege creep: access beyond what the role needs, especially admin rights.
4. Segregation-of-duties conflicts I listed, plus any obvious ones you spot (mark as suggested).
5. Shared, generic, or service accounts without a named owner.
6. Role mismatches: people who changed jobs but kept old access.

Return:
- A findings table: User | Finding type | Current access | Recommended action (remove / reduce / confirm with manager) | Risk (high/medium/low).
- A list of questions for each manager to certify their team's access.
- A short evidence summary I can file for auditors (scope, date, reviewer, results, actions).

Do not recommend removing access without listing it for manager confirmation first, except clear leavers.
variables: PASTE current employees with department and title
what each job should have - or "infer and mark as assumption"

title: Screen where my business may owe sales tax
description: Maps sales by state against economic and physical nexus factors and lists the questions to resolve with a tax advisor.
content:
Help me screen where a business may have sales tax obligations in the US.

**What we sell:** [products/services - note digital goods, SaaS, services, shipping]
**Sales by state, last 12 months:** [PASTE - revenue and number of transactions per state]
**Physical presence:** [offices, employees or contractors, inventory (including in marketplace warehouses), trade shows]
**Sales channels:** [own website / Amazon / Etsy / wholesale / other marketplaces]
**Where we're registered now:** [STATES]

Steps:
1. For each state, compare our sales and transaction counts to that state's economic nexus threshold. Do not state thresholds from memory as fact - list them as [VERIFY THRESHOLD] with the figure you believe applies.
2. Note physical nexus triggers from what I listed.
3. Note where marketplace facilitator rules likely mean the marketplace collects for those sales, and whether those sales still count toward our threshold.
4. Flag product taxability questions (e.g. SaaS and digital goods are taxed in some states and not others).

Return:
1. A table: State | Our sales | Our transactions | Threshold to verify | Physical presence? | Likely status (registered / likely obligated / watch / unlikely) | Notes.
2. The top priorities and why.
3. Questions to take to a sales tax advisor, including whether a voluntary disclosure agreement makes sense for any past exposure.

This is a screening aid, not tax advice. Rules change often - confirm with a qualified sales tax professional before registering or filing.
variables: PASTE - revenue and number of transactions per state
own website / Amazon / Etsy / wholesale / other marketplaces

title: Set up OSHA safety recordkeeping and compliance tracking
description: A practical system for OSHA logs, training records, inspections, and incident investigations, with owners, schedules, and tools that fit your size.
content:
Help me set up a system to manage and document OSHA compliance.

**Industry and operations:** [e.g. "metal fabrication shop", "construction subcontractor", "distribution center"]
**Number of employees and sites:** [DETAILS]
**State:** [STATE - note whether it runs its own OSHA-approved state plan]
**Current setup:** [e.g. "paper sign-in sheets and a shared drive", "nothing formal"]
