**Ideas we already have:** [PASTE LIST, rough is fine]
**Traffic/volume per month:** [so we know what is testable]
**Team capacity:** [e.g. "1 engineer half-time, 1 designer, me"]

Steps:
1. Find the biggest leak in the funnel from my numbers and point most experiments there.
2. Add 5-10 new ideas of your own, spread across acquisition, activation, monetization, and retention.
3. Write each as a hypothesis: "Because we saw [evidence], we believe [change] will improve [metric] for [segment]."
4. Score with ICE (Impact, Confidence, Ease, 1-10 each) and explain the Confidence score in one phrase.
5. Flag any experiment my traffic can't support to a clear result in 4 weeks, and suggest a bolder version or a different metric.

Return a table: Rank | Experiment | Hypothesis | Funnel stage | Primary metric | Guardrail metric | I | C | E | Score | Notes.
Then list the top 3 to start this month and what to stop doing to make room.

Use only the funnel numbers I give; mark missing data as [NEED] and label your Impact estimates as judgments, not forecasts.

title: Check whether a discount or promotion will actually pay off
description: A break-even and margin analysis for a proposed promotion, including the extra sales it needs and hidden costs.
content:
Help me work out whether a planned discount or promotion is worth running.

**Promotion:** [e.g. "25% off sitewide for 5 days", "buy 2 get 1", "first month free"]
**Normal price and unit cost:** [PRICE, COGS or variable cost per unit]
**Typical sales in the same period without a promotion:** [UNITS or revenue]
**Other costs:** [ad spend for the promo, free shipping, payment fees, extra staffing, affiliate commissions]
**Goal:** [e.g. clear inventory, acquire new customers, hit a revenue target, reactivate lapsed customers]
**Past promotion results, if any:** [DETAILS]

Calculate and explain:
1. Contribution margin per unit before and during the promo.
2. Break-even sales lift: how many more units I must sell just to earn the same profit as without the promotion.
3. Hidden costs: sales pulled forward from future weeks, discounting to customers who would have paid full price, higher return rates, training customers to wait for sales, brand perception.
4. For customer acquisition promos: what LTV the new customers need for this to pay back, and how to check their repeat rate later.

Then suggest:
- Smarter alternatives (targeted offer to lapsed or new customers only, bundle, gift with purchase, threshold discount) and why they might protect margin.
- How to measure the true result (control group or comparison period).

Show your math step by step using my numbers only. Mark assumptions with [ASSUMPTION].
variables: PRICE, COGS or variable cost per unit

2. 12-15 pitch questions that expose real capability: who will actually work on the account and their time allocation, a relevant result with numbers and how it was measured, how they'd approach our first 90 days, reporting, how they handle underperformance, fee model and markups on media or tools, contract term and exit terms, ownership of ad accounts, data, and creative.
3. Red flags to listen for (vague attribution claims, senior team in the pitch but juniors on the work, owning our ad accounts, long lock-ins).
4. A weighted scorecard: Criterion | Weight | Score 1-5 | Evidence, covering strategy, relevant experience, team, measurement, cost, fit.
5. Reference-check questions for their current clients.

content:
Help me choose a webinar topic and title that will get registrations and qualified leads. This is step 1 of a 5-step webinar pack; later steps (registration page, reminders, follow-up, repurposing) can use what we decide here.

2. **Score them** on: urgency for the buyer, link to what I sell, speaker credibility, and how differentiated it is from free content already out there.

4. **Timing:** day and time considerations for my audience's time zones.

Be honest if a topic is too broad or too self-promotional to attract the people I want.

title: Clean up search terms and build a negative keyword list
description: A review of your paid search terms report with negatives to add, keywords to promote, and wasted spend to cut.
content:
Help me review my paid search terms report.

**Business and what we sell:** [PRODUCTS/SERVICES, and what we don't offer]
**Locations served:** [AREAS]
**Search terms report:** [PASTE: search term, matched keyword, match type, clicks, cost, conversions, conversion value]
**Target CPA or ROAS:** [NUMBER]

Do this:
1. Group terms by intent: buying, researching, wrong product, job seekers, free/DIY, competitor brand, support or existing customers, irrelevant locations.
2. Flag wasted spend: terms with cost above [e.g. 2x target CPA] and no conversions, and irrelevant terms at any cost.
3. Recommend negatives with the right match type and level (campaign vs. account list), and warn when a negative would block good traffic (e.g. "cheap" blocking "cheap [our product]").

title: Create a brand messaging framework and voice guide
description: Core messages, proof points, and a voice and tone guide so everything sounds on-brand.
content:
Role: Act as a brand manager building the messaging framework and voice guide for [BRAND].

Context: What we do and for whom: [WHAT_WHO]. Target audiences: [AUDIENCES]. Category and main alternatives: [CATEGORY_ALTS]. Differentiators and proof: [DIFF_PROOF]. Brand personality attributes: [PERSONALITY]. Existing copy samples (good and bad): [COPY_SAMPLES]. Words we own / avoid: [LEXICON].

Goal: Give every writer and agency a single reference so brand copy is consistent, distinctive and true to how we actually sound.

Task: Produce: (1) a positioning statement and category frame; (2) 3-4 message pillars, each with a one-line claim, supporting points and proof; (3) audience-specific value messages; (4) a voice guide: 4-5 principles, each with a 'we sound like / we don't sound like' pair and a rewritten before/after example drawn from the samples; (5) the lexicon (use / avoid).

Constraints: Every claim must trace to a differentiator or proof point I provided, no aspirational claims we cannot support. Voice principles must be specific enough to change a sentence, not adjectives like 'friendly'. Keep the whole guide under ~900 words.

Examples: Voice principle shape: 'Plain over clever - We sound like: "Set it up in ten minutes." We don't sound like: "Onboarding has never been more frictionless."' Pillar shape: 'Claim -> 3 support points -> proof.'

Format: Sections: Positioning | Message pillars | Audience messages | Voice guide (principles + before/after) | Lexicon.

Verification: List any pillar or claim that lacks a proof point, and any voice principle that is really just an adjective.

Validation: Apply the voice guide to the 'bad' copy sample: does following it actually fix the sample? If not, sharpen the relevant principle.

title: Create a lead magnet people want

title: Critique my marketing copy and fix what hurts conversions
description: A conversion-focused teardown of your copy with prioritized fixes and a rewritten version.
content:
Critique my marketing copy for conversion and show me how to fix it.

**Copy:** [PASTE]
**Where it appears:** [landing page / ad / email / product page / sales page]
**Audience and awareness level:** [e.g. "problem-aware, never heard of us"]
**The one action I want:** [e.g. "start a free trial"]
**Traffic source:** [where readers arrive from]

Score 1-5 and explain, quoting the copy:
1. Clarity: can a reader say what this is and who it's for in 5 seconds?
2. Relevance: does it match the awareness level and the promise that brought them here?
3. Specificity: concrete outcomes, numbers, and details vs. vague claims ("powerful", "seamless").
4. Proof: testimonials, data, credentials, demos; is every claim backed?
5. Objections: are the main reasons not to act handled?
6. Friction and CTA: one clear next step, low-risk framing, consistent CTA.
7. Readability: scannable, short sentences, benefit-led subheads.

Return:
- Scores table and the 3 changes most likely to lift conversions.
- A rewritten version with changes marked.
- 2 A/B test ideas with a hypothesis each.

Don't invent proof; where proof is needed, write [ADD PROOF: e.g. customer result].
variables: landing page / ad / email / product page / sales page

title: Defend my marketing budget to the CFO with a revenue case
description: A finance-ready case that connects marketing spend to pipeline and revenue, with honest caveats and asks.

Help me build a case to protect (or increase) my marketing budget with finance.

**Budget I'm asking for and change vs. last year:** [AMOUNT, % change]
**What finance is questioning:** [e.g. "brand spend", "event costs", "why CAC rose"]
**Results I can show:** [PASTE: spend, marketing-sourced and -influenced pipeline, revenue, CAC, payback, win rates, by channel if possible]
**Company targets:** [revenue, growth, efficiency goals]
**What happens if cut:** [my honest estimate]

Build:

2. The efficiency story: CAC, payback period, and LTV:CAC trends, using only my numbers. Separate sourced from influenced pipeline and say which is which.
3. Spend split into: proven (keep), scaling (fund with targets), and experimental (cap and measure).
4. Scenarios: flat, cut 20%, and requested budget, with the expected pipeline impact and the lag before it shows.
5. Pre-empt the 5 toughest CFO questions with direct answers, including where the data is weak.
6. Commitments I'll make: metrics, reporting cadence, and triggers to pull back spend.

Format: a one-page memo plus a table of the scenarios. Use finance vocabulary, no marketing jargon. Mark any figure I need to verify with [CONFIRM]; never invent numbers.

title: Diagnose ad creative fatigue and plan a creative refresh

Help me find out whether my ads are fatigued and plan what to replace them with.

Analyze:

Then plan the refresh:

Use only the data I share; label hypotheses as hypotheses.

title: Diagnose email deliverability and falling open rates
description: A step-by-step check of authentication, sender reputation, list health, and content to get emails back in the inbox.
content:
Help me diagnose why my marketing emails are underperforming or landing in spam.

**Email platform:** [TOOL]
**What changed:** [e.g. "open rate fell from 32% to 18% over 6 weeks", "Gmail sending to promotions/spam"]
**Recent metrics:** [opens, clicks, bounces (hard/soft), spam complaints, unsubscribes - by send if possible]
**Sending setup:** [domain, dedicated or shared IP, SPF/DKIM/DMARC status if known]
**List practices:** [how contacts are collected, double opt-in?, last cleaned, purchased lists?, sending to inactive contacts?]
**Volume and frequency:** [sends per week, any recent spike]

Work through:
1. Measurement first: whether privacy features (like automatic image loading) inflate or distort open rates, and why clicks and conversions are better signals.
2. Authentication: SPF, DKIM, DMARC alignment, and current bulk-sender requirements from major mailbox providers (one-click unsubscribe, low complaint rates). Tell me how to check each.
3. Reputation: complaint rate, bounce rate, volume spikes, sending to old or unengaged contacts, spam traps.
4. Content and format: link domains, image-to-text ratio, misleading subject lines.
5. Engagement: segment by recent activity and stop mailing long-inactive contacts after a re-permission attempt.

Return a prioritized fix list (do today, this week, this month), a sunset policy for inactive subscribers, and a warm-up plan if volume needs rebuilding. Note which checks I need my email tool's docs or an expert to verify.
variables: sends per week, any recent spike

title: Explain an interest rate change to my clients in an email
description: A clear, compliant client email that explains a central bank rate move and what it may mean for buyers, sellers, or borrowers.
content:
Write an email to my client list about a recent interest rate change.

**My role:** [e.g. real estate agent, mortgage broker, financial advisor]
**Market:** [city, region, country]
**The change:** [which rate, old and new level, date announced - paste the official announcement or a news summary]
**Who is on my list:** [first-time buyers, homeowners, sellers, investors, past clients]
**Local market facts I can share:** [e.g. recent sales, inventory, days on market - from my own sources]
**My call to action:** [e.g. book a call, get a pre-approval review, request a home valuation]
**Tone:** [warm, calm, professional]

The email should:
1. Open with the news in one or two sentences, in plain language.
2. Explain what it may mean for each group on my list: affordability, monthly payments (with a simple illustrative example clearly marked as an example), fixed vs. variable borrowers, and buyer and seller behavior.
3. Stay balanced: what could change, what probably won't change quickly, and that outcomes vary by person.
4. End with one clear next step.

Rules:
- Use only the facts I provide. Mark anything I need to fill in as [ADD] and any figure to verify as [CONFIRM].
- No predictions presented as certain, no pressure tactics ("buy now before it's too late").
- Include a short disclaimer that this is general information, not personal financial or mortgage advice, and remind me to check my regulator's and brokerage's rules for client communications.

Return 3 subject lines, the email (under 300 words), and a 2-sentence version for text or social.
variables: e.g. real estate agent, mortgage broker, financial advisor

title: Find the selling points in a product photo
description: Turns a product image into a ranked list of visual selling points, with copy angles and the photos you are still missing.
content:
Look at the product photo I've attached and pull out the selling points a buyer would notice.

**Product:** [WHAT IT IS - e.g. "insulated stainless water bottle"]
**Target buyer:** [WHO - e.g. "commuters who want something leak-proof for a bag"]
**Where this will be used:** [product page / marketplace listing / ad / social post]
**Main competitors or alternatives:** [OPTIONAL - what buyers compare it to]
**Facts I can confirm:** [OPTIONAL - materials, sizes, certifications]

Steps:
1. Describe only what is actually visible: shape, materials, finish, color, details, scale cues, included items.
2. Translate each visible feature into a buyer benefit for my target buyer ("wide mouth" -> "fits ice cubes, easy to clean").
3. Rank the selling points by how much they would matter to that buyer.
4. Flag anything that looks like a weakness or could raise doubts (looks cheap, unclear size, missing angle).

Return:
- A table: Visible feature | Buyer benefit | Strength (high/med/low) | How to show it better.
- The top 3 selling points written as short benefit lines for [WHERE THIS WILL BE USED].
- A list of claims I should NOT make from the photo alone (e.g. "waterproof", "BPA-free") marked [CONFIRM] until I verify them.
- 3-5 extra shots I should add (angles, close-ups, scale or in-use photos).

Never state specs, certifications, or performance you can't see; ask me or mark them [CONFIRM].
variables: WHAT IT IS - e.g. "insulated stainless water bottle"
product page / marketplace listing / ad / social post
OPTIONAL - what buyers compare it to

title: Give an agency clear feedback on creative against the brief
description: Specific, actionable creative feedback tied to the brief and goals, so revisions improve instead of going in circles.
content:
Help me give feedback on creative work from my agency or design team.

**The brief (or key points):** [OBJECTIVE, audience, single message, mandatories, channel and format]
**The work:** [PASTE copy, describe the visuals, or list concepts A/B/C]
**Brand guidelines that apply:** [tone, logo use, colors, claims rules]
**Stakeholder comments I've received:** [PASTE, including conflicting ones]
**Round and deadline:** [e.g. "round 2 of 3, final due Friday"]

Do this:
1. Evaluate each piece against the brief: Does it land the single message within 3 seconds? Is it right for the audience and the channel (thumb-stopping on mobile, legible at small sizes, works without sound)? Is the call to action clear?
2. Separate objective issues (off-brief, brand violations, legal or claims risks, accessibility like contrast and text size) from subjective preferences.
3. Consolidate conflicting stakeholder comments into one direction and note which I need to resolve before sending.
4. Write feedback as problems to solve, not solutions to execute ("The offer gets lost behind the image" rather than "make the logo bigger"), unless a mandatory is broken.

Return:
- A verdict per piece: proceed / revise / drop.
- Prioritized feedback (must fix, should fix, consider), max 8 points per piece.
- The feedback message to send, warm and direct, under 250 words.

tone, logo use, colors, claims rules

title: Grow my fan base and bookings as a DJ or musician

Help me grow my audience and get more bookings as a DJ or musician.

**Weekly hours and budget:** [DETAILS]

Give me:

2. A social media plan: the 2-3 platforms that matter for my genre, content types (mix clips, behind the scenes, crowd moments, production breakdowns), and a realistic weekly posting schedule.
3. A booking plan: how to build a list of venues, promoters, and agencies; an outreach email template; how to follow up; and how to use each gig to land the next one.

6. A 90-day plan as a table: Week | Focus | Actions | Metric.

title: Improve an underperforming affiliate program using its data
description: A diagnosis of your affiliate program's metrics with prioritized fixes for recruitment, commissions, and fraud leaks.
content:
Help me diagnose and improve my affiliate program.

**Business:** [what I sell, average order value, margin]
**Program basics:** [network or platform, commission structure, cookie window, number of affiliates]
**Performance data:** [paste or summarize: clicks, conversions, revenue, commission paid, earnings per click (EPC), conversion rate, reversal or refund rate, active vs. inactive affiliates, revenue by affiliate type]
**Affiliate mix:** [content sites, coupon/deal sites, influencers, loyalty/cashback, comparison sites]
**Goal:** [e.g. "more incremental new customers", "lower cost per sale", "reactivate dormant partners"]

Analyze:
1. **Health check:** active affiliate rate, concentration (share of revenue from the top 10 partners), EPC against any benchmarks I provide (do not invent category benchmarks), and reversal rate.
2. **Incrementality:** where commissions may be paid on sales I would have made anyway (coupon sites intercepting checkout, brand-term bidding, last-click cookie overwriting).
3. **Fraud and quality signals:** unusual conversion spikes, high reversal rates, cookie stuffing patterns.
4. **Commission design:** tiers, new-customer bonuses, category-specific rates, and performance incentives.
5. **Recruitment and activation:** which partner types to add and how to reactivate dormant ones.
6. **Partner enablement:** creative, product feeds, exclusive offers, and communication cadence.

Output: a findings table (Finding | Evidence | Impact | Fix), then a 90-day action plan ranked by expected impact and effort.

Use only the numbers I provide; mark missing data as [NEED DATA] and say what it would tell us.
variables: what I sell, average order value, margin

title: Improve free trial to paid conversion for my SaaS product

Help me improve free-trial-to-paid conversion for my SaaS product.

2. Trial design choices to test: trial length, card upfront vs no card, reverse trial (premium trial that drops to free), and the trade-offs for my model.
3. A day-by-day trial journey table: day | trigger (behavior-based where possible) | channel (in-app, email, sales) | message goal | copy draft.

5. Upgrade moments: where to show pricing and limits in context without blocking value.

title: Improve my property listing on Booking.com, Expedia, or Airbnb

**Performance data:** [views, conversion rate, review score, common review complaints]

Steps:
1. Diagnose the funnel: is the problem visibility (search ranking), click-through (photo, price, score), or conversion (content, policies, price)?
2. Rewrite the title and description for that guest type, leading with what they search and filter for.
3. Rewrite room descriptions so bed sizes, room size, and views are exact; mismatches drive bad reviews.
4. Recommend a photo order (first five matter most) and missing shots.
5. Audit amenities and filters: missing ticks that hide me from searches, and anything ticked that should not be.
6. Address recurring review complaints honestly in the listing (e.g. stairs, street noise).

Return the rewritten content, the photo order, an amenity fix list, and 3 platform settings to test (e.g. flexible rate plan, mobile rate, minimum stay). Do not add claims I have not confirmed; mark them [CONFIRM].

title: Measure brand awareness and share of voice

Help me measure brand awareness and share of voice.

Build a measurement plan with:
1. Leading proxies I can track now: branded search volume vs. competitors, direct and branded organic traffic, share of search, social mentions and sentiment, earned media mentions, self-reported "How did you hear about us?".

4. Linking awareness to business outcomes: what changes in conversion rates, CAC, or pricing power to watch.
5. Pitfalls: seasonality in branded search, news spikes, survey wording bias, small samples.

Return:

- A 10-question brand tracking survey.
- A quarterly reporting template.
Don't invent benchmark figures; if suggesting typical ranges, label them as rough and to verify.

title: Mine customer reviews for the words to use in my copy

title: Plan a browse and cart abandonment recovery campaign
description: Segments, flows, copy, discount rules, and measurement to win back shoppers who browsed or added to cart but did not buy.
content:
Plan a campaign to convert people who showed interest in a product but didn't buy.

**What I sell and average order value:** [DETAILS]
**Interest signals I can track:** [product views, cart adds, checkout started, wishlist adds, pricing page visits, quote or demo requests]
**Channels and tools:** [email platform, SMS, push, retargeting ads, sales team]
**Consent I have:** [who has opted in to email and SMS]
**Common reasons people don't buy:** [price, shipping cost, unsure about fit, comparing options - give your best guess if unknown and I'll confirm]
**Discount policy:** [allowed or not, maximum %]

Build:
1. **Segments** by intent strength (browsed once, viewed repeatedly, added to cart, started checkout), with entry and exit rules. Anyone who buys exits immediately.
2. **A flow for each segment:** timing, channel, goal, and content for each touch. Lead with help and reassurance (reviews, sizing, returns, delivery dates) before discounts.
3. **Draft copy** for the cart and checkout abandonment emails: 3 subject lines each, body, and call to action.
4. **Discount rules:** when to offer one, if ever, and how to avoid training customers to abandon carts to get a code.
5. **Frequency caps and suppression rules** so no one is flooded across channels.
6. **Measurement:** recovery rate, revenue per recipient, incremental lift against a holdout group, and unsubscribe rate.

Only message people who have consented to each channel, and follow the privacy and marketing rules for my region (e.g. GDPR, CAN-SPAM, TCPA).
variables: email platform, SMS, push, retargeting ads, sales team
who has opted in to email and SMS

title: Plan a co-marketing campaign with a partner company

Help me plan a co-marketing campaign with a partner company.

2. 3 campaign concepts that give our shared audience real value, with the best one recommended.
3. Roles and responsibilities: content creation, design, promotion commitments (e.g. "2 emails + 3 social posts each"), landing page, and approvals.
4. Lead and data sharing: who owns registrants, consent language that names both companies, how leads are split and followed up, and what each side may not do with the data.
5. Timeline from kickoff to post-campaign report.
6. Shared success metrics and a debrief format.

Return the campaign plan, a 1-page partnership brief to send the partner, and a checklist of terms to put in writing (data sharing, brand use, costs, approvals). Recommend checking data-sharing terms with legal or privacy colleagues.

email list, social following, customers - approximate

title: Plan a holiday or seasonal sale with the right offer and timeline

title: Plan a product launch and go-to-market
description: Launch messaging, audiences, channels, timeline, and success metrics.
content:
Role: Act as a product marketer leading the go-to-market for a launch.

Context: What is launching and why now: [LAUNCH_WHAT_WHY]. Target audiences and their current alternative: [AUDIENCES_ALT]. Top 3 benefits with proof: [BENEFITS_PROOF]. Positioning vs competitors: [POSITIONING]. Launch tier / ambition: [TIER]. Date and constraints: [DATE_CONSTRAINTS]. Sales and channel context: [SALES_CONTEXT].

Goal: Give the launch team one aligned story and a clear plan so messaging, sales and channels all say the same thing on day one.

Task: Produce: (1) the launch narrative (problem, shift, our answer, why believe, call to action); (2) messaging by audience (headline, 3 talking points, one-liner); (3) an objection/FAQ set; (4) a GTM brief: channels and their role, asset checklist with owners, internal enablement needs, timeline milestones, and the success metrics (leading and lagging).

Constraints: Benefits must map to the proof I gave; flag any that do not. Keep the narrative under 250 words. No competitive claims that need Legal review without flagging them. Asset list must fit the launch tier.

Examples: Narrative shape: 'Today [problem]. That's because [old way]. [Product] changes it by [shift]. It works because [proof]. [CTA].' Message-by-audience row: 'Audience | Headline | 3 points | One-liner.'

Format: Sections: Launch narrative | Messaging by audience (table) | Objections/FAQ | GTM brief (channels / assets / enablement / timeline / metrics). ~900 words.

Verification: List every claim needing Legal, Security or benchmark verification before launch.

Validation: Test the narrative on someone outside the product team: can they retell it in two sentences? If not, simplify the shift.

title: Plan a trade show presence that pays back its cost

title: Plan and moderate a focus group

**Decision this will inform:** [WHAT WE WILL DO WITH THE RESULTS]
**Who we need:** [PARTICIPANT PROFILE, who to exclude]
**Format:** [in person / online, number of groups, length]
**Stimulus to show:** [concepts, prototypes, ads, packaging, none]
**Incentive and budget:** [DETAILS]

Deliver:
1. **Whether a focus group is the right method,** or if interviews or a survey would answer this better.
2. **Recruiting screener:** 8-12 questions that qualify the right people without revealing what we want to hear.
3. **Discussion guide** with timings: warm-up, broad exploration, specific topics, stimulus reactions, wrap-up. Use open, neutral questions.
4. **Techniques to get honest, varied opinions:** individual writing before group discussion, projective exercises, ranking tasks, asking for disagreement, how to handle a dominant participant and draw out quiet ones.
5. **Moderator rules:** avoid leading questions, do not defend the product, watch for groupthink and politeness bias.
6. **Logistics and ethics checklist:** informed consent, recording permission, observer etiquette, data privacy.
7. **Analysis template:** a table for themes, supporting quotes, how many participants raised each point, and implications, plus a note on what focus groups cannot tell us (they show reasons and reactions, not how many customers feel this way).

title: Respond to an online patient review without violating HIPAA

**Who will post it:** [e.g. practice manager, office]

The public reply must:
- Not confirm or deny that the reviewer is or was our patient, even if they identified themselves. No names, dates, visit details, diagnoses, treatments, or billing details.
- Not argue with facts, even if the review is inaccurate.
- Speak about our general policies in neutral terms (e.g. "Our practice aims to return calls within one business day").
- Invite the person to contact us directly, by role, not by a clinician's name.
- Stay under 80 words, warm and professional.

Return:
1. Two reply options: one brief, one slightly fuller.
2. A version for a positive review that thanks them without confirming a care relationship.
3. Internal next steps: log as a complaint if it describes a care or service issue, who should investigate, and when to escalate to the privacy officer or risk management.
4. A short note on when to request platform removal (e.g. reviews containing another patient's information or threats).

Have our privacy officer approve any reply template before it is used widely.

**Last 2-3 quarters by channel:** [PASTE: channel, spend, leads/customers, CAC or ROAS, pipeline or revenue]

**Known limits:** [e.g. "search volume is capped", "team can run 2 new channels max"]
**Sales cycle length:** [e.g. "same day", "90 days"]

Steps:
1. Rank channels by marginal efficiency, not average: flag where more spend is likely hitting diminishing returns (rising CPA, high frequency, capped impression share).
2. Separate always-on demand capture (search, retargeting) from demand creation (paid social, content, events), and note the lag before the latter shows results.
3. Hold back 10-20% as a test budget unless I say otherwise.
4. Show what changes if the budget is cut by 20% or raised by 20%.

Return:
- A table: Channel | Last quarter spend | Proposed spend | Change | Expected result (range) | Why.
- The test budget: 2-3 specific experiments with a success threshold each.
- Leading indicators to check at week 3 and week 6 to reallocate mid-quarter.

Use only the numbers I give. Where a forecast is a guess, give a range and say so.

**What I want to use this for:** [content ideas / product decisions / strategy]

- What's happening and the evidence (signals, examples, data — cite sources if you can browse; otherwise mark as "to verify").
- Is it a short-lived fad or a durable shift? Why?
- What it means for my business: opportunity or threat.
- One concrete action I could take.

Finish with the 2 trends I should prioritize and one I should probably ignore despite the hype.

title: Turn a completed remodel into a project showcase
description: Portfolio copy, social posts, a photo shot list, and local SEO touches from one finished remodeling or home improvement job.
content:
Turn a completed remodeling or home improvement project into marketing content that wins new clients.

**Project:** [type - e.g. "kitchen remodel", "primary bathroom", "deck", "whole-home renovation"]
**Client's starting problem:** [what wasn't working before]
**What we did:** [scope, materials, finishes, fixtures, clever solutions]
**Timeline and budget range:** [only if the client agreed to share]
**Result:** [how the space works now; a client quote if they gave one]
**What sets my company apart:** [e.g. "in-house cabinetry", "fixed-price quotes", "design-build"]
**Photos available:** [before, after, during]
**Where it will be used:** [website portfolio, Google Business Profile, Instagram, Houzz, email newsletter]

Create:
1. **Portfolio write-up (200-300 words):** challenge, solution, result. Describe materials and design choices concretely (e.g. "quartz waterfall island with three brass pendants"), not with vague praise.
2. **Social posts:** a before-and-after carousel caption, a 30-second video script showing the transformation, and a Google Business Profile update.
3. **Photo shot list** for future jobs of this type: the angles and details that sell the work.
4. **AI image prompt** for a concept rendering of a similar space, clearly labeled as a concept, not a completed project.
5. **Local SEO:** a page title, meta description, and service-plus-city keywords.

Rules: describe only work we actually did, and never present AI images or stock photos as our projects. Get the client's permission before using their name, photos, quote, address, or budget.
variables: scope, materials, finishes, fixtures, clever solutions
only if the client agreed to share
how the space works now; a client quote if they gave one

title: Turn a spec sheet into benefit-led product bullets
description: Converts technical specifications into clear benefit bullets that explain what each feature means for the buyer.
content:
Turn my product specifications into benefit-led bullet points.

**Product and category:** [DETAILS]
**Spec sheet:** [PASTE]
**Target buyer and what they care about most:** [DETAILS]
**Number of bullets:** [5 / 7]

Task:
1. For each important spec, write what it means for the buyer (feature → benefit).
2. Order the bullets by what the buyer cares about most.
3. Start each bullet with the benefit, then the supporting spec in a few words.
4. Keep each bullet under 25 words.
5. Add a feature → benefit table showing your reasoning, so I can check it.

Rules: every benefit must follow from a spec I gave; no exaggerated claims; keep units and numbers exactly as in the spec sheet.

title: Turn product features into benefits and proof points
description: A feature-to-benefit ladder that gives you outcome-led messaging and the proof needed for each claim.
content:
Help me turn a list of product features into benefit-led messaging.

**Product:** [WHAT IT IS]
**Features:** [LIST]
**Audience segments:** [e.g. "IT admins", "small-business owners"]
**Main alternatives they use today:** [competitors, spreadsheets, doing nothing]
**Proof I have:** [customer results, data, reviews, awards - or "none yet"]

For each feature, build a ladder:
- Feature: what it is.
- Advantage: what it does better than the alternative.
- Benefit: what the user gains (time, money, risk, status, ease).
- Emotional payoff: how it feels.
- Proof: which of my proof points supports it, or [PROOF NEEDED].

Return:
1. A table with those columns, per audience segment where benefits differ.
2. The top 3 benefits to lead with, and why.
3. Example copy: 5 headlines, 5 bullet points, and one short paragraph using the top benefits.
4. Claims to avoid until I have proof.

Use plain language and specifics. Never fabricate results or percentages.
variables: customer results, data, reviews, awards - or "none yet"

title: Win back inactive or lost customers
description: A win-back sequence that re-engages lapsed customers with the right message and offer.
content:
Help me win back inactive customers.

**Business:** [WHAT YOU SELL]
**Who's lapsed:** [e.g. "no purchase in 90 days", "cancelled subscription"]
**Likely reasons they left:** [what you know or suspect]
**What's new or improved since:** [CHANGES]
**Offer I can make (if any):** [INCENTIVE]

Deliver:
1. A 3-email (or email + SMS) sequence with timing: reconnect → value/what's new → final offer or goodbye.
2. Subject lines and full copy for each.
3. A one-question survey to learn why they left.
4. How to measure success and when to stop emailing (protect deliverability).

title: Write a campaign brief and channel plan
description: A campaign brief with objective, audience, message, channels, timeline, and measurement.
content:
Role: Act as a growth marketer scoping a new acquisition or activation campaign.

Context: Objective and target metric: [OBJECTIVE_METRIC]. Audience: [AUDIENCE]. Offer / hook: [OFFER]. Budget and timeframe: [BUDGET_TIME]. Channels available: [CHANNELS]. Constraints: [CONSTRAINTS]. What we learned from the last campaign: [PRIOR_LEARNINGS].

Task: Write the brief: objective, audience, single-minded proposition, key messages, mandatories, success metrics and guardrail metrics. Then a channel plan: role of each channel, rough budget split, sequencing, and one clearly-scoped experiment with a hypothesis and how you will read it.

Format: Sections: Campaign brief (headed) | Channel plan (table) | Experiment (hypothesis / setup / read). ~450 words.

Verification: Check the budget split sums to the stated budget and that every message ladders to the single proposition. Flag any channel that cannot realistically move the target metric.

Validation: Pressure-test the experiment: is it powered to give a usable read in the timeframe, or is it too small? Adjust and say what you changed.

title: Write a capabilities statement for my consultancy or agency
description: A one-page overview of services, differentiators, proof, and team that I can attach to proposals or send to new prospects.
content:
Write a one-page capabilities statement for my consulting firm, agency, or freelance practice.

**Business name and what we do:** [SUMMARY]
**Who we serve best:** [INDUSTRIES, company sizes, buyer roles]
**Core services:** [LIST]
**How we're different:** [approach, specialism, speed, methodology]
**Proof:** [client results, notable clients I'm allowed to name, years in business, certifications]
**Team:** [key people and relevant expertise]
**Where it will be used:** [e.g. proposals, procurement portals, government contracting, introductions]

Create:
1. A headline that states who we help and with what outcome.
2. A 2-3 sentence overview.
3. Core services: each as a short line describing the client result, not just the activity.
4. Differentiators: three, each backed by a specific proof point.
5. Selected results: 3-4 short outcome statements.
6. Team snapshot, contact details block, and any company identifiers or certifications I list.
7. A layout suggestion for one page.

Also give me a 50-word version for email introductions.

Rules: only use results, clients, and credentials I've provided; mark gaps with [ADD PROOF]. Remind me to confirm I have permission before naming any client. No buzzwords like "synergy" or "best-in-class".

title: Write a case for support for a fundraising campaign
description: The core argument for why donors should give now, organized so you can reuse it in proposals, appeals, and campaign materials.
content:
Help me write a case for support for my nonprofit's campaign.

**Campaign:** [e.g. capital campaign for a new clinic, endowment, 3-year program expansion, general operating]
**Goal and timeline:** [AMOUNT, dates]
**Problem we address:** [the need, with data sources]
**Our approach and why it works:** [program model, evidence, track record]
**What the money will do:** [budget breakdown by use]
**Proof:** [outcomes, evaluations, testimonials, partners]
**Readers:** [major donors, foundations, board, community]

Structure:
1. The need: urgent, specific, sourced.
2. Our response: why we are positioned to solve it.
3. The vision: what is different when the campaign succeeds.
4. The plan and budget: how the money is used, including overhead honestly.
5. Evidence of impact.
6. Why now, and why this donor.
7. Giving opportunities: gift levels or a gift range chart (often a lead gift of about 10-20% of goal), and naming opportunities if any.
8. The ask.

Return:
- A full case (1,200-1,800 words).
- A one-page summary version.
- A list of every claim that needs a source, marked [SOURCE NEEDED].

Do not invent statistics, research findings, or beneficiary quotes. Avoid deficit language that strips people of dignity; describe the people we serve as people with goals, not problems.

title: Write a countdown email and SMS sequence for my sale
description: A phased email and SMS sequence from teaser to last call, with subject lines and segment variations.
content:
Write the email and SMS sequence for my seasonal sale. This is step 3 of a seasonal campaign pack; it works on its own, but paste your timeline (step 1) and offer messaging sheet (step 2) if you have them.

**Offer, dates, and exclusions:** [DETAILS]
**Featured products:** [LIST]
**Email list segments:** [e.g. VIP/repeat buyers, one-time buyers, subscribers who never bought]
**SMS list size and consent status:** [DETAILS - only people who opted in to marketing texts]
**Brand voice:** [DETAILS]
**Shipping cutoff date:** [DATE]

Return a sequence table first: Send date/time | Channel | Segment | Purpose.

Then write:
1. **Teaser email** (2-5 days before): what's coming and when; early access invitation for VIPs.
2. **Early access email** (VIPs only).
3. **Launch email:** offer up front, hero products, clear CTA.
4. **Mid-sale email:** a different angle, e.g. a gift guide, bestsellers, or a customer favorite.
5. **Shipping cutoff email** (if relevant).
6. **Last-chance email:** sent when the sale actually ends soon.
7. **SMS messages (3-4):** under 160 characters with brand name, offer, link, and opt-out wording ("Reply STOP to opt out").

For each email: 3 subject lines, preview text, body under 150 words, one CTA.

Rules: Respect frequency; suggest suppressing recent purchasers from "last chance" messages. Follow SMS quiet hours and consent rules for my region. Never say "final hours" unless it's true.
variables: DETAILS - only people who opted in to marketing texts

title: Write a creative brief with one single-minded proposition
description: A one-page agency creative brief built around a real insight and one sharp proposition, ready for the creative team.
content:
Write a creative brief my creative team can work from.

**Client and brand:** [BRAND, category, where it stands today]
**Business problem:** [what has to change commercially - e.g. "lapsed buyers are not coming back after the first purchase"]
**Target audience:** [WHO, what they currently think, feel, and do about the brand]
**Research and insights I have:** [DATA, quotes, social listening, strategy work - paste or summarize]
**Mandatories:** [logos, legal lines, product shots, brand assets, tone rules]
**Channels and deliverables:** [e.g. "30s online video, 6 social cutdowns, OOH 48-sheet"]
**Budget band and timing:** [ROUGH BUDGET, key dates]

Structure the brief with these sections, each kept tight:
1. Why are we advertising? (the business problem in one or two sentences)
2. Who are we talking to? (a person, not a demographic)
3. What do they think now, and what do we want them to think, feel, or do?
4. The insight: a human truth that creates tension - not a statistic or a product feature.
5. The single-minded proposition: one sentence, no "and".
6. Reasons to believe: only proof that exists.
7. Tone, mandatories, deliverables, budget, and timings.
8. How we will measure success.

Then:
- Give me 3 alternative propositions and say which is strongest and why.
- Flag where the brief is trying to say too many things, and what to cut.
- List the questions the creative team will ask that this brief does not yet answer.

Keep the brief to one page. Do not invent research findings or claims; mark gaps as [ADD INSIGHT] or [CONFIRM PROOF].
variables: BRAND, category, where it stands today
WHO, what they currently think, feel, and do about the brand
logos, legal lines, product shots, brand assets, tone rules
e.g. "30s online video, 6 social cutdowns, OOH 48-sheet"

title: Write a customer case study

Write a customer case study.

**Customer quotes (real only):** [QUOTES]
**Format and length:** [web page / PDF / short social version]

Structure: headline with the key result → snapshot box (customer, industry, results) → challenge → why they chose us → solution → results → what's next → CTA.

Use only the facts and quotes I provide. Mark missing data as [NEED: …]. Never invent quotes or metrics.
variables: web page / PDF / short social version

title: Write a fair-housing-safe property listing description
description: MLS remarks and a longer website description that sell the home's features without discriminatory or risky wording.
content:
Write a property listing description for me.

**Property basics:** [TYPE, BEDS, BATHS, SQ FT, LOT, YEAR BUILT]
**Standout features:** [UPGRADES, LAYOUT, VIEWS, OUTDOOR SPACE, SYSTEMS - with years, e.g. "roof 2021"]
**Location facts:** [DISTANCES TO TRANSIT, PARKS, SHOPPING - facts only]
**Known limitations I must not hide:** [e.g. busy street, HOA restrictions, needs updating]
**MLS character limit for public remarks:** [e.g. 1,000]
**Brokerage or MLS wording rules:** [ANY RULES - or "none"]

Rules:
- Describe the property, not the people who should live there. No words that signal a preferred buyer by race, religion, sex, familial status, disability, national origin, or other protected class (avoid "perfect for young families", "exclusive neighborhood", "walking distance to church", "bachelor pad").
- Name schools and amenities only as facts; do not rate neighborhoods or describe who lives there.
- No claims I have not given you (square footage, permits, "new" systems). Mark gaps as [CONFIRM].
- No puffery that could read as a misrepresentation ("flawless", "no issues").
- Lead with the single strongest feature; keep sentences concrete.

Return:
1. MLS public remarks within the character limit (state the count).
2. A 200-250 word website and portal description.
3. Five feature bullets for flyers.
4. A list of any phrases you avoided or that I should double-check with my broker for fair-housing or MLS compliance.
variables: TYPE, BEDS, BATHS, SQ FT, LOT, YEAR BUILT
DISTANCES TO TRANSIT, PARKS, SHOPPING - facts only
e.g. busy street, HOA restrictions, needs updating

title: Write a hotel pre-arrival email that sells upgrades and add-ons
description: A pre-arrival email and in-stay message that collect arrival details and offer relevant upgrades without feeling pushy.
content:
Write a pre-arrival email and an in-stay message for my hotel guests.

**Hotel and style:** [TYPE, LOCATION, BRAND VOICE]
**Guest segment this version is for:** [e.g. leisure couples, families, business travelers, long stays]
**Upgrades and add-ons available, with prices:** [ROOM UPGRADES, EARLY CHECK-IN, LATE CHECK-OUT, PARKING, BREAKFAST, SPA, AIRPORT TRANSFER, DINNER RESERVATION]
**Inventory rules:** [e.g. upgrades only when the higher room type has availability; early check-in is not guaranteed]
**What we need from guests before arrival:** [arrival time, special requests, ID or registration details required by local law, online check-in link]
**Send timing:** [e.g. 7 days and 2 days before arrival]
**Booking channel:** [direct / OTA guests - OTA guests may have masked emails and different policies]

Requirements:
- Lead with helpful information (arrival, parking, check-in time, directions), then offer a maximum of three add-ons chosen for the segment.
- Show the upgrade as the difference per night and the total, and say clearly what is confirmed vs. requested.
- Use one clear call to action per offer and a link placeholder [LINK].
- Never ask for card details or passwords by email; direct payments to a secure link.
- Respect marketing consent: this is a service email; keep promotional content limited and relevant to the stay.

Return:
1. 3 subject lines.
2. The pre-arrival email (under 200 words).
3. A short in-stay text or app message sent on day one.
4. Suggested metrics to track: upgrade take rate, revenue per arrival, and pre-arrival form completion.
variables: e.g. 7 days and 2 days before arrival

title: Write a launch-day run-of-show with posts and a reply plan
description: An hour-by-hour launch-day schedule with ready-to-post social copy, monitoring duties, and escalation rules.
content:
Create a launch-day run-of-show for me. This is step 4 of a launch pack; it works on its own, but paste your countdown plan (step 1) and announcement copy (step 2) if you have them.

**What's launching and the main link:** [DETAILS]
**Launch date and time zone:** [DATE, TIMEZONE]
**Channels going live:** [e.g. email, LinkedIn, X, Product Hunt, community, partners]
**Team on duty and their hours:** [NAMES/ROLES + availability]
**Key assets ready:** [blog post, demo video, screenshots, offer code]
**Known risks:** [e.g. signup bugs, server load, payment issues]
**Target reply time for comments and questions:** [e.g. within 30 minutes]

Return:
1. **Run-of-show table:** Time | Action | Channel | Owner | Copy or asset | Check (link works, tracking tag present).
2. **Ready-to-post copy:** one post per channel in that channel's native format (LinkedIn: story-led, under 1,300 characters; X: a hook post plus a short thread; community: helpful, non-salesy). Include a team version that colleagues can personalize, not copy-paste.
3. **Monitoring rota:** who watches comments, support inbox, and dashboards, and how often.
4. **Reply guidelines:** respond within my target reply time; thank, answer, or route; never argue in public.
5. **Escalation rules:** what counts as a launch-stopping issue (e.g. checkout broken), who decides to pause promotion, and a holding message to post if something breaks.
6. **End-of-day snapshot:** the 5 numbers to record before signing off.

Use [CONFIRM] for any time, link, or number I haven't given.
variables: e.g. email, LinkedIn, X, Product Hunt, community, partners
blog post, demo video, screenshots, offer code
e.g. signup bugs, server load, payment issues

title: Write a mission, vision, and values statement

3. **Values** — 4–6 values, each with a one-line definition and 2 concrete behaviors ("we do X, we don't do Y").

variables: WHAT YOU DO, who you serve, size
IN YOUR OWN WORDS — messy is fine

title: Write a post-sale recap with lessons for next year
description: A results recap of your seasonal sale, what drove revenue and margin, and a ready playbook for next year.
content:
Write a recap of my seasonal sale and the lessons for next time. This is step 5 of a seasonal campaign pack; it works on its own, but paste your original plan and goal from step 1 if you have them.

**Campaign and dates:** [DETAILS]
**Goal:** [TARGET]
**Results:** [revenue, orders, average order value, discount cost, gross margin, new vs. returning customers, by day if possible]
**Channel results:** [email, SMS, social, ads: sends/spend, clicks, conversions, revenue]
**Last year's comparable numbers:** [OPTIONAL]
**Operational issues:** [stockouts, shipping delays, site problems, support volume]
**Customer feedback:** [NOTES]

Analyze:
1. Result vs. goal, and whether revenue came with acceptable margin after discounts.
2. New-customer acquisition vs. pulling forward sales from people who would have bought anyway.
3. Which phases, offers, products, and channels did the work. Note where attribution overlaps (e.g. email and ads claiming the same sale).
4. Operational problems and their cost.
5. What customers said.

Return:
- A one-page recap for my team or manager: headline numbers, what worked, what didn't, and decisions.
- A table: Channel | Spend | Revenue | Margin after discount | Verdict.
- A "next year playbook": dates to start prep, offer to repeat or change, list-building to do before the season, and 5 things to fix.
- A 30-day follow-up plan for new customers acquired in the sale, so they buy again at full price.

Use only my numbers; label any estimate clearly.
variables: stockouts, shipping delays, site problems, support volume

title: Write a press release and media pitch
description: A newsworthy press release plus a short pitch email for journalists.
content:
Role: Act as a PR and communications lead writing for trade and business media.

Context: Announcement: [ANNOUNCEMENT]. Why it matters and to whom: [SIGNIFICANCE]. Key facts (figures, dates, names, quotes approved): [KEY_FACTS]. Spokesperson and title: [SPOKESPERSON]. Target outlets / journalists and their beat: [TARGETS]. Boilerplate: [BOILERPLATE]. Embargo / timing: [TIMING].

Task: Write: (1) a press release - headline, dateline, strong first paragraph (who/what/why it matters), supporting paragraphs, one approved quote, boilerplate, contact; (2) a 120-word pitch email to one named target that leads with the angle relevant to their beat.

Format: Two blocks: Press release | Pitch email. AP-style, no marketing adjectives.

Verification: Use only facts and quotes from the brief; mark anything missing as [TO CONFIRM]. Do not add claims, metrics or names not supplied.

Validation: Read the first paragraph as a busy journalist: is there a real story in the first two sentences, or is it buried? Rewrite the lead if buried.

title: Write a product description for a luxury or premium product

title: Write a product launch email for a new product

title: Write a promotional email or SMS campaign

title: Write a size, fit and care section that reduces returns

title: Write a technical product datasheet engineers will trust
description: A spec-led datasheet for an industrial product with complete specifications, test standards, certifications, and selection guidance, free of marketing fluff.
content:
Write a technical datasheet for an industrial product.

**Product and model range:** [NAME and variants]
**Main use and target buyer:** [e.g. "maintenance engineers specifying pumps for food plants"]
**Specifications:** [PASTE every spec you have: dimensions, materials, ratings, performance curves, operating ranges, tolerances, weight]
**Test standards and conditions:** [e.g. "tested to ASTM D638 at 23 C", "IP67 per IEC 60529"]
**Certifications and compliance:** [UL, CE, ATEX, RoHS, REACH, FDA food contact, NSF, etc., only those actually held]
**Options and ordering codes:** [how the part number is built]
**Key differences from competing products:** [only claims we can prove]

Structure:
1. Product name and a 2-sentence description of what it does and where it is used.
2. 3-5 key features, each tied to a specific spec, e.g. "Runs to 120 C continuous (see operating range)".
3. A complete specification table with units, conditions, and test standards. Separate typical values from guaranteed minimums/maximums, and label them.
4. Dimensional drawing and performance curve placeholders [ADD DRAWING].
5. Certifications and compliance with certificate numbers [ADD].
6. Ordering information and part number breakdown.
7. Installation, compatibility, and limits of use (what it is not suitable for).

Also list any spec a buyer would expect that I haven't provided.

title: Write a TV or radio spot timed to length with legal supers

Rules:
- TV: use a two-column format (video | audio) with shot-by-shot visuals, voiceover, dialogue, music, and SFX cues.
- Radio: one column with voice, SFX, and music cues; name the brand early and at least twice.

Return:
1. The script.
2. A tighter alternate version.
3. A clearance checklist: every claim, the substantiation needed, and every super or disclaimer.
4. Lines likely to be questioned by a network or clearance body, with safer wording.

Do not invent product facts, prices, or proof; mark them [CONFIRM]. Have legal or the clearance body review before production.

title: Write a year-end fundraising appeal letter

2. Five bullet points.
3. A product description.
4. Backend search terms within the size limit [CONFIRM current limit]: no words repeated from the title, no competitor brands, no subjective claims.

6. A list of every claim I must be able to substantiate.

title: Write an effectiveness or creative awards entry for a campaign
