2. 10 meal ideas in a table: base | add-ons per person | what to keep separate | prep time.
3. Cross-contact safety for any allergy: separate utensils and surfaces, cooking order, and label-checking habits. Remind me that "may contain" warnings matter for serious allergies.
4. Simple swaps that let one dish fit more people (e.g. a dairy-free sauce everyone can eat).
5. A weekly shopping list organized so restricted items are easy to spot.

Never suggest an ingredient that conflicts with a stated allergy. Where a family member follows a medical diet, tell me to confirm specifics with their doctor or a registered dietitian.
variables: e.g. "severe peanut allergy - carries an epinephrine pen"

title: Cook simple healthy meals in a dorm or tiny kitchen
description: Easy, cheap, balanced meals you can make with a microwave, kettle, or one burner and minimal storage.
content:
Help me eat well with a very basic kitchen setup.

**Equipment I have:** [e.g. "microwave and mini fridge", "one hot plate and a kettle", "shared kitchen I use twice a week"]
**Storage:** [e.g. "half a mini fridge, one shelf"]
**Weekly food budget:** [AMOUNT]
**Meal plan or dining hall access:** [e.g. "lunch covered on weekdays"]
**Foods I like and can't stand:** [LISTS]
**Dietary needs:** [LIST or "none"]
**Time I'll realistically spend cooking:** [e.g. "10 minutes, most days"]

Give me:
1. A starter pantry and fridge list that fits my storage and budget, with what each item can turn into.
2. 12 meals (breakfast, lunch, dinner, snacks) using only my equipment, each with ingredients, steps, and time.
3. How to make each meal more balanced (adding protein, fiber, or vegetables cheaply, e.g. frozen veg, canned beans, eggs).
4. Microwave and food safety tips: heating evenly, leftovers, how long things keep in a small fridge.
5. A late-night or exam-week option list that beats takeout.

Keep it realistic: no specialty equipment, no ingredients I'd have to buy in bulk and waste.
variables: e.g. "half a mini fridge, one shelf"

title: Coordinate care for an aging parent with my siblings
description: A shared care plan dividing tasks, appointments, and costs among family, with a check-in routine.
content:
Help me set up a care plan for my aging parent that my family can share.

**Parent's situation:** [AGE, LIVING ARRANGEMENT, WHAT THEY CAN AND CAN'T DO ALONE]
**Health conditions and care needs (as told by their doctors):** [LIST]
**Family members and what each can give:** [NAMES, DISTANCE, TIME, MONEY, SKILLS]
**Current tasks:** [e.g. "appointments", "medications", "groceries", "bills", "house upkeep", "companionship"]
**Parent's wishes:** [WHAT THEY WANT - e.g. "stay at home"]
**Tension or gaps:** [e.g. "one sibling does everything", "no one manages finances"]

Create:
1. A task table: task | how often | who owns it | backup | notes.
2. A shared calendar structure for appointments and visits.
3. A one-page "care binder" outline: contacts, medications, doctors, insurance, legal documents to look into (e.g. healthcare proxy, power of attorney), and where originals are kept.
4. A monthly family check-in agenda and a fair way to raise imbalance without blame.
5. Signs that more support may be needed and the kinds of local services to research (home care, adult day programs, respite care).
6. Caregiver self-care: how to share load and avoid burnout.

Keep my parent's voice central. For legal and financial documents, tell us to confirm requirements with a qualified professional where we live.
variables: AGE, LIVING ARRANGEMENT, WHAT THEY CAN AND CAN'T DO ALONE
WHAT THEY WANT - e.g. "stay at home"
e.g. "one sibling does everything", "no one manages finances"

title: Create a co-parenting schedule and communication plan
description: A parenting-time calendar with handoff routines, holiday rotation, and ground rules for communicating after separation.
content:
Help me draft a co-parenting schedule and communication plan to discuss with my co-parent.

**Kids and ages:** [DETAILS]
**Distance between homes and to school:** [DETAILS]
**Each parent's work schedule:** [DETAILS]
**Arrangement we're considering:** [e.g. "week on/week off", "2-2-3", "weekdays with one parent"]
**Holidays, birthdays, and special days to plan:** [LIST]
**Current tension points:** [e.g. "late handoffs", "different rules at each house", "arguing by text"]
**Existing court order or agreement:** [yes / no; key terms]

Give me:
1. 2-3 schedule options suited to my children's ages, each shown as a 2-week calendar, with pros and cons for the kids.
2. A holiday and vacation rotation table for alternating years.
3. Handoff routines that keep kids calm: where, when, what travels with them.
4. Communication ground rules: preferred channel, response times, topics for writing versus calls, never using the kids as messengers.
5. A short list of rules to keep consistent across both homes (bedtime, screens, homework).
6. A process for changes and disagreements.

Keep the focus on the children's needs and neutral language. This is general information, not legal advice; any existing court order takes priority, and I should confirm arrangements with a family lawyer or mediator. If there is any risk of abuse or violence, recommend local support services and emergency help.
variables: e.g. "week on/week off", "2-2-3", "weekdays with one parent"

title: Create a food allergy or dietary card for travel
description: A clear, translated card explaining your allergy or diet to restaurant staff, plus a plan for eating safely while traveling.
content:
Help me eat safely while traveling with a food allergy or dietary need.

**Destination and language(s):** [COUNTRY and LANGUAGE]
**My allergy or dietary need:** [e.g. severe peanut allergy, celiac disease, vegan, halal, kosher, diabetes]
**Severity:** [e.g. anaphylaxis risk - carry epinephrine / intolerance / preference]
**Cross-contact concerns:** [e.g. shared fryers, same cutting boards, traces]
**Local dishes I'm curious about:** [LIST - optional]

Give me:
1. A short restaurant card in English and the local language: what I can't eat, hidden sources to watch for, cross-contact concerns, and a polite thank-you. Keep it to 5-6 sentences.
2. A list of common local ingredients and dishes that often contain my allergen or don't fit my diet, and safer dishes to ask about. Present these as things to confirm with staff, since recipes vary.
3. Questions to ask when ordering.
4. A travel plan: safe snacks to pack, grocery and kitchen options, telling the airline and hotel in advance.
5. For severe allergies: carry my emergency medication in hand luggage with a doctor's note, know the local emergency number, and have a translated phrase for "I'm having an allergic reaction, call an ambulance".

Note that translations should be checked by a native speaker or professional translator if the allergy is severe. This is general information; ask my doctor or allergist about a travel action plan.
variables: e.g. shared fryers, same cutting boards, traces

title: Create a gratitude practice that doesn't feel forced
description: A short gratitude routine with varied formats and prompts that stays fresh and feels genuine, even on hard days.
content:
Help me build a gratitude practice that feels real, not forced.

**Why I'm interested:** [e.g. "I focus on the negative", "want to feel more content", "I've read it can lift my mood"]
**What I've tried:** [e.g. "listing 3 things a day got repetitive"]
**Time available:** [e.g. "2 minutes at night"]
**Who's in my life:** [FAMILY, PARTNER, KIDS, FRIENDS, COWORKERS - optional]
**What's going on right now:** [e.g. "a hard season", "things are fine"]

Give me:
1. A simple core routine that takes the time I have.
2. 5 different formats to rotate so it doesn't go stale (e.g. one specific detail, a person and why, something I usually take for granted, a thank-you message, a small win).
3. 20 specific prompts that go beyond "I'm grateful for my family".
4. A version for hard days that doesn't deny what's difficult ("both/and" rather than "look on the bright side").
5. One way to share it with others, such as a family dinner question or a thank-you note, with a short example.
6. A way to look back after a month to notice any change.

Keep it warm and down to earth. Gratitude isn't a substitute for getting help with depression; if I describe a persistently low mood, suggest I talk to a doctor.
variables: e.g. "listing 3 things a day got repetitive"
FAMILY, PARTNER, KIDS, FRIENDS, COWORKERS - optional

title: Create a workout plan
description: A progressive training plan for your goal, level, schedule, and equipment.
content:
Create a workout plan for me.

**Goal:** [build strength / lose fat / run a 5K / improve mobility / general fitness]
**Current level:** [beginner / intermediate / advanced; what I can do now]
**Days per week and minutes per session:** [DETAILS]
**Equipment:** [gym / home dumbbells / bodyweight only]
**Injuries or limitations:** [DETAILS]
**Age (optional):** [AGE]

Deliver: a weekly schedule; each session with warm-up, exercises, sets, reps, rest, and cool-down; form cues for each exercise; a 4–8 week progression; easier and harder substitutions; and how to track progress.

Start conservatively. If I have health conditions or pain, check with a doctor or physical therapist first, and stop any exercise that causes sharp pain.
variables: beginner / intermediate / advanced; what I can do now

title: Create an emergency health information sheet for my family
description: A one-page medical info sheet per family member for emergencies, babysitters, and caregivers.
content:
Help me create an emergency health information sheet for each person in my household.

**For each person:** [NAME, DATE OF BIRTH, BLOOD TYPE IF KNOWN]
**Conditions diagnosed:** [LIST]
**Medications and doses (from labels):** [LIST]
**Allergies and reaction type:** [e.g. "penicillin - hives", "peanuts - anaphylaxis, carries epinephrine pen"]
**Doctors and pharmacy:** [NAMES AND PHONE NUMBERS]
**Insurance:** [PROVIDER AND MEMBER ID - or leave a blank line to fill in by hand]
**Emergency contacts:** [NAMES, RELATIONSHIP, PHONE]
**Important notes:** [e.g. "uses hearing aids", "has a pacemaker", "advance directive kept in X"]

Create:
1. A one-page sheet per person, with the most critical information (allergies, conditions, medications) at the top in a clear layout a stranger could read in 30 seconds.
2. A version for a babysitter or caregiver that adds routines and what to do in common situations, plus "call emergency services" instructions and my address written out.
3. A wallet-card version with only essentials.
4. A reminder schedule for reviewing and updating the sheets.

Copy medication details exactly as I gave them; mark anything missing [ADD]. Remind me where to store copies (fridge, wallet, phone) and to think about who should see sensitive details.
variables: NAME, DATE OF BIRTH, BLOOD TYPE IF KNOWN

title: Cut back on phone and screen time without going cold turkey
description: A realistic plan to reduce mindless phone use with app changes, phone-free zones, and better things to do instead.
content:
Help me use my phone and screens less.

**Current daily screen time (if known):** [HOURS - from my phone's screen time settings]
**Apps or habits that eat the most time:** [e.g. "short videos", "news", "games", "checking email"]
**When I scroll most:** [e.g. "in bed", "first thing in the morning", "when bored at work"]
**What I actually need my phone for:** [WORK, FAMILY, NAVIGATION]
**What I'd rather do with the time:** [READ, SLEEP, HOBBIES, FAMILY]
**My goal:** [e.g. "under 2 hours of social media a day", "no phone at dinner"]

Give me:
1. The likely reasons I reach for my phone, based on my answers (boredom, avoidance, habit, connection).
2. Phone setup changes: notifications to turn off, home screen changes, app limits, grayscale, logging out. Keep it general so it works on any phone.
3. 2-3 phone-free zones or times that suit my life.
4. A list of quick replacements for the moments I usually scroll.
5. A 3-week step-down plan, cutting gradually rather than all at once.
6. How to handle the fear of missing out and people expecting fast replies (with a sample message).

Keep it realistic; I'm not aiming for zero screens.
variables: HOURS - from my phone's screen time settings

title: Cut back on sugary drinks or caffeine without crashing
description: A gradual taper plan with swaps and side-effect tips for reducing soda, energy drinks, or coffee.
content:
Help me cut back on what I drink without feeling awful.

**What I drink now:** [e.g. "3 sodas a day", "2 energy drinks", "5 cups of coffee"]
**When I drink each:** [TIMES AND SITUATIONS]
**Why I want to cut back:** [e.g. "sleep", "sugar", "jitters", "cost"]
**My goal:** [e.g. "one coffee before noon", "no soda on weekdays"]
**What I've tried:** [DETAILS]

Give me:
1. A gradual taper schedule over 2-4 weeks (cutting suddenly can cause headaches, tiredness, and irritability from caffeine withdrawal).
2. Swaps for each drink and situation (e.g. sparkling water with fruit, half-caf, tea) and what to expect taste-wise.
3. Ways to handle the energy dip: timing, short walks, light, meals, and sleep.
4. How to handle triggers (the vending machine, the afternoon slump, social drinks).
5. A simple daily tracker.

Keep the advice general. If I'm pregnant, have a heart condition, high blood pressure, anxiety, or take medication, remind me to ask my doctor or pharmacist about caffeine limits for me.
variables: e.g. "3 sodas a day", "2 energy drinks", "5 cups of coffee"
e.g. "one coffee before noon", "no soda on weekdays"

title: Cut down on robocalls, spam texts, and junk mail
description: A practical plan to reduce unwanted calls, texts, emails, and paper mail using phone settings, opt-outs, and safe habits.
content:
Help me reduce the unwanted calls, texts, emails, and mail I get.

**What bothers me most:** [e.g. daily robocalls, spam texts with links, telemarketers, catalogs, credit card offers, junk email]
**My phones:** [mobile make and model, landline yes/no, carrier]
**Country:** [LOCATION - opt-out services differ]
**What I've tried:** [e.g. blocking numbers one by one, answering to say "stop"]
**Anyone else in the household affected:** [e.g. an older parent who answers every call]

Give me a plan in order of impact:
1. Phone settings: built-in spam filtering, silencing unknown callers, and call screening - with honest notes on the tradeoff (I might miss a doctor's office or delivery). Mark menu paths [CHECK ON MY PHONE].
2. Carrier tools: free spam-blocking features or apps my carrier may offer [CONFIRM WITH CARRIER].
3. Official opt-out lists for calls and mail in my country [CONFIRM - name the type of service, and only name a specific service if you're sure it exists].
4. Safe habits: don't answer unknown numbers, never press a key or say "yes", don't reply STOP to suspicious texts, report spam texts to my carrier, don't click links.
5. Email: unsubscribe safely (only from senders I recognize), filters, and a separate address for shopping.
6. Paper mail: opting out of prescreened credit offers and catalogs, and contacting senders directly.

End with a 20-minute setup checklist and what to expect: unwanted contact usually drops but rarely stops completely.
variables: mobile make and model, landline yes/no, carrier
e.g. blocking numbers one by one, answering to say "stop"
e.g. an older parent who answers every call

title: Cut my grocery bill without eating worse
description: Specific ways to spend less on groceries based on how you actually shop, with a target and a simple tracking method.
content:
Help me spend less on groceries without lowering the quality of what we eat.

**Household:** [WHO EATS AT HOME - ages, appetites]
**Current monthly grocery spend:** [AMOUNT, or "not sure"]
**Target:** [AMOUNT or percentage, e.g. "save $100/month"]
**Where I shop and how often:** [STORES, delivery vs in-person, number of trips]
**Typical cart:** [WHAT WE BUY OFTEN - snacks, meat, convenience foods, drinks]
**Food we throw away:** [e.g. "bagged salad", "bread", "leftovers"]
**Constraints:** [diet needs, time to cook, no car, storage space]

Give me:
1. The 3-5 biggest likely savings for my situation, ranked by money saved per effort, each with a rough estimate I can check against my receipts (label estimates clearly; don't present them as facts).
2. Swaps that keep nutrition steady (e.g. frozen vegetables, dried beans, store brands), noting where the cheaper option isn't worth it.
3. A food-waste plan: what to buy less of, how to store it, and "use it up" meal ideas.
4. A simple shopping routine: list template, a weekly budget, and when to check unit prices.
5. A 4-week tracking sheet (week | spend | waste | notes).

Don't suggest anything that would cut needed nutrition for kids, pregnancy, or medical diets.
variables: WHO EATS AT HOME - ages, appetites
STORES, delivery vs in-person, number of trips
WHAT WE BUY OFTEN - snacks, meat, convenience foods, drinks
diet needs, time to cook, no car, storage space

title: Decide when and how to clear snow from my driveway
description: A timing and method plan for clearing snow that reduces effort, refreezing, and slip risk on your specific driveway.
content:
Help me decide when and how to clear snow from my driveway.

**Location:** [CITY/REGION]
**Forecast:** [paste the hourly forecast: snowfall totals, timing, temperatures, wind, and what happens over the next 48 hours]
**Driveway:** [length, surface (asphalt / concrete / gravel / pavers), slope, curves, shade vs. sun]
**Where snow can go:** [space for piles, obstacles like trees, fences, or walls]
**My equipment:** [shovel / snow blower / plow service / none]
**Melt products on hand:** [rock salt, calcium chloride, sand, none]
**Constraints:** [when I need to leave, my physical ability, health limits, help available]

Work through:
1. **Timing:** Should I clear during the storm, right after, or wait? Weigh total depth, wet vs. dry snow, the end-of-driveway plow ridge, and whether temperatures will drop below freezing afterward (refreeze risk).
2. **Method:** Best technique for my surface and slope (for gravel, leave a base layer; for slopes, clear the steepest section first and keep traction).
3. **Melt and traction:** What to use, how much, and when, given the forecast low and my surface (avoid products that damage new concrete or pavers; sand for traction below roughly 15 F / -10 C when salt stops working).
4. **Snow storage:** Where to pile it so it doesn't drain back across the driveway and refreeze.
5. **Safety:** Pacing, lifting technique, and when not to shovel at all.

Output: a short recommendation up top ("Clear at ___ because ___"), then a step-by-step plan with times, then a checklist for the next 48 hours.

If I mention heart conditions, high blood pressure, or I'm not used to exertion, tell me plainly that heavy shoveling can trigger heart problems and suggest alternatives. Base advice only on the forecast I give; if it's missing, ask for it.
variables: space for piles, obstacles like trees, fences, or walls
shovel / snow blower / plow service / none
rock salt, calcium chloride, sand, none

title: Decide whether to keep renting or buy a home
description: A side-by-side comparison of renting and buying based on your numbers, timeline, and priorities, with questions to settle first.
content:
Help me think through whether to keep renting or buy a home.

**Current rent and what it includes:** [AMOUNT, utilities, maintenance]
**Homes I'm looking at:** [price range, area, type]
**Savings for a down payment and closing costs:** [AMOUNT]
**Household income and existing debts:** [AMOUNTS]
**How long I expect to stay in the area:** [YEARS]
**Job and life stability:** [e.g. "stable job", "might relocate", "planning kids"]
**Quotes or estimates I have:** [mortgage rate, property tax, insurance, HOA fees - or "none"]
**What matters most to me:** [flexibility, stability, building equity, space, control over the home]

Give me:
1. A monthly cost comparison: rent vs. the full cost of owning (mortgage payment, property tax, insurance, HOA, maintenance reserve). Mark anything I didn't provide as [GET ESTIMATE].
2. Upfront costs of buying beyond the down payment, and the costs of selling later.
3. How my expected time in the home changes the answer, explained simply.
4. Non-money factors on both sides.
5. A readiness checklist: emergency fund after the down payment, stable income, credit, debt levels.
6. A clear lean (rent, buy, or wait) based on my inputs, with the 2-3 assumptions that would change it.

Don't invent interest rates, prices, or tax figures. This is general information; suggest I speak with a housing counselor or qualified advisor before committing.
variables: mortgage rate, property tax, insurance, HOA fees - or "none"

title: Decide whether to lend money to family or a friend
description: A clear-headed decision on lending money, plus kind words for yes, no, or a smaller amount, and terms if you lend.
content:
Help me decide whether to lend money to someone close to me, and how to say it.

**Who is asking and my relationship with them:** [e.g. "my brother", "a close friend"]
**Amount and what it's for:** [DETAILS]
**Their history with borrowed money:** [e.g. "paid me back last time", "still owes me", "never borrowed before"]
**My financial situation:** [savings, debts, upcoming costs]
**How I'd feel if I never got it back:** [fine / upset / it would hurt my finances]
**What I'm leaning toward:** [yes / no / a smaller amount / not sure]

Give me:
1. A quick decision check: can I afford to lose this money? Would I lend it as a gift? What does this mean for the relationship either way?
2. Alternatives to a straight loan: a smaller gift, helping in another way (such as paying one bill directly or helping them make a budget), or pointing them to other resources.
3. Three short, kind scripts: saying yes with clear terms, saying no without over-explaining, and offering a smaller amount or different help.
4. If I lend: simple written terms to agree on (amount, repayment schedule, what happens if a payment is missed) and a friendly way to bring that up.
5. One sentence to agree now on how we'll handle a missed repayment, so it's settled before it happens.

Keep it compassionate and non-judgmental. Do not pressure me either way.
variables: fine / upset / it would hurt my finances
yes / no / a smaller amount / not sure

title: Decline an invitation without guilt or over-explaining
description: Warm, short replies to turn down a social invitation, event, or request while keeping the relationship intact.
content:
Help me decline an invitation in my personal life.

**The invitation:** [e.g. "bachelorette weekend", "birthday dinner", "volunteering at my kid's school", "weekly game night"]
**From whom, and how close we are:** [RELATIONSHIP]
**My real reason (only for your context):** [e.g. "can't afford it", "need rest", "don't enjoy it", "schedule clash"]
**How much of the reason I'm comfortable sharing:** [none / a little / all of it]
**Do I want to offer an alternative?** [e.g. "yes, coffee next week" / "no"]
**Channel:** [text / call / email / in person]

Rules:
- Say no clearly in the first sentence or two. No "maybe" if I mean no.
- Thank them and show I value the invitation or the person.
- Give no more reason than I chose to share; don't invent an excuse.
- If I'm offering an alternative, make it specific; if not, don't hint at one.

Return:
1. Three versions: very brief, warm, and one with an alternative (if I want one).
2. A reply if they push back or ask why.
3. A version for declining something recurring (so I don't have to say no every time).
variables: none / a little / all of it

title: Declutter a room without getting overwhelmed
description: A step-by-step decluttering session for one space, with clear keep-or-go rules and where to send what leaves.
content:
Help me declutter one space in my home.

**Space:** [e.g. "bedroom closet", "garage", "kids' playroom", "kitchen drawers"]
**What's in it:** [ROUGH DESCRIPTION OF THE STUFF]
**Why I want to declutter:** [e.g. "can't find anything", "moving", "new baby coming"]
**What makes it hard:** [e.g. "sentimental items", "'might need it someday'", "it belongs to my partner"]
**Time and energy:** [e.g. "two 1-hour sessions", "I get overwhelmed fast"]

Give me:
1. A session plan broken into 15-30 minute chunks, starting with the easiest wins (trash, duplicates, expired items).
2. A sorting setup: Keep / Donate or sell / Recycle / Trash / Decide later, with a time limit for "decide later".
3. Decision questions tailored to what I said is hard (e.g. "Have I used it in the last year?", "Would I buy it again?", "Can a photo keep the memory?").
4. Where items should go: donation, resale, recycling, and safe disposal for things like batteries, electronics, medication, and paint (check my local rules).
5. How to talk about shared items with family members without throwing out their things.
6. A 5-minute daily habit to keep the space clear.

Be encouraging and practical. No guilt, no minimalism lectures.

title: Design the life I want
description: A guided exercise to picture your ideal life across key areas and work backwards to today.
content:
Guide me through designing the life I want.

**Life areas to include:** [health, relationships, career, money, home, learning, fun, contribution — choose]
**Time horizon:** [e.g. 3 years, 10 years]

Ask me reflective questions for each area, one area at a time: what an ideal ordinary day looks like, what I'd be proud of, and what I'd regret not doing.

Then write:
1. A vivid one-page vision of my life at the time horizon, in present tense.
2. The 3 areas with the biggest gap between now and the vision.
3. For each, one goal and the first step this month.
4. What I need to say "no" to in order to make room.

title: Dial in espresso on my home machine
description: A step-by-step routine to set grind, dose, and timing on your home setup, plus fixes for sour, bitter, or watery shots.
content:
Help me dial in espresso at home and build a consistent routine.

**Machine:** [MODEL or type - e.g. "single-boiler with pressurized basket", "heat exchanger"]
**Portafilter and basket size:** [e.g. "51 mm, double basket"]
**Grinder:** [MODEL or type - e.g. "flat burr, stepped", "blade"]
**Tools I have:** [scale, tamper, distribution tool, milk pitcher, WDT needle, etc.]
**Beans:** [roast level, roast date if known]
**Drinks I make:** [e.g. "straight espresso", "flat whites", "iced lattes"]
**What my shots taste like now:** [sour / bitter / thin / gushing / choking / inconsistent]

Give me:
1. A starting recipe for my basket: dose, target yield (brew ratio), and target shot time, with the reasoning.

3. A dial-in method: change one variable at a time, what to adjust first, and how big each change should be.
4. A taste troubleshooting table: Symptom | Likely cause | What to change.
5. If I make milk drinks: how to steam and texture milk for those drinks, with common mistakes.
6. A short cleaning and maintenance routine (daily, weekly, monthly), including backflushing only if my machine supports it.
7. A one-page cheat sheet I can keep next to the machine.

If my grinder or basket limits what I can achieve (e.g. a blade grinder or pressurized basket), say so plainly and suggest the cheapest upgrade with the biggest impact. Follow my machine's manual for descaling and anything involving pressure or electrics.
variables: MODEL or type - e.g. "flat burr, stepped", "blade"
roast level, roast date if known
sour / bitter / thin / gushing / choking / inconsistent

title: Discover my core values and use them to guide choices
description: Guided questions to identify your top personal values, define them in your own words, and check how your life lines up.
content:
Help me figure out my core personal values.

**Moments I felt proud or most like myself:** [2-3 EXAMPLES]
**Moments I felt frustrated, angry, or uneasy:** [2-3 EXAMPLES - these often show a value being crossed]
**People I admire and why:** [NAMES OR TYPES + QUALITIES]
**A decision I'm facing (optional):** [DECISION]

Guide me through:
1. From my examples, suggest 8-10 values that seem to show up (e.g. honesty, freedom, family, growth, security, creativity, fairness), with the example that points to each.
2. Ask me to narrow to my top 5. Then help me write a one-sentence personal definition for each, since "family" or "success" means different things to different people.
3. A values check: a table with Value | How much my current life reflects it (1-10) | One small change to live it more.
4. Where my values pull against each other (e.g. security vs. adventure) and how to hold both.
5. If I gave a decision, test each option against my top 5 values and show which fits best and why.

Ask questions instead of assuming. Don't tell me what my values should be.

title: Downsize my home before a move
description: A gentle, step-by-step plan to sort a lifetime of belongings and move into a smaller space.
content:
Help me downsize before moving to a smaller home.

**Current home:** [SIZE, rooms, storage areas like attic, garage, basement]
**New home:** [SIZE, rooms, storage available - include a floor plan or room sizes if you have them]
**Timeline:** [MOVING DATE]
**Who's involved:** [e.g. "just me", "my adult children will help", "I'm helping my parents"]
**Hardest categories:** [e.g. "photos", "furniture", "collections", "my late spouse's things"]
**Physical limits:** [e.g. "can't lift heavy boxes", "stairs are hard"]

Give me:
1. A room-by-room order, starting with areas that hold little emotional weight, and a realistic weekly pace for my timeline.
2. A "will it fit" method: measure the new rooms and choose furniture first, then everything else.
3. Gentle decision questions for sentimental items, plus ways to keep memories without keeping everything (photograph items, choose a few favorites, pass items on to family with a story).
4. A plan for what leaves: offering items to family with a deadline, selling, donating, estate sale services, and safe disposal of medications, chemicals, and old electronics.
5. How to protect important documents and valuables during the process.
6. How family helpers can support without taking over decisions.

Keep the tone warm and unhurried. Suggest a senior move manager or professional organizer if the job is too big.

e.g. "can't lift heavy boxes", "stairs are hard"

Help me eat healthier without spending more on groceries.

2. Money-saving tactics that actually work: unit pricing, store brands, frozen vs. fresh, buying whole vs. pre-cut, using leftovers.

4. Ways to reduce food waste (storage tips, a "use it up" night).

Keep the meals realistic for my time and equipment. No specialty "superfoods."

title: Estimate what my trading cards or collectibles are worth
description: A method for pricing cards, sealed products, or collectibles from real sold data, with grading and selling guidance.
content:
Help me estimate what my trading cards or collectibles are worth.

**Items:** [LIST — name, set, number, edition or print run, year]
**Condition:** [raw or graded; if graded, the company and grade; describe wear, centering, edges, surface, or sealed packaging condition]
**Where I'm located:** [COUNTRY]
**Goal:** [sell now / hold / insure / trade / decide whether to grade]
**Price data I have:** [paste recent sold listings, or say "none"]

Work through:
1. **Comparable sales:** explain how to find recent sold prices (not asking prices) on major marketplaces and price-tracking sites for the exact item, condition, and grade. If I pasted data, summarize it: number of sales, date range, low, median, high.
2. **Value range:** a realistic range for each item based only on the data provided, with a note on how thin or noisy the data is. If there is no data, say so instead of guessing a number.
3. **Price drivers:** condition, grading, print run, demand cycles (new set releases, reprints, anniversaries), and seasonality.
4. **Grading decision:** whether grading is likely worth the fee and wait time, based on condition and the price gap between raw and graded copies.
5. **Selling options:** marketplace, local shop, auction, or consignment, with fees and the net amount I would actually receive.
6. **Trend check:** how to tell whether a recent price drop is a lasting trend or noise.

This is a pricing method, not investment advice. Collectible prices are volatile; don't buy or hold anything on the expectation of future gains.
variables: LIST — name, set, number, edition or print run, year
sell now / hold / insure / trade / decide whether to grade
paste recent sold listings, or say "none"

title: Explain a hard topic to my child in age-appropriate words
description: Gentle, honest words for talking with your child about death, divorce, illness, or scary news, plus answers to likely questions.
content:
Help me talk with my child about something difficult.

**Topic:** [e.g. "grandparent died", "we're separating", "I'm having surgery", "a frightening news event", "our pet is dying"]

**What they already know or have overheard:** [DETAILS]
**Our family's beliefs or values to respect:** [religious or cultural views, or "none"]
**Who will be there and when:** [SETTING]

Give me:
1. Key principles for this age: how much to say, what words to use and avoid (for example, avoid "went to sleep" for death with young children).
2. A short script to open the conversation (under 150 words), honest and simple.
3. The questions my child is likely to ask, with brief, truthful answers I can adapt, including "Is it my fault?" and "Will it happen to me or you?"
4. Signs of how they are coping, and what is normal for their age over the next few weeks.
5. Ways to keep the conversation open: books, drawing, rituals, routines.

Do not tell me what to believe; follow my family's values. If my child shows lasting distress, changes in sleep or eating, talks about harming themselves, or I'm worried, suggest speaking to their pediatrician, school counselor, or a child therapist. If there is any immediate danger, contact emergency services.

title: Figure out what a confusing text or message really means
description: Read the possible meanings of an ambiguous message, check your assumptions, and choose a calm reply.
content:
Help me understand a message I received and decide how to reply.

**The message (exactly as written):** [PASTE]
**Who sent it and our relationship:** [e.g. "friend of 10 years", "someone I've been dating a month", "my brother"]
**Context:** [WHAT HAPPENED BEFORE, previous messages if relevant]
**How they usually text:** [e.g. "always short", "lots of emojis normally", "slow to reply"]
**How it made me feel and what I'm worried it means:** [YOUR READ]

Give me:
1. **Possible readings:** 3-4 realistic interpretations, from most to least likely given what I've told you, and the clues for each. Point out where I might be reading tone into text that isn't there.
2. **What I don't know:** facts that would change the meaning.
3. **Reply options:** three replies matched to different approaches: (a) light and neutral, (b) a gentle clarifying question, (c) addressing it directly. Keep each short.
4. **Whether to wait, call, or talk in person** instead of replying by text.
5. **What to avoid:** e.g. over-analyzing in a long message or sending several texts in a row.

Don't claim certainty about what they meant; be clear these are possibilities.
variables: WHAT HAPPENED BEFORE, previous messages if relevant

- Learning curve: how soon I'd make something I'm pleased with.
- How it suits my physical considerations, with adaptations if needed (e.g. larger crochet hooks, ergonomic tools).

- A way to do it with other people (classes, clubs, library or community center groups).

Finish with a simple 4-week "try it" plan for my top 2 picks, so I can find out what I enjoy before buying much.

Help me find purpose and stay connected in retirement.

title: Find tech and services that help me keep living independently at home
description: A tailored shortlist of devices, services, and simple changes that support safe, independent living for an older adult.
content:
Help me find technology and services that make it easier to keep living independently at home.

**Living situation:** [alone or with someone, house or apartment, stairs, rural or city]
**Daily tasks that are getting harder:** [e.g. remembering medications, getting to appointments, shopping, cooking, cleaning, hearing the doorbell, reading small print]
**Safety worries:** [e.g. falls, wandering, leaving the stove on, being alone at night]
**Tech comfort and devices already owned:** [e.g. smartphone, no internet, tablet]
**Budget and support:** [e.g. limited income, family can help pay, open to free community services]

Give me:
1. A shortlist matched to each task or worry, mixing low-tech and high-tech options: e.g. pill dispensers with alarms, medical alert devices, video doorbells, smart speakers for reminders and calls, large-button phones, grocery and prescription delivery, ride services, meal programs, home care help.
2. For each: what problem it solves, how easy it is to use, typical cost range marked [CHECK CURRENT PRICE], and privacy considerations.
3. Community services worth checking, such as an area agency on aging or local senior center [CONFIRM FOR MY LOCATION].
4. A start-small plan: the 3 changes with the biggest benefit for the least effort and cost.
5. Questions to ask before buying any monitoring device or subscription (contract length, monthly fees, what happens in an emergency).

Respect the person's choices - recommend discussing every option with them, especially anything that monitors them. Don't invent product names or prices. If falls, confusion, wandering, or missed medications are already happening, suggest asking their doctor for a home safety or care needs assessment; for a fall with injury or sudden confusion, call emergency services.

title: Find ways to cope with grief after a loss
description: Gentle, practical support for grieving: what to expect, how to get through hard days, and where to find more help.
content:
Help me cope with grief.

**Who or what I lost:** [e.g. "my father", "a close friend", "my dog", "a pregnancy", "my marriage"]
**When it happened:** [TIMEFRAME]
**How I'm doing:** [SLEEP, EATING, WORK, MOOD, WHAT'S HARDEST]
**Support around me:** [PEOPLE, COMMUNITY, FAITH - or "not much"]
**Upcoming hard days:** [e.g. "birthday next month", "first holidays"]

Please respond with care and keep it practical:
1. Acknowledge my loss briefly and sincerely.
2. Explain in plain words that grief has no fixed timeline or order, and that common experiences include waves, numbness, anger, guilt, and trouble concentrating.
3. Suggest 5-6 small things that can help on hard days (basic routines, letting people help, ways to talk about the person).
4. A plan for one upcoming hard day.
5. 3-4 ideas for remembering or honoring them, if I want that.
6. How to tell people what I need (a short message I can send to friends or my employer).
7. Types of support to consider: grief support groups, counselors, faith communities, hospice bereavement services.

Don't push me to "move on" or use clichés. If I mention not wanting to live, being unable to function for a long time, or using alcohol or drugs to cope, encourage me to contact a doctor or crisis line (in the US, call or text 988).
variables: SLEEP, EATING, WORK, MOOD, WHAT'S HARDEST

title: Fix a computer, phone, or app problem
description: Patient, step-by-step tech support for everyday device and software problems.
content:
Help me fix a tech problem.

**Device and system:** [e.g. Windows 11 laptop, iPhone 15 on iOS 18, Mac, router, printer]
**What's happening:** [PROBLEM, exact error messages]
**When it started and what changed:** [updates, new apps, drops]
**What I've tried:** [STEPS]
**My comfort level:** [beginner / comfortable / advanced]

Walk me through fixes one step at a time, starting with the simplest and safest. After each step, ask me what happened before moving on. Explain technical terms. Warn me before anything that could delete data, and remind me to back up first.

Never ask for my passwords. If this sounds like a scam (e.g. a pop-up asking me to call "support"), tell me.

title: Fix or maintain something at home
description: Diagnoses household problems and guides safe DIY fixes — or tells you when to call a pro.
content:
Help me with a problem at home.

**Details:** [age of the item, when it started, sounds, smells, photos]
**My skill level and tools:** [DETAILS]
**Renting or owning:** [STATUS]

Give me:
1. Likely causes, from most to least likely.
2. Safe checks I can do myself.
3. Step-by-step fix instructions if it's a reasonable DIY job (tools, parts, time).
4. When to stop and call a professional — and what to ask them.

Safety first: for gas smells, electrical work beyond basics, structural issues, or anything involving a risk of injury, tell me to call a professional.
variables: age of the item, when it started, sounds, smells, photos

title: Get a lower rate on my phone, internet, or insurance bill
description: A prepared call script and talking points to ask a provider for a better rate, plus when to switch.
content:
Help me ask a provider to lower one of my regular bills.

**What I actually use:** [e.g. "I work from home, need fast upload", "two phones, little data"]
**Competitor offers I've found:** [OFFER DETAILS with prices, or "none yet"]
**Am I willing to switch?** [yes / maybe / no]

Give me:
1. A 10-minute prep checklist: what to look up before calling (contract end date, early termination fees, current promotions, my usage).
2. A short, friendly call script: opening line, the specific ask, how to use competitor offers honestly, and asking for the retention or loyalty team if the first person can't help.
3. Responses to likely pushback ("that's our best price", "that promo is for new customers only").
4. Things to ask about besides price: removing unused add-ons, equipment fees, bundling, paperless or autopay discounts.
5. A note on what to get in writing before I hang up.
6. A simple rule for when switching is worth the hassle.

Only use the offers I provide; don't invent prices or promotions. For insurance, remind me to compare coverage and deductibles, not just the premium.
variables: PLAN NAME, monthly cost, what's included
OFFER DETAILS with prices, or "none yet"

title: Get conversation starters for a party or social event
description: Tailored openers, follow-up questions, and graceful exits for a specific social event so small talk feels easier.
content:
Help me handle small talk at an upcoming event.

Give me:
1. 8 openers that fit this specific event (not "So, what do you do?" on repeat).
2. How to keep a conversation going: follow-up questions, and how to share a little about myself so it isn't an interview.
3. Ways to join a group that's already talking.
4. 4 polite ways to exit a conversation.
5. Deflections for topics I want to avoid, and for nosy questions.
6. A quick trick for remembering names.

Keep every line short and natural enough to say out loud.

starting / keeping it going / ending / remembering names

title: Get mentally ready for a situation that makes me nervous
description: A short confidence plan for an upcoming nerve-wracking event: reframes, rehearsal, a calming routine, and a backup plan.
content:
Help me prepare mentally for something that makes me nervous.

**The situation:** [e.g. "first day at a new job", "a hard conversation", "a party where I know nobody", "a medical procedure"]
**When it is:** [DATE/TIME]
**What I'm most afraid will happen:** [WORST-CASE THOUGHTS]
**What I'd like to happen:** [BEST REALISTIC OUTCOME]
**What usually happens to me when I'm nervous:** [e.g. "mind goes blank", "talk too fast", "avoid it"]

Give me:
1. **Reality check:** my worst fear vs. what's most likely, and what I'd do if the worst did happen (a calm, specific coping plan).
2. **Preparation:** 3-5 practical things to do before the day that reduce uncertainty.
3. **Rehearsal:** a short visualization I can run through, including handling one thing going wrong.
4. **On the day:** a 10-minute pre-event routine (breathing, posture, a grounding phrase).
5. **In the moment:** 3 quick resets if nerves spike.
6. **Afterward:** 3 questions to reflect on what went well, so confidence builds.

Keep it practical and encouraging, not hype. If nervousness is stopping me from doing everyday things or causing panic attacks, suggest I talk to a doctor or therapist; anxiety is very treatable.
variables: e.g. "mind goes blank", "talk too fast", "avoid it"

title: Get my family moving more together
description: Fun, low-cost ways to build more physical activity into family life, with a weekly plan everyone can enjoy.
content:
Help my family get more active together.

**Family members and ages:** [DETAILS]
**What we do now:** [e.g. "mostly screens on weekends", "kids do soccer, adults do nothing"]
**What each person enjoys:** [INTERESTS]
**Where we live:** [e.g. "apartment, small park nearby", "suburb with a yard", "cold winters"]
**Time available:** [WEEKDAYS AND WEEKENDS]
**Budget:** [AMOUNT or "free only"]
**Limits:** [e.g. "toddler in a stroller", "grandparent with bad knees", "one child uses a wheelchair"]

Give me:
1. 20 activity ideas sorted by indoor/outdoor and time needed (10 minutes, 30 minutes, half a day), each adaptable to everyone's ability.
2. A weekly plan that fits our schedule, mixing short daily movement with one bigger weekend activity.
3. Ways to make it stick: letting kids choose, simple challenges or charts, linking activity to routines (walking to school, after-dinner walks).
4. Bad weather backup options.
5. How to keep it positive - focused on fun and feeling good, not weight or appearance.

Keep suggestions safe for the youngest and least mobile person. If anyone has a health condition, suggest checking with their doctor about suitable activities.

title: Get my home ready to recover after surgery
description: A practical home setup, supply list, and support schedule for recovering after a procedure.
content:
Help me prepare my home and routine for recovery after a surgery or procedure.

**Procedure and date:** [TYPE AND DATE]
**What my care team has told me so far:** [e.g. "no lifting over 10 lb for 6 weeks", "crutches for 2 weeks", "no stairs"]
**My home:** [e.g. "second-floor apartment, bathroom upstairs", "pets", "live alone"]
**People who can help and when:** [NAMES, AVAILABILITY]
**Responsibilities to cover:** [e.g. "school pickups", "dog walking", "work"]

Give me:
1. A home setup checklist: a recovery spot with essentials in reach, clear walkways, bathroom safety, and moving things I'll need to waist height.
2. A supply list (comfort, hygiene, easy meals, anything my care team mentioned), marked by priority.
3. A meal plan for the first week using freezer-friendly or no-cook options.
4. A helper schedule template covering rides, meals, and chores, plus a message I can send to friends asking for specific help.
5. A list of questions to ask my surgical team before discharge (activity limits, wound care, pain management, driving, when to call).

Base all medical limits on what my care team said; don't add new ones - mark gaps [ASK CARE TEAM]. Remind me to call my care team or emergency services for warning signs they give me, such as fever, increasing pain, or trouble breathing.

title: Get my personal finances in order
description: A budget, savings plan, and priorities based on your income, spending, and goals.
content:
Help me get my finances in order.

**Savings and debts:** [balances, interest rates]

Give me:
1. A clear picture of where my money goes and what stands out.
2. A realistic budget (e.g. needs/wants/savings split adapted to my situation).
3. A priority order: emergency fund, high-interest debt, retirement contributions, goals — and why.
4. 5 specific ways to free up money.
5. A simple monthly money routine.

General education, not personalized financial advice — check big decisions with a qualified advisor.
variables: emergency fund, pay off debt, buy a home, travel…

title: Get my voice and song ready for a live singing performance
description: Singing-specific prep for a live song: key and arrangement fit, vocal warm-ups, lyric security, mic technique, and sound check questions.
content:
Help me get a song ready to sing live.

**Song and original artist:** [TITLE - ARTIST]
**Event:** [open mic, wedding, school concert, outdoor gig, karaoke night - crowd size, indoor or outdoor]
**Accompaniment:** [backing track / guitarist or band / I play myself / a cappella]
**My voice:** [range if known, voice type, training, where the song feels hard - e.g. "chorus feels too high", "run out of breath in verse 2"]
**Sound setup:** [house PA with sound person / small speaker / no mic / not sure]
**Time until the performance:** [e.g. "3 weeks"]

Give me:
1. **Key and fit check:** how to tell whether the original key suits my voice, how to test and choose a better key (and tell my accompanist or change the backing track), and simple arrangement changes - shorter intro, lower harmony line, softer bridge - that play to my strengths.
2. **Problem spots:** for each hard section I named, a specific practice method (slow practice, breath marks, vowel shaping, singing on a lip trill first).
3. **Rehearsal schedule:** from now to the show - sections, full runs, practice with the accompaniment, and at least two full run-throughs standing, with a mic or a stand-in, as if live.
4. **Vocal care:** a 10-minute warm-up, breathing for long phrases, hydration, and what to avoid in the 24 hours before.
5. **Lyric security:** memorization techniques and a plan for what to do if I blank mid-song.
6. **Mic and monitors:** mic distance for loud vs. quiet passages, avoiding feedback, what to ask in the sound check, and how to signal that I need more of myself in the monitor.
7. **The last 30 minutes:** a short warm-up and calm-down routine.

Don't reproduce the song's lyrics; refer to sections like "verse 1" or "the bridge". If I get hoarse, lose my voice, or feel pain when singing, tell me to rest and see a doctor or voice specialist rather than push through.

title: Get permission to handle a parent's accounts and calls for them
description: Explains the options for helping a parent with banks, utilities, and agencies, and drafts the request letters and conversation.
content:
Help me get the right permission to help my parent manage accounts and talk to companies on their behalf.

**Organizations involved:** [LIST]

**My country or state:** [LOCATION]

Give me:
1. The common options, from lightest to strongest, explained simply: being added as an authorized contact or third party on a single account, a trusted contact person at a bank, a representative or appointee for benefits, a financial power of attorney, and court-appointed options. For each: what it allows, what it doesn't, and what's typically needed. Mark rules and form names [CONFIRM FOR MY LOCATION].
2. Which options fit our situation and why.
3. A short letter or message my parent can sign authorizing a specific company to speak with me.
4. Talking points for discussing this with my parent in a way that respects their control and choices.
5. A tracker: Organization | Permission type | Date set up | Contact | Notes.

Stress that permissions should be set up while my parent can consent, and only with their agreement. This is general information, not legal advice; for a power of attorney, recommend an elder law attorney or legal aid.

Help me with my style.

Recommend something for me.

Give me 10 recommendations: a few safe bets close to my taste, a few stretches, and one wildcard. For each, explain in one line why it matches what I love. Don't repeat what I've listed.

e.g. light read for vacation, something thought-provoking

title: Get unstuck on a government website or online account
description: Troubleshoots login, identity check, and navigation problems on a government or official online portal, with safe workarounds.
content:
Help me get past a problem on a government or official website.

**Website or service:** [e.g. tax portal, benefits account, pension account, driver's license renewal, health insurance marketplace]
**What I'm trying to do:** [e.g. create an account, verify my identity, upload a document, find my letter, renew something]
**Where I'm stuck:** [the step, and the exact error message - remove personal details]
**Device and browser:** [e.g. iPhone with Safari, Windows laptop with Chrome]
**What I've tried:** [LIST]
**Deadline:** [if any]

Steps:
1. Explain what the error or step likely means in plain words.
2. Give fixes to try, simplest first: a different browser or device, clearing cache, turning off pop-up blockers, checking the format of names and dates, file type and size for uploads, waiting out a lockout, using the official help page.
3. For identity checks: explain why they're used, what documents are usually needed, and what alternatives often exist (in-person, phone, or mail verification) [CONFIRM ON THE OFFICIAL SITE].
4. If online won't work, how to get the task done another way and before the deadline.
5. Safety checks: make sure I'm on the official website (look at the web address and avoid look-alike sites from ads), and never pay a third party to do something the official site does for free.

Return: the likely cause, a numbered fix list, a short script for calling the help line, and what to write down (reference numbers, time of call). Never ask me for passwords or full ID numbers.
variables: e.g. iPhone with Safari, Windows laptop with Chrome

title: Get unstuck on a personal goal
description: Coaching conversations that turn a vague goal into clarity, a plan, and accountability.
content:
Coach me on a personal goal.

**The goal or area:** [e.g. confidence, fitness, finishing a project, a relationship, finding purpose]
**Where I am now:** [CURRENT SITUATION]
**What's getting in the way:** [OBSTACLES]
**Why it matters to me:** [REASON]

Coach me — don't lecture:
1. Ask questions to clarify what I really want and why (one at a time).
2. Help me see options I haven't considered.
3. Turn it into a specific goal and 3 next actions.
4. Help me plan for the obstacle most likely to stop me.
5. End by asking how I'll hold myself accountable, and offer to check in.

Be encouraging but honest; call out excuses kindly.

title: Handle a parenting challenge

3. What to do in the moment vs. preventing it ahead of time.
4. How to stay consistent with other caregivers.
5. Signs this needs a pediatrician or child specialist.

title: Handle drama or being left out in my friend group
description: Sort out friend-group tension, exclusion, or gossip, and get words for talking to the people involved.
content:
Help me deal with a problem in my friend group.

**My age and setting:** [e.g. "16, high school", "college freshman in a dorm"]

**How long it's been going on:** [TIME]

4. What not to do (screenshots, venting in group chats, subtweeting) and why.
5. Ways to widen my circle so I'm not dependent on one group.
6. How to look after my mood while this is going on.

If it involves threats, sharing private photos, repeated bullying online or in person, or I feel unsafe or very low, tell me to talk to a trusted adult, school counselor, or resident advisor, and to contact a crisis line if I'm thinking about hurting myself.

FIRST NAMES OR ROLES, how close I am to each

title: Help my picky eater try new foods

content:
Help me support my picky eater in trying new foods.

**Child's age:** [AGE]

**What mealtimes look like now:** [e.g. "battles every night", "separate meals for them"]
**What I've tried:** [e.g. "bribing with dessert", "hiding vegetables"]
**Family schedule and cooking time:** [DETAILS]

Give me:
1. A short explanation of why picky eating is common at this age and what usually helps (repeated low-pressure exposure, division of responsibility, modeling).
2. A "food bridge" list: new foods that are similar in taste, color, or texture to the ones they already accept.
3. A 3-week plan: how often to offer a new food, how to serve it alongside a safe food, and how to track exposures.
4. Phrases to use and phrases to avoid at the table.
5. Ways to involve them (shopping, washing, choosing) that build curiosity.
6. How to handle refusal without a battle or a separate meal every night.

Tell me plainly to talk to my child's doctor if they eat a very limited number of foods, are losing weight or not growing, gag or choke often, or show strong distress around food - these can need professional support.
variables: e.g. "battles every night", "separate meals for them"

title: Improve my sleep

Help me sleep better.

Help me find and choose a babysitter or nanny.

title: Keep a symptom diary to share with my doctor
description: A simple daily symptom tracker and a one-page summary that helps your doctor see patterns, without guessing at causes.
content:
Help me set up a symptom diary I can share with my doctor.

**Symptom(s) I want to track:** [e.g. "headaches", "stomach pain", "fatigue", "joint stiffness"]
**When it started:** [DATE OR ROUGH TIMEFRAME]
**Things I suspect might be related:** [e.g. "certain foods", "sleep", "stress", "my cycle", "weather"]
**How I'll record it:** [paper / phone notes / spreadsheet]
**Appointment date:** [DATE - optional]

Create:
1. A daily log template with columns that matter for my symptom: date, time, severity (0-10), duration, what I was doing, food and drink, sleep, medications taken, and anything that helped or worsened it.
2. A short guide on how to rate severity consistently.
3. A one-page summary template for the appointment: when it started, how often, worst episode, patterns noticed, what I've tried, and my top 3 questions.
4. Once I paste my log entries, help me summarize patterns factually (e.g. "4 of 6 headaches followed less than 6 hours of sleep") without suggesting a diagnosis.

Do not diagnose or name possible conditions. Tell me to seek urgent care or call emergency services for sudden severe pain, chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of stroke (face drooping, arm weakness, speech trouble), fainting, or any symptom that feels like an emergency.

title: Learn local customs and etiquette before I visit a country
description: A respectful, practical briefing on greetings, dress, dining, tipping, and common faux pas so you fit in and avoid offending anyone.
content:
Give me a practical etiquette briefing for an upcoming trip.

**Country or region:** [WHERE - be specific if customs vary by region]

**What I'll be doing:** [e.g. sightseeing, visiting religious sites, staying with a local family, a business meeting, a wedding]

Cover:
1. Greetings and forms of address.
2. Dress expectations, especially for religious sites and rural areas.
3. Dining manners: ordering, eating, sharing, who pays, and tipping norms.
4. Gestures, body language, and topics to avoid.
5. Photography etiquette: when to ask permission.
6. Being a guest in someone's home: gifts, shoes, arriving on time.
7. Bargaining: where it's expected and where it isn't.
8. 5 common mistakes visitors make, and how to recover gracefully if I slip up.

Rules: avoid stereotypes, note where customs vary between cities, generations, or communities, and say where something is a general tendency rather than a rule. If any local laws affect visitors (e.g. dress codes, alcohol, public behavior), flag them and tell me to confirm with official travel advice.

Format as short sections I can skim on my phone, ending with a 10-line cheat sheet.
variables: WHERE - be specific if customs vary by region
WHERE I'M FROM, so you can point out the biggest differences

title: Learn the etiquette for a cultural or religious event I'm attending
description: What to wear, do, bring, and say at a wedding, funeral, or celebration from a tradition you're unfamiliar with.
content:
Help me prepare for an event from a culture or religion I'm not familiar with.

Give me a practical guide:
1. **What to expect:** the general flow, how long it may last, and moments when guests participate or simply observe.
2. **What to wear:** including colors or items to avoid, and whether to cover head, shoulders, or legs.
3. **Gifts or contributions:** whether they're expected, typical forms, and appropriate ways to give them. Don't state specific amounts as fact; say norms vary and suggest asking.
4. **Greetings and phrases:** what to say to the hosts or family, with pronunciation.
5. **Food and drink customs.**
6. **Common guest mistakes** to avoid.
7. **Questions I could politely ask the host** to check anything unclear.

Note that customs vary a lot by family, region, and denomination, so treat this as a general guide and follow the lead of the hosts. Flag anything you're unsure about as [CONFIRM WITH HOST].
variables: CITY/COUNTRY, VENUE, WORDING ON THE INVITE

title: Let go of a resentment I keep replaying
description: Helps you work through a lingering hurt or grudge, decide what you need, and stop it from taking up so much space.
content:
Help me let go of a resentment that keeps replaying in my head.

**What happened and who was involved:** [SITUATION]
**How long ago:** [TIMEFRAME]
**What still hurts most:** [e.g. "they never acknowledged it", "it felt unfair", "I trusted them"]
**My current relationship with them:** [still in contact / no contact / unavoidable, e.g. family or coworker]
**What I've tried:** [e.g. "talking to them", "avoiding them", "venting"]

Guide me through:
1. Naming the hurt precisely and the need or value that was crossed.
2. What I'm hoping for when I replay it (an apology, justice, understanding, being heard) and whether that's realistic to get from them.
3. My options, each with pros and cons: talk to them (with a short opening line), set a boundary, accept and move on without reconciling, or seek help from a mediator or counselor.
4. What letting go does and doesn't mean: it's not saying it was okay, and it doesn't require reconnecting.
5. Practices for when it replays: a short unsent letter exercise, a phrase to interrupt the loop, and redirecting attention.
6. A small action this week that moves me forward.

Don't push me to forgive. If the situation involved abuse or I'm still at risk, prioritize safety and point me to appropriate support services.

title: Lower my home energy bills
description: A ranked list of energy-saving changes for your home, from free habits to upgrades, with what to check first.
content:
Help me lower my home energy bills.

**Home:** [e.g. "1980s house, 1,800 sq ft", "apartment on top floor"]
**Own or rent:** [OWN / RENT]
**Climate:** [e.g. "hot summers, mild winters"]
**Heating, cooling, and water heating:** [e.g. "gas furnace, window AC units, electric water heater"]
**Recent bills:** [MONTHLY AMOUNTS or usage, especially the highest months]
**Habits:** [thermostat settings, laundry, who's home during the day, devices left on]
**Budget for upgrades:** [AMOUNT, or "free changes only"]

Give me:
1. Where my money is likely going, based on what I've shared (label as estimates; my utility bill or a home energy audit gives the real picture).
2. Free changes this week (thermostat schedule, laundry in cold water, unplugging standby devices, closing curtains at the right times).
3. Low-cost fixes under $100 (weatherstripping, door sweeps, LED bulbs, smart power strips), with renter-friendly options marked.
4. Bigger upgrades worth getting quotes for (insulation, heat pump, water heater) and how to check payback time.
5. Where to look for help: my utility's free or low-cost energy audit, rebates, and government incentive programs. Tell me to confirm current eligibility on official sites; don't invent amounts.
6. A simple monthly tracking table to see what's working.

Safety: never use an oven or outdoor heater to heat the home, keep space heaters away from anything flammable and plugged directly into the wall, and keep carbon monoxide alarms working.
variables: e.g. "1980s house, 1,800 sq ft", "apartment on top floor"
e.g. "gas furnace, window AC units, electric water heater"
MONTHLY AMOUNTS or usage, especially the highest months

title: Make a checklist of documents I need to file my taxes

Help me get organized to file my personal taxes this year.

**Last year's return available?** [yes / no]

Give me:
1. A checklist grouped by: identity and household, income records, deductions and credits I might qualify for, accounts and payments, and last year's information. Explain each item in one plain line and why it's needed.
2. Items specific to the life changes I listed that people often forget.
3. A short list of credits or deductions worth asking about for my situation - framed as questions to check, not promises that I qualify.
4. Key dates to confirm, marked [CONFIRM DATE] instead of stated as fact.
5. A simple folder system (paper or digital) to keep everything together next year.
6. Signs that I should get help from a qualified tax professional.

Keep it practical and calm. Tax rules change and differ by location, so tell me to verify specifics with official tax authority guidance or a qualified preparer.
variables: myself with software / a tax preparer / not sure

title: Make a healthier version of my favorite recipe
description: Rewrites a recipe you love with smart swaps that keep the flavor while cutting what you want less of.
content:
Help me make a healthier version of a recipe I love, without ruining it.

**Recipe:** [PASTE INGREDIENTS AND STEPS]
**Servings it makes:** [NUMBER]
**What I want to change:** [e.g. "less saturated fat", "less sugar", "more vegetables", "more protein", "lower sodium"]
**What must not change:** [e.g. "it has to stay crispy", "my kids must still eat it"]
**Kitchen and budget limits:** [EQUIPMENT, INGREDIENTS I CAN GET]
**Allergies or foods to avoid:** [LIST or "none"]

Steps:
1. Identify the 3-5 ingredients or techniques that contribute most to what I want to change.
2. Suggest swaps for each, rated "barely noticeable", "slight change", or "noticeable change", and explain how each affects taste, texture, and cooking (e.g. baking chemistry, browning, moisture).
3. Avoid swapping everything at once - recommend which 2-3 changes to try first.

Return:
1. A swap table: original | swap | why | effect on taste/texture.
2. The full rewritten recipe with updated steps and timings.
3. A rough before/after comparison of the nutrients I care about, labeled as an estimate.
4. A "if it didn't turn out right" troubleshooting list.

Don't invent exact nutrition figures; label all numbers as approximate. If I'm changing this recipe for a medical condition (e.g. diabetes, kidney disease, a heart condition), follow my doctor's or registered dietitian's specific targets over these general swaps.
variables: e.g. "it has to stay crispy", "my kids must still eat it"

title: Make a money plan after losing my job or income
description: A calm first-30-days plan after a job loss or income drop: a bare-bones budget, bills to prioritize, and help to apply for.
content:
Help me manage my money after a sudden drop in income.

**What happened:** [e.g. "laid off", "hours cut", "business slowed down", "can't work due to illness"]

**Savings available:** [AMOUNT]
**Monthly costs:** [housing, utilities, food, insurance, debt payments, subscriptions, other]
**Location:** [COUNTRY and state or region]
**People who depend on me:** [DETAILS]

Give me:
1. A bare-bones budget: essentials only, and how many months my savings plus expected income will last.
2. A bill priority list: what to protect first (housing, utilities, food, insurance, transport for job hunting) and what can wait or be negotiated.
3. A first-week checklist: apply for unemployment or income support, check health coverage options, review any severance terms, call lenders about hardship options before missing payments.
4. Types of assistance worth checking in my area (food, utility, rent help), phrased as things to look up with [CONFIRM] markers.
5. Spending cuts in order, from easiest to hardest.
6. A short weekly check-in to update the plan as things change.

Keep the tone calm and steady. Don't invent benefit amounts or eligibility rules. If I mention feeling hopeless or unsafe, encourage me to reach out to someone I trust or a local crisis line right away.
variables: severance, unemployment benefits, partner's income, other

title: Make a packing list for my trip
description: A tailored packing checklist based on your destination, weather, activities, and luggage limits, so you pack light and forget nothing important.

Help me make a packing list for my trip.

Rules:

- Include the easily forgotten: plug adapters, copies of documents, a pen for arrival forms, refillable water bottle.

Return:
1. A checklist grouped by: Documents and money, Carry-on essentials, Clothes, Toiletries, Tech, Health, Extras for my activities.
2. Quantities for clothing items.
3. A "buy there if needed" list of things not worth packing.
4. A 5-item last-minute check for the morning I leave.

WHAT I KNOW - or "please tell me what to check"

just me / me and a partner / family with kids - ages

title: Make a plan to drink less alcohol
description: A personal, non-judgmental plan to cut back on drinking, with goals, triggers, and support options.
content:
Help me make a plan to drink less alcohol.

**What I drink now:** [TYPES, AMOUNTS, DAYS PER WEEK - estimates are fine]
**When and where:** [e.g. "wine every evening after work", "heavy weekends with friends"]
**Why I want to change:** [e.g. "sleep", "health", "money", "how I feel the next day"]
**My goal:** [e.g. "alcohol-free weekdays", "a 30-day break", "no more than X drinks on a night out"]
**What makes it hard:** [TRIGGERS, SOCIAL PRESSURE, STRESS]

Give me:
1. A clear, specific goal and how to track it (drink count, alcohol-free days).
2. How "a standard drink" is measured where I live, so my tracking is accurate - tell me to confirm with my local health authority's guidance.
3. A trigger plan: for each trigger I named, an alternative and a script for declining a drink.
4. Alcohol-free drinks and activities for the moments I usually drink.
5. A weekly check-in template and what to do after a slip (no all-or-nothing thinking).

Safety: if I've been drinking heavily every day, warn me that stopping suddenly can cause dangerous withdrawal and I should talk to a doctor before cutting down. If drinking feels out of my control, point me to a doctor or a local alcohol support service or helpline.
variables: TYPES, AMOUNTS, DAYS PER WEEK - estimates are fine
e.g. "sleep", "health", "money", "how I feel the next day"

title: Make a plan to handle my anger better
description: A personal anger plan covering your triggers, early warning signs, in-the-moment cool-down steps, and repair afterward.
content:
Help me make a practical plan for handling my anger.

**Recent times I got angry:** [2-3 EXAMPLES - what happened, what I did or said]
**Who's usually around:** [e.g. "my partner", "kids", "coworkers", "other drivers"]
**Early signs I notice (if any):** [e.g. "jaw clenches", "voice gets louder", "heart races"]
**What tends to make it worse:** [e.g. "being tired", "hunger", "feeling ignored"]
**What I want to change:** [e.g. "stop yelling", "stop sulking for days"]

Build my plan:
1. **Patterns:** the common triggers and the feelings that may sit under the anger (hurt, fear, embarrassment, unfairness).
2. **Warning scale:** a 1-10 scale with my own signs at 3, 6, and 8, and what to do at each level.
3. **Cool-down steps:** 4-5 things I can do in under 2 minutes (breathing, stepping away, a phrase to say).
4. **Time-out script:** words to pause a heated conversation respectfully and agree to come back to it.
5. **Repair:** how to come back to the person and talk about it calmly.
6. **Prevention:** 3 changes to lower my baseline (sleep, food, workload, stress).

Keep it non-shaming. If my anger has involved physical aggression, threats, or someone feeling afraid of me, tell me clearly to get support from a counselor or anger management program, and put safety first.

title: Make a plan to pay off debt
description: Compares payoff strategies and builds a month-by-month plan.

Help me pay off my debt.

**Debts:** [for each: type, balance, interest rate, minimum payment]

3. Ways to speed it up (negotiating rates, balance transfers, consolidation) with their risks.
4. How to avoid new debt while paying this off.

Educational only. If I'm struggling with payments, point me to free, reputable debt advice services in my country.

title: Make a potty training plan for my toddler

Help me potty train my child.

**Past attempts:** [WHAT HAPPENED]

Give me:

title: Make a scam-safety plan together with my older parent
description: A respectful scam-protection plan for an older relative, with a fridge cheat sheet, a family code word, and agreed safety settings.
content:
Help me create a scam-safety plan with my older parent or relative.

**Who it's for:** [relationship, age, lives alone or with others]
**How they use technology:** [e.g. landline only, smartphone, email, social media, online banking]
**Scams they've faced or nearly fallen for:** [e.g. fake grandchild calls, tech support pop-ups, romance scams, prize letters]
**Their attitude:** [e.g. open to help, proud and independent, embarrassed after a past scam]
**Memory or health considerations:** [optional]
**Who else in the family can help:** [NAMES OR ROLES]

Create:
1. Talking points for a respectful conversation that treats them as capable, not as a victim. Include how to start the talk and what to avoid saying.
2. A large-print, one-page cheat sheet for the fridge or by the phone: the top warning signs (urgency, secrecy, gift cards, wire transfers, crypto, remote access requests, threats of arrest), and the rule "hang up and call back on a number you already know."
3. A family code word and a plan for verifying calls that claim to be from a grandchild or relative in trouble.
4. Practical safeguards to discuss, with their agreement: call blocking, bank alerts, a trusted contact on accounts, spending limits.
5. A short script they can use to end a suspicious call.
6. What to do if they think they've been scammed, with the people to call first.

Respect their independence and privacy - every safeguard should be agreed with them, not set up behind their back.
variables: relationship, age, lives alone or with others

Help me decide what to buy.

title: Make a travel documents checklist for my trip abroad
description: A personal checklist of passport, visa, transit, and health-entry items with deadlines and the official sources to verify each one.

Help me make a travel documents checklist for an international trip.

**My citizenship(s):** [COUNTRY or COUNTRIES]

**Destination(s), including transit stops:** [COUNTRIES and airports]
**Travel dates:** [DEPARTURE and RETURN]
**Purpose:** [tourism / visiting family / business / study]
**Passport expiry date:** [DATE]
**Traveling with:** [e.g. a child, a child without both parents, a pet, prescription medications]

Give me:
1. A checklist of what to confirm: passport validity rules (some countries require several months beyond departure and blank pages), visa or electronic travel authorization, transit visas for layovers, proof of onward travel or funds, vaccination or health requirements, and customs rules for medications.
2. A timeline working back from my departure date, with when to start each item.
3. Extra documents for my situation, such as a consent letter for a child traveling without both parents.
4. A list of the official sources to verify each item: the destination's government or embassy website and my own government's travel advice page.

Important: entry rules change often and depend on nationality. Present everything as what to check, not as final answers, and mark anything uncertain as [VERIFY WITH OFFICIAL SOURCE]. Never suggest third-party visa sites as the primary source.

title: Make an emergency plan for losing my passport, wallet, or phone abroad
description: A before-you-go backup setup and a clear step-by-step plan for lost documents, cards, or phone while traveling.
content:
Help me prepare for, and handle, losing important things while traveling.

**Destination:** [COUNTRY or COUNTRIES]
**My citizenship:** [COUNTRY]
**What I carry:** [passport, ID, credit/debit cards, phone, cash, driver's license]
**Situation:** [preparing before the trip / it has just happened - describe what was lost or stolen and where I am]

If I'm preparing, give me:
1. A backup setup: photos of my passport and cards stored securely and offline, a paper copy kept separate, a second card stored apart from my main wallet, emergency cash in another bag, card and bank phone numbers written down, and my embassy or consulate's address and phone saved.
2. Phone protection: screen lock, find-my-device turned on, a backup of my contacts and two-factor codes.
3. A one-page emergency sheet I can print.

If it's happening now, give me numbered steps in priority order:
1. Get somewhere safe and contact someone I trust.
2. Freeze or cancel cards using the bank app or phone number.
3. Report it to local police and get a report reference if possible (often needed for insurance).
4. Contact my embassy or consulate about an emergency travel document; mark details [CHECK EMBASSY WEBSITE].
5. Lock or erase a lost phone and change key passwords from a secure device.
6. Contact my travel insurer and keep all receipts.

Keep the steps short and calm. If I'm in danger or injured, call local emergency services first.

title: Make my home safer to prevent falls
description: A room-by-room fall-prevention checklist with low-cost fixes and a plan for what to do if you fall.

Help me make my home safer so I'm less likely to fall.

Give me:

5. Questions to ask my doctor at my next visit (medication side effects that affect balance, vision and hearing checks, whether a physical therapist could help).

If someone has fallen and hit their head, can't get up, or is in severe pain, call emergency services.

title: Make my home Wi-Fi faster, more reliable, and more secure
description: Troubleshoots slow or patchy home internet and tightens router security with clear steps you can follow without being an expert.
content:
Help me improve my home Wi-Fi and make it more secure.

**The problem:** [e.g. slow in the evenings, no signal upstairs, drops during video calls, not sure it's secure]
**My setup:** [internet provider, plan speed if known, router make and model, whether my provider supplied it, how old it is]
**Home:** [size, floors, thick walls, where the router sits]
**Devices:** [roughly how many, e.g. phones, laptops, TV, smart speakers, cameras]
**Speed test results:** [optional - near the router and in the problem room]
